notes.teaches: Material value is not just about points; two minor pieces often outperform a rook and pawn due to their coordination. Recognize when a tactical sequence leads to a favorable material imbalance.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has sacrificed a pawn to obtain two pieces for a rook and a pawn. The two pieces are worth six points, while the rook and pawn are also six points, but the two pieces coordinate better and control more squares, making them more valuable.
notes.teaches: When considering trades, evaluate not just material count but the coordination and potential of the pieces. Two minor pieces often outperform a rook and pawn because they can work together to control the board.
notes.plans: Black aims to use the bishop pair to control key diagonals and files, and to launch an attack on the king, especially since White's king is exposed on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's moves are all gaining tempos: a5 attacks the knight, then Bishop d7 attacks the queen, and a4 will attack the knight again. White is forced to respond, giving Black time to develop and improve their position.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development or a material imbalance, look for forcing moves that gain time and keep the opponent on the defensive.
notes.plans: Black continues to harass White's pieces while completing development, castling, and preparing to bring rooks to open files.

notes.explains: White's queen has taken a pawn on b5, opening files on the side where White's king is. This gives Black long-term attacking chances against the king, even though the king is still in the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent opens files near their own king, it can be a strategic weakness that you can exploit later, even if the king is not immediately in danger.
notes.plans: Black will castle, then bring rooks to the open files and use the bishop pair to create threats against White's king.

notes.explains: Black's position is so good that even if White tries aggressive moves like Queen b7, Black can respond with a4, and after Knight a5, there is a tactical sequence leading to a winning endgame with two pieces for a rook.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, it's important to calculate concrete variations, but also to trust your intuition when you have multiple advantages (bishop pair, active pieces, safer king).
notes.plans: Black continues with a4, forcing the knight to a1, then castles to complete development and prepare an attack.

notes.explains: After castling, Black's position flows naturally: the queen can move, rooks come to open files, and the bishop can go to e6, supporting pawn advances like f5-f4 or f5-e4, and the bishop can enter the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and better piece activity, your pieces often find their best squares without forcing moves; just complete development and improve your worst pieces.
notes.plans: Black will play Bishop e6, Queen c7, and then bring rooks to the open files, preparing a kingside attack.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian structure, Black's pieces are harmoniously placed: the bishop on e6 eyes the center, the queen on c7 supports the c-pawn, and the rooks are ready to occupy open files. White's light-squared bishop is absent, so Black's light-squared bishop is a permanent asset.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are naturally well placed, your position flows without deep calculation; trust that good squares lead to good moves.
notes.plans: Continue developing with moves like Rfc8, preparing to pressure the c-file and support pawn breaks like f5-f4 or f5-e4.

notes.explains: White's idea of c4 is met by Bb5, pinning the knight and attacking the c4 pawn, which is defended only by the queen on c7. The queen cannot recapture because it would leave the pawn en prise, so the pawn is lost.
notes.teaches: A pin can be a powerful resource when the defender is tied to a valuable piece; look for pins that target weak pawns.
notes.plans: If White plays c4, respond with Bb5 to win the pawn or force concessions.

notes.explains: Black must be wary of White's c5 break, which would advance the pawns and create threats. If Black captures, d6 follows with a double threat on the queen and rook, so the pawn cannot be taken safely.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a central pawn break, evaluate whether capturing is safe; sometimes it's better to avoid the break altogether.
notes.plans: Prevent c5 by maintaining control of that square or be ready to meet it with a piece move rather than a pawn capture.

notes.explains: White's king on b1 is a common safety move, but here it's less effective because White lacks the light-squared bishop, leaving the king vulnerable to attacks on the light squares, such as g6 or f5-f4.
notes.teaches: King safety is relative: a castled king can still be exposed if the opponent controls the bishop's color complex.
notes.plans: Exploit the missing light-squared bishop by aiming for light-square breaks like f5-f4, opening lines for the bishop on f5.

notes.explains: Black's pieces are all active: rooks on strong files, the light-squared bishop unchallenged, and the dark-squared bishop ready to join later. This harmony invites setting up tactical tricks for the opponent.
notes.teaches: When all your pieces are well placed, look for dynamic moves that create threats or traps; initiative often leads to tactics.
notes.plans: Consider moves that create immediate threats, such as a pawn break or a piece maneuver, to force the opponent into errors.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian position, black wants to keep the position open to attack the white king. A move like a3 by black can provoke weaknesses or trades, but the opponent may respond with a3 or Nb4 to block the queenside, which would be annoying for black's attacking plans.
notes.teaches: When you have an attack, prefer moves that keep the position open and avoid trades that reduce your attacking potential. Consider your opponent's possible responses and whether they can block the position.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Rb8 to maintain pressure, but be ready for a3 and Nb4 ideas. The immediate a3 is a concrete try to force a favorable trade or create weaknesses.

notes.explains: After black plays a3, if white captures with the pawn, black should not recapture with the rook because the knight remains active. If white captures with the knight, black can trade it off, which is good because the knight is a key defender.
notes.teaches: When choosing recaptures, consider which piece you eliminate. Removing a defender is often more valuable than regaining material.
notes.plans: If white takes with the knight, recapture and eliminate the knight. If white takes with the pawn, look for other moves like Qa5 or Bf6 to continue the attack.

notes.explains: In this position, black has several candidate moves: Qa5, Ba4, Qxc3, or Bf6. Qxc3 trades queens, which is undesirable because black has the attack and needs the queen for pressure. Bf6 is a strong idea because it prepares e4 and then a capture on c3, activating the bishop and coordinating all pieces against the c3 pawn.
notes.teaches: When attacking, avoid unnecessary queen trades. Look for moves that improve your worst-placed piece and coordinate all your forces against a single weakness.
notes.plans: Play Bf6, then e4, and follow up with a capture on c3, bringing the bishop into the attack. The queen stays to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: After Bf6, black is two pawns down but the position is completely winning because white's king is exposed, the files around it are open, and black has the bishop pair. The bishop on d7 is unrivaled because white has no counterpart.
notes.teaches: Material is not the only factor; king safety and piece activity can outweigh pawn deficits. A powerful bishop pair and an exposed enemy king can make a position winning despite being down material.
notes.plans: Continue the attack, using the bishop pair and the active pieces to target the white king. The concrete tactic is to strike now with forcing moves.

notes.explains: When the opponent takes on a3 with the knight, black has a tactical opportunity to strike. The principle is to look for forcing moves: checks, captures, and threats in that order.
notes.teaches: In a position where you have a winning attack, calculate forcing moves first. Look for checks, captures, and threats to find the most direct continuation.
notes.plans: Find the tactical blow that exploits the knight on a3 and the exposed king. Execute the forcing sequence to win material or checkmate.

notes.explains: The rook sacrifice on a3 opens the a-file and clears the b-file, while the queen and rook are aligned on the c-file. The immediate threat is to deflect the queen from defending a key pawn, allowing the queen to enter for mate.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can serve to open lines and improve piece activity. Even when giving up material, each move should improve your position or create a concrete threat.
notes.plans: Play Bf5, attacking the queen and gaining space on the diagonal, while maintaining the threat of Qxc3.

notes.explains: After Bf5, the queen cannot capture the bishop because Qxc3 would be mate. The opponent's queen retreats to d2, but then the bishop can go to b5, creating multiple threats that are impossible to parry simultaneously.
notes.teaches: When two bishops work together on adjacent diagonals, they can control a huge portion of the board. Creating multiple threats can overload the defense.
notes.plans: Continue with Bb5, maintaining the attack and exploiting the coordination of the bishops.

notes.explains: With the b-file open, the rook can be brought to b8, connecting with the bishop on b5 to threaten mate on b1. This final move seals the deal, as the opponent cannot defend all the threats.
notes.teaches: After opening files, use your major pieces to invade and create mating nets. Look for ways to connect your pieces on key squares.
notes.plans: Play Rb8, threatening mate on b1 and forcing the opponent to deal with the unstoppable attack.

notes.explains: In this position, the bishop and rook lines converge on b1, creating a mating threat. The queen is overloaded, having to defend c3 and also provide an escape square for the king on d2.
notes.teaches: When a single piece has multiple defensive duties, it can become overloaded. Look for ways to create threats that force the opponent's pieces to abandon their key defensive roles.
notes.plans: Play Rook b1 next move to deliver checkmate, or force the opponent to give up material to prevent it.

notes.explains: Even though the side with the attack has less material, all their pieces are actively placed and have clear threats, making it impossible for the opponent to defend everything.
notes.teaches: Material count is not the only factor; piece activity and coordination can outweigh a material deficit. When your pieces are all working together, the opponent may be unable to meet all threats.
notes.plans: Continue pressing the attack, forcing the opponent to give up material or be checkmated.

notes.explains: The game continued with the opponent giving up the queen to stave off immediate mate, but the resulting endgame was still winning for the attacking side, and there were additional tactical resources.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, be prepared for the opponent to sacrifice material to prolong the game. The resulting position may still be winning if your pieces remain active and your threats persist.
notes.plans: Convert the material advantage or continue exploiting tactical weaknesses in the opponent's camp.

notes.explains: The attacking player had set up the position many moves in advance, waiting for the moment when the tactic would work. The opponent missed a defensive resource, but the point is that the threats were overwhelming.
notes.teaches: Long-term planning and patience are key in chess. Set up ideas in the position and wait for the right moment to strike, rather than forcing tactics prematurely.

notes.explains: In a Najdorf Sicilian, the battle often revolves around control of the d5 square. White may try to establish a knight on d5, while Black seeks to challenge it with pieces like the bishop pair and a knight maneuver to f6.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, the d5 square is a critical outpost. Both sides should be aware of the fight for this square and plan their piece placements accordingly.
notes.plans: Black can aim to trade off the knight on d5 by playing ...Nf6, while using the bishop pair to create dynamic counterplay.

notes.explains: The player values the bishop pair and seeks to use it to maintain initiative. The opponent's knight on d5 is a key piece to eliminate, so the plan is to play ...Nd7 and ...Nf6 to trade it off.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong centralized knight, consider maneuvering your own knight to challenge and exchange it, especially if you have the bishop pair.
notes.plans: Play ...Nd7 and ...Nf6 to remove the knight on d5, then proceed with active piece play.

notes.explains: After resolving the d5 knight, the d6 pawn is no longer weak, and the opponent's knight on c1 is misplaced, blocking rook connection. The player now has active pieces and aims to make moves with tempo to keep the opponent reacting.
notes.teaches: A misplaced piece (like a knight on c1) can be a long-term liability; use tempo moves to prevent the opponent from regrouping.
notes.plans: Continue making threats with tempo, such as pushing a5-a4 to drive back opponent's pieces, and avoid giving the opponent time to coordinate.

notes.explains: Playing f4 is risky because it puts pawns on the same color as the bishop, reducing its scope, and if the center closes, the knight may become better than the bishop. However, there are tactical ideas, such as Qb6 with threats on the king and b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: Be cautious about placing pawns on the same color as your bishop; consider whether the resulting pawn structure favors your pieces or your opponent's.
notes.plans: Use the queen to create threats (e.g., Qb6) and force the opponent to react, while keeping the position open to maintain the bishop's activity.

notes.explains: The queen is not suited for defense; if it is used to defend, it becomes a target because any threat to the queen must be answered. The player's queen on f3 is vulnerable, and they plan to attack it with Qb6.
notes.teaches: Avoid using the queen for defensive duties when possible; it is a powerful attacking piece and can be harassed if forced to defend.
notes.plans: Play Qb6 to attack the b2 pawn and create threats, forcing the opponent to respond and keeping the initiative.

notes.explains: The player plans to open the e-file with ...e4, sacrificing a pawn to activate the rook and bring all pieces into the attack. They also consider ...f3 first to prevent the queen from returning to f3, keeping the position open.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn to open lines and activate pieces can be worth it if it leads to a sustained attack and forces the opponent to defend multiple threats.
notes.plans: Play ...f3 to prevent Qf3, then ...e4 to open the e-file, followed by ...Re8 to support the pawn and join the attack.

notes.explains: Playing f3 first prevents the queen from retreating to f3 and keeps opening the position. The key issue for the opponent is that they will not have enough time to react to all the threats at once.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development or a space advantage, open the position to increase the number of threats and overload the opponent's defense.
notes.plans: Continue to open lines and create multiple threats, forcing the opponent to respond to each one.

notes.explains: After f3, if the pawn takes, the position opens up, similar to a previous a3 idea where pawns become dispersed and files open. Here, Rook to e8 makes the position tricky for White despite fewer pieces.
notes.teaches: Pawn advances can be used to open files and diagonals, even at the cost of pawn structure, to activate pieces and create tactical chances.
notes.plans: If the pawn captures, play Rook to e8 to increase pressure on the open file.

notes.explains: The opponent is playing very fast, which makes it a perfect opportunity to set up a tactic or trap a few moves ahead that the opponent won't see.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is playing quickly, it's a good time to create tactical complications and hidden threats that they may overlook.
notes.plans: Set up a tactical sequence that exploits the opponent's speed and lack of deep calculation.

notes.explains: The queen is the piece holding White's position together, so we need to attack it. h5 is a move that attacks the queen indirectly, and if the queen takes on f3, there is a dangerous Bishop to d4 with many threats.
notes.teaches: Identify the key defensive piece in the opponent's position and target it to break down their defense.
notes.plans: Continue to attack the queen and create threats that overload the defense.

notes.explains: If the queen takes on h5 instead of f3, there is a big change. We always look for checks, captures, and threats first. There is a checkmate idea involving a long-range check.
notes.teaches: Always consider forcing moves like checks and captures first, as they can lead to tactical finishes.
notes.plans: Look for a check that leads to a checkmate or a decisive material gain.

notes.explains: The queen was moved from g4 to h5 to enable the sacrifice on f2, because otherwise the queen on g4 would defend the d4 square after bishop to d4. The bishop was forced to f6 earlier to make this possible.
notes.teaches: Before executing a combination, ensure that the opponent's pieces cannot defend the critical squares. Sometimes you need to deflect or move your own pieces to clear the path.
notes.plans: The immediate plan is to execute the queen sacrifice on f2, leading to a forced mate or material gain.

notes.explains: The alternative queen takes f3 was analyzed, but it leads to bishop to d4 and pressure on f2. If the queen goes to g2, rook takes f2 exploits the back rank; if the queen goes to d1, bishop to f2 and king g2 gives white a scary position with compensation for the material.
notes.teaches: When considering a sacrifice, analyze the opponent's defensive resources. Even if not immediately decisive, there may be sufficient compensation in the form of pressure and attacking chances.
notes.plans: If the opponent declines the sacrifice, there are ideas like queen to e3, h4-h3, and continued pressure on f2.

notes.explains: After a tournament block, individual game analysis alone misses the bigger picture. Reviewing each game for isolated mistakes is useful, but the real lessons come from stepping back and looking at the whole set of games as one dataset.
notes.teaches: Treat a tournament or a series of games as a single sample. Look for recurring patterns: which openings caused trouble, which endgame types you scored well in, and how your time management varied between events.
notes.plans: After returning from a tournament, group your games by opening, phase, and time usage. Identify one or two recurring weaknesses and make those the focus of your next training block.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: When facing an opponent of nearly identical rating, it is hard to predict their opening knowledge or style, unlike when facing much weaker or stronger players.
notes.teaches: Prepare for equal-strength opponents by focusing on your own solid opening repertoire and understanding typical plans, rather than trying to guess their preparation.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, White's early e3 is critical because it leads to many distinct lines. Black's choice of when to take on c3 matters: taking after a3 is preferable to avoid annoying bishop checks on a3.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, the timing of capturing on c3 is important; wait for a3 to prevent the bishop from going to a3 with tempo.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: Black has several setups against the Nimzo-Indian: castling first, or playing c5 early. The early c5 aims to meet Nge2 with ...cxd4, gaining a chance to open the center.
notes.teaches: The choice between castling and an early c5 in the Nimzo-Indian depends on whether you want to provoke Nge2 and then trade on d4.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: After the opening moves, Black's light-squared bishop is still undeveloped. The position may look equal, but Black must decide how to develop this bishop: fianchetto, play d5, or prepare d6/e5.
notes.teaches: In closed openings, identify your underdeveloped pieces and choose a plan that gives them a good role, such as fianchettoing or preparing a central pawn break.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop via fianchetto or prepare a central pawn advance (d5 or d6/e5) to activate it.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: After castling, the position appears equal: White has center and space, Black has king safety. The main issue is the undeveloped bishop, which needs a plan.
notes.teaches: When you don't have a clear plan, look at your undeveloped pieces and consider their possible futures.
notes.plans: Choose a development scheme for the bishop: fianchetto (b6), d5, or d6-e5.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: White's setup with e3 and Ne2 has specific ideas: the knight can go to f3-e4 or f4-d5, and it doesn't block the f-pawn. This prevents some Black tactics and makes slow play difficult.
notes.teaches: Recognize the opponent's setup and its typical plans; adapt your own development accordingly.
notes.plans: Avoid giving up the two bishops; choose a solid setup that doesn't allow White's knight to dominate.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: With a3 played, Black decides not to take on c3, as it would trade bishop for knight and give up the bishop pair while the center is still mobile.
notes.teaches: Don't part with a bishop for a knight without a concrete reason; the bishop pair is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: Play Be7 and develop the bishop actively, aiming for d6-e5.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: Bf4 is not good because it blocks the knight, delays development, and delays castling. The bishop looks good on the diagonal but the cost is too high.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that look active but hinder your development and king safety.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f4 instead, and then decide the bishop's fate.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: Black chooses d6 with the idea of e5, rather than b6 or d5. b6 is less appealing because after Bb7 and castling, the bishop can get locked in if the knight goes to d7 and then d5 or Nf6 closes the diagonal.
notes.teaches: When choosing a plan, consider the future of your pieces and whether they might become passive.
notes.plans: Play d6, then e5, and develop the knight to e4 if possible, but be aware of d5 pressure.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: After White plays Be3, Black considers e5. If e5 is met by dxe5, the queens may be exchanged, which could be undesirable.
notes.teaches: Before advancing a pawn, check if it allows unfavorable simplifications.
notes.plans: Consider Qb6 to put pressure on b2, but note that White can play Bd3, and if Black takes on b2, Na4 traps the queen.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In this position, Black considers queen b6, but it is not a real threat because White can simply play bishop d3, and if Black takes on b2, knight a4 traps the queen. Thus, the move lacks a concrete threat and is not effective.
notes.teaches: Before playing a move that appears aggressive, check if it actually threatens something concrete. If the opponent can ignore it or defend easily, the move may just waste time.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: Black considers developing the knight to c6, but this allows White to push d5, which would be annoying. Black would prefer to play e5 to challenge the center, but that leaves the dark-squared bishop passive. The position is uncomfortable for Black, who would rather be White.
notes.teaches: When considering a developing move, always check if it allows the opponent a strong central push. Sometimes you must commit to a pawn break like e5 even if it leaves a piece passive, to avoid a worse alternative.
notes.plans: Black should commit to playing e5, accepting the passive bishop, to prevent White's d5 and to create counterplay.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The pawn structure after e5 is a typical minority/majority situation: White has a queenside pawn majority, Black has a kingside majority. White can push queenside pawns without worrying about king safety, while Black must be cautious pushing kingside because it exposes the king.
notes.teaches: In such structures, the side with the queenside majority can often launch a pawn storm safely, while the side with the kingside majority must weigh the risk to their king. Understanding these plans is crucial in many openings.
notes.plans: Black should aim to use the kingside majority to create attacking chances, but must coordinate pieces and ensure king safety. White will try to push on the queenside.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: White plays knight d5, a strong centralizing move. If White plays passively, Black will develop and have better piece activity and coordination. White must act energetically to maintain pressure.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage or better coordination, you should play actively to increase the pressure. If you allow the opponent to develop freely, they may equalize or even get the better game.
notes.plans: White should continue to press with active moves, possibly targeting weaknesses in Black's camp. Black must find a way to neutralize the knight on d5.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: Black considers developing the knight to c6, but this would require giving up the bishop pair by taking on d5. The bishop pair is valuable, but sometimes you must make such a concession to develop and relieve pressure.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair is an advantage, but not absolute. You must weigh it against the need to develop and the concrete demands of the position. Sometimes you have to give up a bishop to avoid a worse fate.
notes.plans: Black should decide whether to take on d5 with the knight or find another way to develop, considering the long-term value of the bishop pair.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In this position, the choice is between taking the knight with the bishop or moving the bishop away. Taking is not forced immediately, but declining it leads to long-term problems: the opponent's knight can jump around, and the bishop pair is less effective if the opponent keeps a knight to harass it.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, it's often worth trading one bishop for a knight to eliminate the opponent's minor piece, because a lone knight can become a strong outpost. If you keep your own knight while the opponent has two bishops, your knight can be more valuable than their extra bishop.
notes.plans: Take the knight with the bishop, then continue development, aiming to use the remaining bishop and knight actively.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: A concrete tactical point: if you don't take the knight, the opponent can play a knight to c7, trapping your rook. Also, moving the bishop to d6 would allow c5, attacking the bishop and gaining time, so the bishop is misplaced.
notes.teaches: Before declining a capture, check for tactical threats like a knight fork or a pawn attack on the piece. Sometimes a move that seems flexible actually loses time because the opponent can harass your piece.
notes.plans: Take the knight to avoid the tactical threats, then proceed with development.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: After the exchange, the position is critical: you have less material, so you must develop the remaining pieces to active squares. The knight is your key piece because the opponent lacks one, so it must be activated. Knight f5 is better than bishop f5 because the bishop can still go to f3, but the knight needs to find a strong post.
notes.teaches: When you have a minor piece advantage (e.g., a knight vs. no knight), activate that piece to its best square. Don't let a bishop sit passively when a knight can occupy a central outpost.
notes.plans: Play knight f5, aiming to create threats against the opponent's position, possibly targeting the bishop or pawn structure.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The opponent's king move (king d2) invites you to capture the bishop, which would mess up the pawn structure. If white develops instead, you can take the bishop and enjoy better piece activity, as your rook is active and the opponent's bishop is passive.
notes.teaches: In endgames and simplified middlegames, activity matters more than material. A bishop that is stuck behind pawns is often worse than a knight that can jump to active squares.
notes.plans: If white doesn't address the threat, capture the bishop, then play rook d8 to increase pressure, aiming for a favorable endgame with active pieces.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In this endgame, Black's pieces are active while White's bishop is passive. Black can create pressure and potentially win a pawn, but the position is not necessarily winning—just better for Black due to piece activity.
notes.teaches: Piece activity is a key advantage in endgames. A passive piece can be a long-term liability, so aim to keep your pieces active and your opponent's passive.
notes.plans: Black should continue to improve piece activity, possibly by bringing the king into the game or advancing pawns to create weaknesses in White's camp.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: If White develops with king bishop e2, Black can capture on e3, but if White plays king d2 instead, capturing would allow White's king to become active and the bishop to come to d3. That would help White activate pieces, so Black should avoid that capture.
notes.teaches: Avoid helping your opponent activate their pieces. In endgames, king activity is crucial, so don't give the enemy king a free path into the game.
notes.plans: Black should instead develop the bishop to b2 (or d3) and prepare rook d8, aiming to pressure White and maintain piece activity.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: Black has a spatial and activity advantage. The question is how to convert this advantage into something concrete, like a pawn or a better endgame. The idea is to convert the dynamic advantage into a lasting structural one.
notes.teaches: When you have an advantage, you must have a plan to convert it. Think of it like energy conversion: use your activity to create weaknesses or win material, then convert that into a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Black should aim to advance with f5, possibly after improving the bishop, and bring the king into the game. The concrete plan is to increase pressure and force White into passivity.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In the endgame, both having a passed pawn and activating the king are top priorities. Black should consider both when deciding on moves.
notes.teaches: In endgames, prioritize king activity and passed pawns. These are often the decisive factors.
notes.plans: Black should look for ways to create a passed pawn or bring the king to a more active square, while keeping the opponent's pieces tied down.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In this position, the dynamic advantages of piece activity and coordination are temporary. They must be converted into something permanent, like a structural gain, before they fade.
notes.teaches: Use dynamic advantages quickly; if you cannot convert them, they may disappear, leaving you with nothing.
notes.plans: Look for immediate ways to exploit activity, such as pushing f5 or creating threats, before the opponent consolidates.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: When you have a better rook, you should aim to trade rooks to emphasize your advantage. Playing c5 may not achieve that, whereas rook d1 would force the exchange.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the player with the better rook should seek to trade rooks, simplifying to a favorable pawn structure.
notes.plans: Consider rook d1 to force rook exchanges and reduce opponent's counterplay.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In a position without a clear winning plan, you should focus on playing the position accurately and putting pressure on the opponent, rather than searching for a forced win.
notes.teaches: When no forced win exists, rely on general principles and make moves that maintain pressure and limit opponent's options.
notes.plans: Combine ideas like b6 to slow the opponent's pawn, bring the king up, and consider g5 depending on opponent's moves.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The decision to allow the opponent's king activity in exchange for your rook activity is a matter of taste and risk assessment. Some players might accept it, but it's okay to avoid it if you don't trust your position.
notes.teaches: Evaluate trades that give the opponent activity; choose the option that you feel most comfortable with, even if it's not objectively best.
notes.plans: If you avoid the trade, maintain your rook's activity and seek other ways to improve your position.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In this rook and pawn endgame, the key is to avoid giving the opponent counterplay. Advancing pawns prematurely like g5 allows the opponent to activate their rook with d1, followed by d7, exploiting a pinned bishop. The priority is to keep the opponent's pieces passive while improving our own position.
notes.teaches: In endgames, preventing the opponent's activity can be more important than creating your own passed pawns. Restrain the opponent's pieces before pushing your own pawns.
notes.plans: Focus on stabilizing the queenside and defending the center before advancing pawns on the kingside.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: When considering taking on c4, the idea is to open the d-file for the rook, gaining control of the only open file. This is beneficial because it gives the rook activity and puts pressure on the opponent's position, even though it helps the opponent's king by removing a pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, control of the only open file can be worth material concessions. Rook activity often outweighs pawn structure considerations.
notes.plans: After taking on c4, aim to occupy the d-file with the rook and then bring the king into the game.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: Playing b6 is a strong alternative because it attacks the opponent's pawns and bishop while maintaining pressure. The opponent cannot capture due to losing the bishop, and black can continue to harass the queenside pawns, eventually winning material.
notes.teaches: In endgames, creating threats against the opponent's weak pawns can tie down their pieces and yield a material advantage. Use pawn moves to initiate attacks on the opponent's structure.
notes.plans: After b6, continue to pressure the queenside pawns, forcing the opponent to defend passively, then convert the extra pawn.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: When considering king e7 to defend d7, the problem is that after trades, the opponent's king can penetrate to c4, becoming very active. This allows white to dominate the position, so king e7 is not satisfactory. Instead, taking on c5 is better, as it eliminates the opponent's pawn and creates a passed pawn for black, which is beneficial despite being an isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, king activity is paramount. Avoid moves that allow the opponent's king to become active. An extra pawn, even if isolated, can be a decisive advantage if the opponent's king is tied down.
notes.plans: Take on c5, then use the extra pawn to create a passed pawn while keeping the opponent's king passive.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In this endgame, having an extra pawn is beneficial because it also helps to paralyze the opponent's king. The idea is to create a passed pawn and keep the opponent's king tied down.
notes.teaches: An extra pawn in the endgame can be used not only as material but also to restrict the opponent's king, making it harder for them to defend.
notes.plans: Push the pawns on the kingside to create a passed pawn and activate the king.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: When choosing which pawns to keep, it's important to consider which ones will support your king's activity and future pawn breaks. Here, keeping the central pawns (e4 and f4) is preferable because they allow more flexibility and keep the opponent's king out.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, the choice of which pawns to keep is crucial; central pawns often provide better support for king penetration and pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Keep the central pawns and use them to create threats while the opponent's king is tied down.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The opponent's inaccurate play (rushing with a5 and then ignoring the kingside) allowed the black king to become active. The winning idea is to march the king forward and support the pawns, rather than forcing pawn breaks that allow the opponent to block the king's entry.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, king activity is often more important than pawn moves. Avoid pawn moves that allow the opponent to block your king's path.
notes.plans: Bring the king to e5 and then support the pawns, aiming to create a decisive passed pawn.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The move f3 would allow g4, blocking the king's entrance, so taking the pawn on e3 is better because it keeps the king active. The opponent's best try was to play h4 to mess with the pawn structure, but they ignored the kingside and went for the queenside, which was a mistake.
notes.teaches: When your king is active, avoid pawn moves that allow the opponent to block it. Keep your king free to participate in the attack.
notes.plans: After taking on e3, bring the king to e5 and then push the kingside pawns, using the king's activity to win.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The winning move is c4, starting a pawn march with everything. Even if not the most accurate, having a clear plan and following it is important. The king is free to go to the attack.
notes.teaches: In endgames, having a clear plan is essential. Even if you don't play the most accurate move, a consistent plan can guide you to victory.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawn and support it with the king, creating a decisive passed pawn.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: In this pawn endgame, Black has a kingside majority and White has a queenside majority. The immediate push c4 is strong, but the even more accurate move is e2, which brings the king into the game first. By sacrificing the extra pawn, Black activates the king and creates a decisive advantage.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, king activity often outweighs material. Sometimes giving up a pawn to activate your king is the fastest route to victory.
notes.plans: Push the e-pawn to bring the king to the center, then use the kingside majority to create a passed pawn and promote.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The opening came out roughly equal, with both sides having different pawn majorities. The key was not to force a super winning position but to follow a clear plan: activate the king and restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.teaches: You don't always need the most accurate moves; you need a coherent idea and a path to follow. Even from an equal position, a clear plan can guide you to victory.
notes.plans: Continue with the plan of king activation and pawn pushes, while preventing the opponent from freeing their pieces.

notes.opening: French Defense: Classical Variation, Swiss Variation
notes.explains: The game was won not by a single blunder but by the opponent making slightly inaccurate moves. The player had a clear technique and knew exactly what they wanted to achieve.
notes.teaches: You can win by consistently making good moves and following a plan, even if your opponent doesn't make a huge mistake. Patience and technique are valuable.

notes.explains: In endgame studies, material is often misleading; a king trapped by its own pawns can be mated despite a huge material deficit.
notes.teaches: Look for ways to restrict the enemy king's escape squares, even at the cost of material, before counting the position as lost.
notes.plans: Identify the king's potential escape routes and consider sacrifices that force the opponent's pieces to block them.

notes.explains: A series of pawn sacrifices can force the enemy bishop to capture, thereby opening lines and tightening the cage around the king.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be used to deflect defensive pieces and create a mating net, not just to win material.
notes.plans: Push pawns to lure the bishop into taking, then use the cleared squares for your own pieces to deliver mate.

notes.explains: When the enemy king is confined, even a lone bishop and king can deliver checkmate if the opponent's pawns block the escape squares.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a king can be mated by minimal material if the opponent's own pawns are used against them.
notes.plans: Coordinate your king and bishop to control the key escape squares while the opponent's pawns do the rest.

notes.explains: In a queen vs. pieces endgame, the defender's king may be trapped, but you must avoid stalemate while delivering mate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has few moves, be alert to stalemate tricks and look for checkmate patterns that force the king to walk into mate.
notes.plans: Use checks and threats to drive the king into a corner, but ensure the opponent always has a legal move until the final mate.

notes.explains: A knight and bishop can cooperate to create a mating net, even when the opponent has extra pawns, if the king is confined.
notes.teaches: Recognize common mating patterns in studies, such as the 'windmill' or 'epaulette' mate, and look for forcing moves that lead to them.
notes.plans: Coordinate the knight and bishop to control the king's flight squares, then deliver mate with a final sacrifice or quiet move.

notes.explains: Black's king is in a painful zugzwang: every legal move worsens his position, and the only move leads to checkmate. The presence of black's own pawns is what traps the king, as removing any pawn would give black at least a draw.
notes.teaches: In endgame studies, look for zugzwang positions where the opponent's own pawns restrict their king and force self-destruction. Recognize that material advantage can be a liability when it suffocates the king.
notes.plans: If in a similar position, aim to create a mating net by using your pieces to control escape squares, forcing the opponent to move into a checkmate pattern.

notes.explains: Solving endgame studies, especially those with surprising resources, improves calculation and visualization. These positions often cannot be solved by memorized tactical patterns because the key ideas are unconventional.
notes.teaches: Practice with complex studies to enhance board visualization and the ability to find creative resources. Use them as warm-ups to sharpen tactical awareness.

notes.explains: White is down material but has a mating attack. The knight must be brought to g7 to create threats, but the immediate knight to f6 fails because black can deflect with rook takes f4. The correct first move is knight to e8, aiming for g7.
notes.teaches: When building a mating net, choose the piece route that maintains the strongest threats. Sometimes a slower, more indirect approach is necessary to avoid tactical refutations.
notes.plans: After knight e8, if black doesn't address the threat, play knight g7 and bishop f5 mate. If black tries to create escape squares, use sacrifices to seal the king in.

notes.explains: In the study, white sacrifices pieces (h5, f5, g4, bishop f5) to systematically remove black's escape squares and force the rook to block the king. The final position is a checkmate with the knight and pawns, despite white giving up all major pieces.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be justified if they permanently restrict the enemy king. The goal is to eliminate all possible flight squares, even at the cost of material, to achieve a forced mate.
notes.plans: Continue the mating pattern: after the rook is forced to c5, play bishop f5 check, forcing rook takes, then knight g7 with mate to follow.

notes.explains: In another study, white has a material disadvantage but black's pawns are a pressing threat. It might be tempting to accept a draw by giving up the knight to stop the pawns, but white should look for a more active resource.
notes.teaches: When facing dangerous passed pawns, do not automatically settle for a draw. Look for counterplay against the enemy king, as the pawns may also restrict the opponent's own pieces.
notes.plans: Seek a way to use the knight and bishop to create mating threats while dealing with the pawns, rather than passively defending.

notes.explains: In this study, the white knight is under pressure from advancing pawns, and it's tempting to give up the knight to stop them, but that only draws. The key is to find a way to use the knight actively to create mating threats rather than passively defending.
notes.teaches: When defending against passed pawns, look for active counterplay, especially mating threats, rather than accepting material loss for a draw.
notes.plans: Bring the knight to a square where it both stops the pawn and supports a mating net, such as knight b1, then coordinate with the king and bishop to deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: The black pawns are very dangerous, and if white tries to stop them with the bishop alone, black can force a draw. The only winning move is to reposition the knight to a square that both blocks the pawn and sets up a mating pattern.
notes.teaches: In endgames with passed pawns, sometimes the best defense is a counterattack that leads to checkmate, not just blockade.
notes.plans: Play knight b1, then when black advances the king, use the knight and bishop to create a mating net while the pawns are stopped.

notes.explains: White is up a piece, but the material balance is not winning because black has dangerous pawns. If white tries to save both pieces, black can force a draw by winning one back.
notes.teaches: Material advantage is not always enough; you must assess the activity of pieces and the danger of passed pawns.
notes.plans: Use the knight to give a check that forces the black king to a worse square, then try to maintain the material advantage while avoiding black's tricks.

notes.explains: In the second study, white must act decisively because passive play allows black to draw. The knight gives a check, and black must respond, but black has clever resources to try to win back material.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, you must be precise and avoid allowing your opponent to trade off your extra piece.
notes.plans: Continue with the knight check, then if black tries to win a piece, use tactical shots to maintain the advantage and head for a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Black tries to trap the white knight, but white finds a counter-tactic to keep the pieces coordinated. The position remains winning for white because the extra piece is decisive.
notes.teaches: In endgames, keep your pieces coordinated and watch for tactical resources to avoid losing your advantage.
notes.plans: Continue to use the knight and bishop in coordination, avoiding black's traps, and convert the material advantage into a win.

notes.explains: Two knights against a lone king is normally a draw, but with extra bishops on the board, the position can be winning for the side with the extra material. The defender must seek tricks and complications to salvage a draw.
notes.teaches: In endgames with minor pieces, the presence of extra pieces can turn a normally drawn material configuration into a win. The defender should look for stalemate tricks, forks, and perpetual checks to escape.
notes.plans: The side with the extra material should aim to consolidate and avoid tactical pitfalls, while the defender should create maximum counterplay.

notes.explains: A specific defensive setup with bishop and two knights can lead to stalemate if the attacker captures the bishop. The defender repeatedly offers the bishop to force a draw.
notes.teaches: When defending a seemingly lost endgame, look for stalemate patterns where capturing a piece leaves the opponent with insufficient mating material. Sacrificing pieces to reach a drawn fortress is a key defensive resource.
notes.plans: The defender should aim to set up a stalemate net, while the attacker must find a way to avoid the trap and bring the king into the action.

notes.explains: In a mirrored version of the previous setup, the attacker's king is better placed, enabling a win despite the same defensive trick. The king's activity is the decisive difference.
notes.teaches: King activity is often the deciding factor in endgames. A seemingly identical position can be winning or drawing depending on the king's ability to participate in the attack or defense.
notes.plans: The attacker should use the king to support the knights and create mating threats, while the defender must find ways to keep the king out.

notes.explains: Two knights can deliver checkmate when the opponent has extra pieces that block escape squares. The king's proximity enables a forced mate that would be impossible against a lone king.
notes.teaches: Even in endgames with minimal material, checkmate patterns exist when the opponent's pieces obstruct their own king. Always be alert for unusual mating nets.
notes.plans: The attacker should coordinate the knights and king to drive the enemy king to the edge and deliver mate, while the defender must avoid being boxed in.

notes.explains: In a bishop vs knight endgame, the bishops are often the better team due to their long-range power and ability to control both wings. Here, white's pieces are more active, giving winning chances.
notes.teaches: In minor piece endgames, piece activity and coordination matter more than material count. Bishops often outperform knights in open positions, especially when they can target weaknesses.
notes.plans: The side with the bishop should activate it, create threats, and induce weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure. The side with the knight should seek outposts and block the bishop's diagonals.

notes.explains: A seemingly natural bishop move can be a blunder if it allows a stunning pawn break that traps the bishop or wins material. Here, black's b5 move exploits the bishop's vulnerability.
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical resources before committing to a move. A move that looks active may leave a piece en prise to a pawn advance or other tactic.
notes.plans: The side with the initiative should look for pawn breaks to undermine the opponent's pieces, while the defender must anticipate such breaks and keep pieces protected.

notes.explains: In this position, White's last move was a serious mistake, allowing Black a stunning resource. The natural moves like g6, Nf4, or even Ng5 are all reasonable, but there is a much stronger idea that turns the tables immediately.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical resources that exploit the opponent's last move, even when the position seems quiet. A single move like b5 can completely change the evaluation.
notes.plans: After b5, Black threatens Bb7 next move, and White has no good defense, leading to resignation.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, Black is up a pawn but White's rook is actively placed, keeping Black's rook passive and cutting off the black king. Black finds a clever idea with f4+.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rook placement is often more important than material. Be alert to tactical tricks even when the position seems equal.
notes.plans: White should consider Kf2 or other king moves to avoid the tactical blow. If White plays the natural Ke4, Black has Rd6, threatening mate and winning.

notes.explains: White is up a piece and winning, but must convert carefully. The fastest way is to push the h-pawn, but White instead decides to deal with the a-pawn, allowing Black a counterattack.
notes.teaches: When winning, prefer the most direct and forcing plan. Do not give the opponent counterplay by addressing secondary concerns.
notes.plans: White should play g3 and then push the h-pawn, which cannot be stopped. Instead, after Rha7, Black has Rh1! and White is lost.

notes.explains: Black is down material but has a dangerous passed pawn about to promote. White must decide between perpetual check or a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a promotion threat, look for ways to use your own pieces to create mating threats, even if it means sacrificing material.
notes.plans: The bishop should be brought to a square where it can support a mating net, but the queen must be deflected or the key squares must be covered.

notes.explains: When the opponent is about to promote and you are down material, the only winning try is often a direct mating attack. Here, the bishop on g5 is the key move because it covers the critical squares and prevents the black queen from defending both the promotion and the king.
notes.teaches: In positions where the opponent threatens promotion, look for a move that simultaneously creates mating threats and restricts the opponent's defensive resources. A quiet move that covers key squares can be stronger than a flashy check.
notes.plans: If black promotes, white must mate quickly; if black takes the bishop, white wins the h-pawn and the resulting queen endgame is easily winning.

notes.explains: In a race between a mating attack and a promotion, precise move order is crucial. White uses checks to drive the black king to a square where the queen and bishop can deliver mate, even against two queens.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has multiple queens, you must mate immediately; use checks to force the king into a mating net, and coordinate your pieces to cover all escape squares.
notes.plans: White gives a series of checks, forcing the king to g8, then delivers mate with queen and bishop.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent has a dangerous passed pawn, a seemingly natural move like knight e7 can fail to a tactical resource. The opponent's f6 check disrupts the mating net, and the white king is too slow to stop the promotion.
notes.teaches: When trying to mate before a pawn promotes, consider the opponent's defensive checks. A move that looks good may allow a check that breaks the coordination of your pieces.
notes.plans: White must find a more accurate move that prevents the opponent's defensive resources.

notes.explains: The winning idea is to use the king aggressively: king h6 controls the escape squares and supports the knight's mating threats. This prevents the black king from fleeing and allows the knight to deliver mate even after the pawn promotes.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the king can be a powerful attacking piece. Sometimes the only winning move is to bring the king into the attack, cutting off the opponent's escape routes.
notes.plans: White plays king h6, then uses the knight to control g8 and deliver mate, regardless of black's attempts to promote or check.

notes.explains: A similar pattern appears in other endgames: when the opponent checks with f6, the king can step to g6, and the h-pawn becomes a decisive factor. Even if the opponent promotes, the h-pawn advances and supports a mating attack.
notes.teaches: Recognize recurring mating patterns in endgames. The king's ability to cut off escape squares and the support of a passed pawn can turn a lost-looking position into a win.
notes.plans: White uses the king to control key squares and the h-pawn to create mating threats, even against a new queen.

notes.explains: In this endgame, black's king can hide on h7, making it difficult for white to deliver mate. The key is to find the right checking square, such as f6, to force the king to h6 where it becomes trapped.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is hiding, look for checks that force it to a worse square, even if the immediate mate is not apparent. Calculation is important, but understanding the king's hiding squares guides the search.
notes.plans: After forcing the king to h6, use the knights or pawns to deliver mate, as the king has no escape squares.

notes.explains: White has a material advantage (rook for bishop and pawn) but black has a dangerous passed a-pawn. The obvious move rook a5 allows black to hold, but the resource rook g6 is much stronger, restricting the black king and setting up mating threats.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, look for active rook moves that cut off the enemy king and create mating nets, rather than passively defending. Even with a material edge, the most direct winning plan may be to go for checkmate.
notes.plans: After rook g6, if black pushes the a-pawn, white can use the rook to give checks and force mate on the h-file. If black tries to cover with the bishop, white can dominate it and still deliver mate.

notes.explains: In this study, White has king, knight, and pawn versus Black's king and queen, with Black to move. The natural attempts—trapping the queen or promoting the pawn—fail because Black can simply sacrifice the queen for the pawn, resulting in a draw.
notes.teaches: When facing a lone queen with minor piece and pawn, the defender's queen can often be traded for the pawn to draw, so the attacker must seek a mating net that prevents the queen from capturing the pawn.
notes.plans: Set up a position where the knight delivers a checkmate threat, forcing Black to either give up the queen or be mated.

notes.explains: The puzzle is an imagination exercise: the pieces are not placed initially, and solvers must deduce the only winning arrangement. The solution can be mirrored (e.g., pawn on b7, king on b6, queen on h5) but no other arrangement works.
notes.teaches: When solving composed positions, consider the geometry of the board and how the pieces coordinate to create unavoidable threats, rather than relying on generic strategies.
notes.plans: If studying this position, explore mirrored versions to understand the underlying pattern.

notes.explains: In the French Winawer, after e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4, Black's bishop on b4 signals a desire to trade it for the knight on c3, creating doubled c-pawns for White but giving Black long-term dark-square weaknesses. White's most principled response is e5, closing the center and gaining space.
notes.teaches: When facing the Winawer, be ready to accept doubled pawns in exchange for the bishop pair and a space advantage. The closed center means Black can afford some slow maneuvers, but White should look to exploit the dark-square holes left by the bishop's absence.
notes.plans: After e5, White typically aims to build a strong center and prepare kingside play, while Black often tries to undermine the center with moves like ...c5 or ...b6.

notes.explains: After e5, Black's move ...Qd7 is a rare but logical preparation for ...b6, intending to meet White's queen check on g4 with ...f5, protecting the g7 pawn laterally. The queen on d7 does not obstruct Black's development because the light-squared bishop is heading to a6.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a seemingly awkward queen move can be a useful preparatory step. Here, ...Qd7 supports a plan to exchange light-squared bishops and neutralizes White's typical attacking idea of Qg4.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...b6 and ...Ba6, while White must find an alternative plan to exploit the dark-square weaknesses, such as the pawn thrust h4-h5.

notes.explains: White's move h4 is a direct way to target Black's dark-square weaknesses. The idea is to march the pawn to h5 and then h6, since Black's bishop on b4 no longer controls that square. Black should respond with ...h5 to hold the pawn, but then White can use the inclusion of the h-pawn moves to create a powerful knight outpost on f4 in the resulting endgames.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has weakened dark squares, a pawn storm like h4-h5 can be a strong plan, especially if it forces further weaknesses. The timing of pawn moves can be crucial for creating permanent outposts for your pieces.
notes.plans: White will aim to play h5, then possibly h6, and if Black plays ...g6, White can exploit the dark-square holes. The long-term plan involves placing a knight on f4, which becomes a dominant piece.

notes.explains: In the position after ...Qd7, h4, and ...b6, Black's most common move has been ...Bf8, retreating the bishop to its original square. This position has been known for years, with about 30 games in the database, and is generally considered slightly better for White, but practically Black has scored well because White's plan is difficult to execute.
notes.teaches: Engine evaluations don't always translate to practical results, especially in closed positions where long-term plans are hard to find. It's important to understand the typical plans and be prepared for the opponent's resources.
notes.plans: White needs to find a concrete plan to make progress, possibly involving kingside expansion or piece maneuvers, while Black will try to complete development and counter in the center.

notes.explains: In this theoretical position, black has two main ideas: exchanging the light-squared bishop with ...Ba6, which is favorable in this pawn structure, and playing ...c5 to recapture with the b-pawn, which is positionally desirable. Both are hard to meet simultaneously.
notes.teaches: When facing a position with multiple plausible black plans, look for a single move that addresses all of them at once, even if it looks shocking.
notes.plans: White can play b4, which prevents ...Ba6 (as b5 would follow) and makes ...c5 less attractive because the b-file would open against black.

notes.explains: After b4, black's tactical try ...Bxb4 fails because Qxg7 is a serious threat. If ...Bxc3, both Bd2 and Kd1 lead to a winning attack after Qxh8, as the knight on g8 cannot be held due to ...Kf8 Bxh6+.
notes.teaches: Before playing a pawn move like b4, always check if an enemy piece can capture it, and if so, whether the resulting tactics are in your favor.
notes.plans: If black captures on b4, proceed with the queen and bishop attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black's other ideas are also neutralized: ...Ba6 can be met by b5, leaving the bishop on b7 without a future, and ...c5 is met by a capture, opening the b-file which is uncomfortable for black.
notes.teaches: A well-timed pawn push can restrict the opponent's pawn breaks and make their pieces passive.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop the knights to good squares like f3 and f4, and prepare rook b1 to exploit the b-file.

notes.explains: Black's best response is ...f5, leading to an unpleasant endgame for black because ...c5 is never possible and white's knights can go to f3 and f4. In the game, black played ...a6 as prophylaxis, preparing ...c5 without worrying about Bb5.
notes.teaches: In endgames, pawn structure weaknesses are permanent; if the opponent's freeing break is prevented, their position remains difficult.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and consider rook b1 to pressure the b-file, while keeping the knight route to f4 in mind.

notes.explains: After ...a6, white played a3 (not best; Rb1 is better), and black played ...Ne7, ...Bd3, and ...c5, opening the position. White's better development makes the open position favorable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent opens the position, superior development becomes a decisive factor; use it to increase the pressure.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and use the better piece activity to create threats, possibly placing a rook on an open file.

notes.explains: White has a large development lead and black's position is cramped and difficult to play. Black may try tactical pawn sacrifices to free the light-squared bishop and create outposts, but white's activity remains dominant.
notes.teaches: A lead in development can justify aggressive plans, even allowing the opponent temporary pawn activity, as long as your pieces remain more active.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece activity, often by placing rooks on open files and using the bishop pair to pressure black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black's king is stuck in the center because of a knight on g6 preventing castling. This makes black's position very uncomfortable and gives white attacking chances.
notes.teaches: Preventing the opponent from castling is a key strategic goal; it keeps their king vulnerable and restricts their coordination.
notes.plans: Exploit the uncastled king by opening lines and preparing direct attacks against it.

notes.explains: In a tactical sequence, white offers a bishop on b4. Black cannot capture with the knight because of a fork, and capturing with the bishop allows white's knight to become protected and jump into strong squares. Even if black finds a resource, the position remains very difficult for them.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing material, ensure that the resulting position gives you lasting pressure or concrete threats, even if the opponent finds the best defense.
notes.plans: Keep the initiative by maintaining threats against the enemy king and pieces, forcing black to defend passively.

notes.explains: White has a choice between a safe continuation that leads to opposite-colored bishops and a drawish position, and a more forcing move order that creates mating threats and wins material. The forcing line is correct.
notes.teaches: When you have a tactical opportunity, calculate the most forcing sequence; avoid drifting into positions where the opponent can more easily defend.
notes.plans: Use the rook and queen to create threats on the seventh rank, targeting the enemy king and the loose bishop.

notes.explains: In the Winawer French after e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4 e5 c5 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 Ne7, White's main tries are Qg4 and h4, both exploiting Black's missing dark-squared bishop. The move h4 is currently fashionable, aiming to create kingside pressure.
notes.teaches: When your opponent lacks a bishop of one color, target weaknesses on that color complex, especially the king side. The immediate queen sortie to g4 or the pawn thrust h4 are standard ways to exploit the dark-squared bishop's absence.
notes.plans: White will follow up with h5 to gain space and potentially open lines against the black king, while Black must find a safe setup to neutralize this pressure.

notes.explains: In the main line after Nf3 Bd7 Be2 c4, Black's typical plan is ...Kb8, ...Qa5, and bringing pieces to the queenside. The position is roughly balanced, though engines prefer White. White's idea of dxc5 is tempting to open the position for the bishop pair, but it fails tactically because of ...Nxe5 and the discovered check ...Nxf3+.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, opening the position can be good, but you must check for tactical refutations. A discovered check can ruin your plan, so consider prophylactic moves to avoid such tactics.
notes.plans: White might try the artificial-looking Kf1 to avoid the discovered check and keep the position closed, while preparing to activate the rook via h3 or g3. Black will continue with queenside play.

notes.explains: In a closed center with no immediate kingside danger, the white king does not need to castle short. The rook on h1 can find activity through other means, so an artificial-looking move like Kf1 can be useful.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed and the kingside is safe, consider keeping the king in the center to use the rook and prepare a specific threat.
notes.plans: White threatens dxc5, which would be met by Nxe5 and then Bf4, exploiting the pin on the knight. This aims to provoke black into playing c4 early.

notes.explains: After black plays c4, white can respond with a4, allowing the bishop to go to a3 on the a3-f8 diagonal, where it is optimally placed. This is the key idea behind Kf1.
notes.teaches: Provoking a pawn advance can open a diagonal for a bishop to an active square, improving piece activity.
notes.plans: White aims to place the bishop on a3 and continue with the plan of dxc5, even at the cost of tripled pawns, to generate play.

notes.explains: Black's move g5 is designed to force the bishop to g3 after hxg6 and Nxg6, where it is poorly placed and difficult to bring back into play. White is not overly concerned because the position remains solid.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to drive a piece to a bad square, assess whether the piece can be redeployed or if other factors compensate.
notes.plans: White continues with Nd4, ignoring the attack on the pawns, trusting in the activity of the knight and the solidity of the position.

notes.explains: In this sharp French Winawer position, black has several pawns available to capture, but each capture has a downside. For example, taking on a3 or c3 allows white's knight to jump to b5, and if black then takes on c5, tactics like knight a6 fork the queen. Keeping the queen on the a-file leads to a sticky situation after the a-file opens.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has multiple captures, look for tactical refutations that punish the greedy ones. A knight on b5 can be a powerful outpost to harass the queen and create forks.
notes.plans: White should aim to play knight b5, then knight d6, creating forks on b7 and f7, and follow up with f4 to reroute the bishop to f2 with tempo.

notes.explains: Black's queen takes c3 is a serious blunder because it attacks three pieces but walks into a discovered attack on the d-file. White can save both bishops with bishop d3, and black's queen is overloaded: it cannot recapture on b7 due to bishop a6 check winning the queen, and other captures fail to skewers.
notes.teaches: The queen on the d-file in the French can be a liability. Always check for discovered attacks and skewers before grabbing material with the queen.
notes.plans: White should play bishop d3, then exploit the exposed black king with moves like bishop a6, rook b4, and queen b1 to create decisive threats.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, Black's king is exposed on a8 and White's heavy pieces are coordinated against it. Black's defensive resources are limited because the rook on b7 is strongly placed, and attempts to dislodge it often fail tactically.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the corner, prioritize keeping your attacking pieces coordinated and look for ways to cut off the king's escape squares.
notes.plans: Continue to bring more pieces to the queenside and maintain the pressure on the b-file, aiming for a decisive breakthrough.

notes.explains: Black's threat of ...Nb8 would destabilize the bishop on a6 and rook on b7, so White chooses to reposition the rook to c7, where it still supports the attack while avoiding the undermining.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are aligned on a file, be alert to tactical undermining moves that force them to move. Sometimes a lateral retreat is better than stubbornly holding the file.
notes.plans: After Rc7, the rook is safe and the threat of Qb1 becomes decisive, so White should aim to execute that threat.

notes.explains: Black's queen move to b2 allows a tactical sequence: Bb7+ and Rxd7, leaving the c6 knight undefended. This shows that even when material is roughly balanced, the exposed king and loose pieces make Black's position untenable.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for forcing checks and captures that exploit the opponent's loose pieces. Material is less important than the safety of the king.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack, using the lead in development and the exposed black king to create further threats.

notes.explains: Black tries counterplay with ...Rxg3, but White ignores it because after c6, the white king is safe and the attack on the black king is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When your opponent launches a counterattack, evaluate whether your own king is safe. If it is, you can often ignore the material loss and continue your own attack.
notes.plans: Proceed with the attack, using the king's safety to bring more pieces into the assault, such as preparing Rb1.

notes.explains: In the French Winawer, the dark-squared bishop for Black is often a key defender. When it is traded off, Black's position can become precarious, especially with doubled pawns.
notes.teaches: In the Winawer, the fight for the dark squares is crucial. If you can remove Black's dark-squared bishop, you often gain long-term positional pressure.
notes.plans: Develop pieces to exploit the weakened dark squares, such as placing a bishop on a3, and maintain pressure on Black's structure.

notes.explains: Black's position with doubled pawns is difficult to handle in practice, but some players are very skilled at maneuvering around them. The game shows that even when Black is up a pawn, the placement of the pawn can be poor.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always a weakness; they can provide control of key squares. However, if they are isolated or immobile, they can become targets.
notes.plans: In such positions, focus on piece activity and king safety rather than material. Use the pawn structure to your advantage by attacking the weaknesses.

notes.explains: Some players will repeat the same opening even after losing badly in it. This is a psychological factor to be aware of in preparation.
notes.teaches: When preparing for an opponent, do not assume they will avoid a line just because they lost in it before. Be ready for them to try again, possibly with improvements.
notes.plans: Have a solid repertoire that can handle both expected and unexpected choices, and be flexible during the game.

notes.explains: In this position, black has won a pawn but the black king is exposed on c8, and the pawn structure is bizarre with tripled pawns and a protected passed pawn on d6. White's pieces are active, especially the bishop on h3 eyeing e6, and the knight on a4 is immobilized due to the threat of Rxa7.
notes.teaches: Material is not the only factor; king safety and piece activity can compensate for a pawn deficit. A protected passed pawn can be a strength, but if the king is vulnerable, the initiative matters more.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve piece placement, bring the rook to e3 and then e1, and prepare to invade on e6 or exploit the weak light squares around the black king.

notes.explains: Black is missing the dark-squared bishop, which makes the light-squared bishop particularly important. White's bishop on h3 is very active, and black's lack of dark-squared control means that losses involving the light-squared bishop are magnified.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is missing a bishop, the opposite-colored bishop can become a dominant piece. Use it to control key diagonals and target weaknesses that the missing bishop would normally defend.
notes.plans: White should aim to trade or use the light-squared bishop to create threats, while keeping the black king under pressure. The rook lift to e3 and e1 prepares to break through.

notes.explains: In the French Winawer, the maneuver Rook to h3 is a useful preparatory move. It protects the c3 pawn, which is often a target, and prepares to support the bishop's development to d3. This is important because if the bishop goes to d3 without the rook on h3, black can play c4, trapping the bishop on h7 after Nxc5 and Qxd5+.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic thinking: a move like Rh3 can serve multiple purposes—defending a weak pawn and preparing a piece development that would otherwise be punished. Always consider how a move can neutralize the opponent's tactical resources.
notes.plans: After Rh3, white can develop the bishop to d3 with the idea of castling long and then using the rook on h3 to support an attack on the kingside, possibly with Bh7 and Rg3.

notes.explains: In this specific line of the French Winawer, black's typical queen to a5 is not as effective because the rook on h3 already protects the c3 pawn, so the queen's pressure on c3 is neutralized.
notes.teaches: When a move like Qa5 is a standard resource, look for ways to neutralize it by reinforcing the target square. A rook on h3 can be a surprising but effective defender of the queenside pawns.
notes.plans: White should continue with the plan of castling long and building up an attack, while being aware that black may try other moves like ...Bd7 or ...c4 to challenge the setup.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has just played ...Bd7, and White responds with Bd3, exploiting the fact that long castling has left the h7-bishop vulnerable. The rook on h3 is a key resource: it prevents the tactical trick ...Nxe5 because the rook can swing to e3 to block checks and win.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center or has castled long, look for ways to use your rook on the third rank to support a bishop maneuver and create threats against the enemy king's pawn shield.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain pressure on g7 and prepare a decisive breakthrough, while Black must find a way to neutralize the h3-rook and the bishop on d3.

notes.explains: After the queen trade on g7 and ...cxd4, White's center is falling apart, but White has a very good opposite-colored bishop endgame. The h6-pawn is a permanent weakness, and White's pieces are well placed to pressure the dark squares.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop positions, a permanent weakness on the opponent's side can be more important than a damaged pawn structure. Even without queens, an attack can be effective if the pieces coordinate well.
