notes.plans: White will slowly improve the king and pieces, targeting the h6-pawn and the queenside, while Black struggles for counterplay because the f6-advance is no longer possible.

notes.explains: The move Rc3 is excellent because it prepares to improve the knight on e2 via d4. The immediate threat is Nb5, which would be very uncomfortable for Black. Black responds with ...f6 to undermine the e5-pawn and the d6-square.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed, look for a rook move that clears a path for it to reach a better square. A knight on d4 can create strong threats, especially with a rook behind it.
notes.plans: White will continue to press on the dark squares and the h6-pawn, while Black tries to generate counterplay with ...f5 and ...g3, but the position remains very difficult for Black.

notes.explains: In this type of pawn structure, White should generally avoid playing f4 and instead press on the queenside, especially since the b-file is open. The rook on h7 is tied to defense, and Black has very little counterplay after ...f5.
notes.teaches: When you have a lasting advantage, do not rush to force exchanges or create weaknesses. Slowly improve your position, and let the opponent's weaknesses (like the h6-pawn) become more significant over time.
notes.plans: White will continue to improve the king and pieces, maintaining pressure on the queenside and the h6-pawn, while Black remains passive and without counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's f6 advance is no longer possible, leaving h6 as a chronic weakness and the queenside precarious. White's king on d3 is well placed to support slow improvement.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has no counterplay, you can improve your position patiently without rushing exchanges.
notes.plans: White should slowly improve piece placement, keep pressure on h6, and avoid unnecessary exchanges.

notes.explains: White repeats moves to gain time on the clock while maintaining the attack. Black's h5 weakens the g5 square, allowing the white king to infiltrate.
notes.teaches: Repeating moves is a classic technique to gain time when you have an ongoing attack.
notes.plans: White brings the king to g5, preparing a decisive attack, possibly leading to checkmate.

notes.explains: In this position, White's king can march to h6 to support a mating attack, and Black has no reasonable way to prevent it. The king's participation is decisive despite few pieces remaining.
notes.teaches: In endgames with few pieces, the king can be a powerful attacking piece. Use it to join the attack when the opponent cannot stop it.
notes.plans: White should continue with the king march to h6, then use the rook to create mating threats, such as rook b7-b8.

notes.explains: Black tries to deflect the rook from the second rank with a6, but it's not necessary and White can simply capture. The mating attack persists even after material loss.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, don't be distracted by side issues. Keep the initiative and continue with the most direct threats.
notes.plans: White can capture on a6 and continue with the king march, maintaining the mating net.

notes.explains: Black tries to trade rooks to reach an opposite-colored bishop endgame, which is more defensible. White must decide whether to allow the trade or keep rooks on for the attack.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endings, material imbalances and passed pawns matter more than the bishops themselves. Keeping rooks can preserve winning chances.
notes.plans: White should avoid unnecessary trades and continue pressing with the rook, targeting weaknesses like the e6 pawn.

notes.explains: After a trade, the position becomes an opposite-colored bishop endgame. With no a-pawn, the black bishop on c6 is unassailable, and Black can defend the draw.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, the defender can often hold if the pawns are fixed on the same color as the defender's bishop. Passed pawns on the wrong color may not win.
notes.plans: White should try to create passed pawns on both flanks, but Black can set up a blockade.

notes.explains: When a player is hit with a novelty, the natural human reaction is to trade pieces and head for a safe-looking position, especially one with opposite-colored bishops, because such endgames are often drawish.
notes.teaches: A prepared novelty can be chosen precisely because the 'safe' response is deceptively difficult. The defender's instinct to simplify can walk into a worse endgame where the opponent's bishop is unassailable.

notes.explains: A move like Rh3 creates a concrete threat, making it more practical in human games than a computer-generated move that only offers a subtle edge.
notes.teaches: When preparing an opening, prioritize moves that create immediate threats and force the opponent to solve problems, as they are more effective in practice than engine-only ideas.

notes.explains: The prepared position with opposite-colored bishops is extremely deceptive: it looks safe for black, but in reality it is very dangerous, and the defender must navigate it precisely.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, material is not the only factor; the activity and safety of the bishops matter enormously. A seemingly equal position can be winning for the side with the more active bishop.

notes.explains: The novelties in this opening all tie into the same thematic idea: exploiting the dark squares and creating direct threats there.
notes.teaches: When preparing an opening, look for a unifying theme (like dark-square control) and choose novelties that reinforce that theme, making the preparation coherent and easier to remember.

notes.explains: In this endgame, material is equal, but white's king on f3 is much more active than black's king on g8. The black king is not weak because it cannot be attacked effectively with so few pieces on the board; it is simply less active. White's king has several tempos over black's, which is a significant advantage.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, king activity is a crucial factor. A king that is centralized and active can support pawns and restrict the opponent's pieces, while a passive king can be a long-term liability.
notes.plans: White should aim to use the active king to penetrate into black's position, possibly targeting weak pawns or supporting a passed pawn. Black should try to activate the king and coordinate pieces to create counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's b7 pawn is a backward pawn, fixed by white's a4 pawn, and cannot advance to become a passed pawn. It must be defended by pieces, not pawns, making it a potential weakness. White's c3 pawn is better protected, and the bishop on d4 has more mobility than black's bishop on c7.
notes.teaches: A backward pawn on an open file is a structural weakness because it cannot be supported by other pawns and often requires piece defense. Pawn islands are not the only factor; the quality of pawns and their protection matter.
notes.plans: White should pressure the b7 pawn and exploit the better bishop mobility. Black must defend the weakness carefully and seek active piece play to compensate.

notes.explains: The position is close to equal, but white has practical winning chances due to small advantages: better king, better bishop, and a potentially weak black pawn. These factors accumulate if black does not play precisely.
notes.teaches: In endgames, small advantages can be accumulated and converted into a win if the opponent is not accurate. It is important to identify and press on the opponent's weaknesses while improving your own pieces.
notes.plans: White should play actively, improving piece placement and creating threats. Black should aim for solid defense and active counterplay to neutralize white's advantages.

notes.explains: A backwards pawn on b7 is a permanent weakness because it cannot be supported by another pawn and must be defended by pieces, tying them down. The bishop on d4 is more active than the one on c7, which has limited mobility.
notes.teaches: In same-colored bishop endgames, small positional factors like a backwards pawn and a better bishop accumulate into a decisive advantage if the defender does not find active play.
notes.plans: The side with the advantage should increase pressure on the weak pawn and improve piece activity, while the defender must seek counterplay.

notes.explains: With bishops of the same color, pawns should generally be placed on the opposite color of the bishops to avoid being attacked by the enemy bishop. Here, with rooks on the board, the rule is more flexible but still relevant.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, put your pawns on the opposite color of the bishops to reduce their vulnerability.
notes.plans: When deciding pawn moves, consider the bishop color complex and how pawn placement affects both defense and control of key squares.

notes.explains: Black's move h5 is natural because it prevents White from playing g4, which would gain space and control on the kingside. If White plays g4 anyway, Black can trade pawns, which is fine. This move restricts White's plans and is a typical prophylactic idea.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a pawn move like h5 can be a key prophylactic resource to stop the opponent from gaining space with a pawn advance like g4.
notes.plans: Black should consider h5 to limit White's kingside space and keep the position solid.

notes.explains: After Black played b6, the bishop on c7 became tied to defending the b6 pawn, reducing its activity. White then played Rb1 to pressure the pawn, and Black's indirect defense via Rc8 is insufficient because if the pawn falls, the resulting rook vs bishop and pawns endgame is not winning for Black—the pawns will drop later.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is weak, tying a piece to its defense can leave that piece passive. In rook endgames, giving up the exchange for two pawns is often not enough if the remaining pawns are weak and the opponent's rook is active.
notes.plans: White should continue to increase pressure on the weak pawn and improve the rook's activity, while Black must find a way to activate the bishop and avoid further weaknesses.

notes.explains: White's rook on e4 is a strong centralizing move. It controls key squares and prepares to double rooks or invade. Trading rooks with Rb5 might be less effective because Black's rook can go to e6, protecting the pawn and cutting off the king, giving Black active defense.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, centralizing the rook and avoiding unnecessary trades that give the opponent active counterplay is often the best way to convert an advantage.
notes.plans: White should keep rooks on and use the active rook to penetrate Black's position, while maintaining pressure on the weak pawns.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the rook on e4 is strong because it protects the pawns and keeps the enemy king out. Trading rooks would let the white king penetrate and win the pawns, so Black avoids it.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, keep rooks on the board when your king is closer and your pawns are protected; trading can turn a win into a draw.
notes.plans: White can double rooks on the file or bring the king over, while keeping the rook active on e4.

notes.explains: After Black plays f5, White can trade rooks and then play Rb5, now protected by the e4 pawn. This threatens both b6 and a5, and Black cannot defend both.
notes.teaches: Subtle tactics in endgames matter: a protected rook can create double threats that decide the game.
notes.plans: White should execute the rook maneuver to win a pawn on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's g6 weakens the h6 pawn and the light squares, allowing White's g4 to fix the h6 pawn on the bishop's color. This makes the position nearly lost for Black.
notes.teaches: In endgames, avoid pawn moves that create weaknesses without gaining something; fixed weaknesses on the bishop's color are easy targets.
notes.plans: White should play g4 to fix h6 and then attack it with the bishop and king.

notes.explains: Endgames require alertness and practical play; missing a small tactic can be fatal because there are fewer pieces to compensate.
notes.teaches: Stay focused in endgames and study endgame books to improve technique and avoid blunders.

notes.explains: In the endgame, tactical awareness is crucial. A move like f5 may look tempting but fails due to a tactical refutation. Instead, active rook play can win a pawn by exploiting the split pawns.
notes.teaches: Always calculate tactical lines in the endgame; a seemingly good move may have a hidden refutation. Active pieces can create threats that win material.
notes.plans: Use the rook to infiltrate and attack the weak h6 pawn, while keeping the king safe from counterplay.

notes.explains: The move h4 prepares h5, fixing the h6 pawn on the same color as the bishop. Once the pawn is fixed, White can trade pieces and then win the pawn, leading to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: In endgames with minor pieces, fixing your opponent's pawns on the color of your bishop creates a target. If you have a better pawn structure, you can force trades to reach a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Play h5 to fix the h6 pawn, then trade pieces and go after the pawn. Avoid lines where Black can create counterplay, such as bishop g7 ideas.

notes.explains: In this position, a tactical resource like bishop g7 might be tempting, but it fails because after king takes and rook takes, the bishop can take on h4, leaving an unclear endgame. This is why a move like bishop d7 doesn't work.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a tactical sequence, calculate the resulting endgame carefully. If the outcome is unclear or favorable for the opponent, the tactic is not worth it.
notes.plans: Instead, prefer a solid move like bishop d8, preparing to advance the h-pawn and activate the rook.

notes.explains: After bishop d8, white can continue with h5, and if black takes, rook to e7, then rook to g1, aiming for bishop g7 and later taking on h6. Black defends with rook c6, but white can improve with rook g4, then rook e6, and after rook g8, the king advances, and the other rook comes in, winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong initiative, keep improving your pieces and create threats. The rook lift to g1 is a typical maneuver to attack the king side.
notes.plans: Follow this plan: h5, rook e7, rook g1, bishop g7, and then bring the king up.

notes.explains: In the bishop endgame that arises, white has a winning position because the passed pawn on the a-file is unstoppable. The black bishop only has one long diagonal to stop the pawn, but white can use the king to support the pawn's advance, and the bishop cannot cover both key squares.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, a passed pawn on the edge is often winning if the defending bishop lacks a second diagonal to control the promotion square. The attacking king can help escort the pawn.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn, use the king to support it, and if the bishop tries to block, use the king to chase it away.

notes.explains: After bishop d4 and king f8, white's next step is to play f4, then f5, fixing the pawns on the opposite color of the bishop. This makes them immune to bishop attacks, and the rook alone cannot capture them.
notes.teaches: In endgames with bishops of opposite colors, place your pawns on the opposite color of your opponent's bishop to protect them from being attacked. This is a key principle for pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play f4, then f5, and continue to gain space and push black back.

notes.explains: In this rook-and-bishop endgame, White has a passed pawn on the g-file. The immediate plan is to activate the rook to g7 or g8 to support the pawn's promotion, while the bishop on e5 and king on d5 coordinate to restrain Black's pieces. This setup gives White a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, prioritize bringing your rook behind it or to the seventh rank to support its advance, and use your king and bishop to control key squares.
notes.plans: Play Rg1, then Rg7 or Rg8, supporting the g-pawn. Keep the bishop on e5 and king on d5 to limit Black's activity.

notes.explains: After trades, the position reduces to a bishop endgame where White has a passed a-pawn. The critical choice is between Bb4 and Bc5. Bc5 allows Bxc5, Kxc5, and then Black's king reaches a8, drawing because the bishop is the wrong color for the a-pawn's promotion square.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, a rook pawn (a- or h-file) is drawn if the bishop cannot control the promotion square. Always check the bishop's color relative to the corner pawn.
notes.plans: Choose Bb4 to keep the bishop on the correct color to support the a-pawn's promotion, avoiding the drawing mechanism.

notes.explains: With a central pawn, the bishop can waste tempos to gain opposition and force the enemy king to the wrong side, allowing your king to penetrate and support the pawn. This is winning, unlike the rook-pawn case.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames with a central pawn, use the bishop to triangulate and gain opposition, forcing the king away and then entering with your own king.
notes.plans: If the pawn is central, maneuver the bishop to lose a tempo when needed, then bring the king to support the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: In the actual game, White played Bb4, then advanced the pawns to c6 and a6, forcing Black's king to a8. The next stage is to bring the king around to support the pawn's promotion, using the bishop to keep Black's king confined.
notes.teaches: Technical endgames often proceed in stages: first secure the pawns and confine the enemy king, then bring your king to assist the pawn. Knowing these stages prevents converting a win into a draw.
notes.plans: After pushing the king to a8, bring your king to c4, then to a5, and use the bishop to maintain the confinement while the king approaches the pawn.

notes.explains: In a bishop-and-pawn endgame, the winning method is to bring the king around to support the pawn while the bishop guards the queening square from a safe diagonal. The key is to avoid pushing the pawn too early, as that allows the defender to sacrifice the bishop and force stalemate.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, first improve your king's position and use the bishop to control the promotion square. Do not rush the pawn push; a premature advance can throw away the win.
notes.plans: March the king toward the pawn's queening square, use the bishop to cover the promotion square from a long diagonal, and only push the pawn when the king is ready to support it.

notes.explains: Technical endgames are those where the result is theoretically known and the winning or drawing method can be memorized, such as rook and pawn versus rook. Practical endgames are less forced and require general principles and pawn-structure understanding.
notes.teaches: Study technical endgames thoroughly so you can execute the correct technique under time pressure. Practice them against a computer to internalize the method.

notes.explains: In equal endgames, playing passively to secure a draw gives the opponent chances to seize the initiative. Active moves keep the opponent under pressure and may induce mistakes.
notes.teaches: Do not play for a draw in equal endgames; play actively and try to win. If you are inferior, then it is correct to aim for a draw, but otherwise keep creating problems for the opponent.
notes.plans: Look for active king moves, piece activity, and pawn breaks to maintain pressure and avoid passive defense.

notes.explains: In equal endgames, players often aim for a draw and play passively, which can lead to missed opportunities and giving the opponent chances.
notes.teaches: Keep making active moves in endgames to pressure the opponent and induce mistakes, even against higher-rated players.
notes.plans: Look for ways to improve piece activity and create threats, rather than simplifying to a draw.

notes.explains: Planning in chess can feel intimidating, but it is not always necessary to have a grand, long-term plan. Sometimes the best approach is to focus on improving your pieces and placing them on their best squares, which naturally leads to good play.
notes.teaches: You do not need a detailed long-term plan to win; instead, make short-term, flexible improvements to your position, adapting as the game evolves.

notes.explains: In the second puzzle, it is black to move, and the position should be assessed by noting what is good and bad. The bishop is not well placed, and there are other imbalances to consider.
notes.teaches: Before choosing a plan, take a moment to evaluate the position: identify strong and weak pieces, pawn structure, and potential targets. This helps form a short-term plan.

notes.explains: Before choosing a plan, take a few minutes to survey the position: identify which pieces are poorly placed, which squares are weak, and what the opponent is trying to do.
notes.teaches: Always start by evaluating the position: note bad pieces, weak squares, and the opponent's intentions before deciding on a plan.

notes.explains: In this closed position, both sides have poorly placed bishops, and black's d6 pawn is weak. White's rooks are not connected, and white may aim for an outpost on d5 or a pawn break with f4.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, piece activity and outposts matter more than material; look for squares where your pieces can be improved and where the opponent's pieces are restricted.
notes.plans: Black should consider improving the bad bishop and finding a better square for the knight, while also addressing the weak d6 pawn and potentially preventing white's f4 break.

notes.explains: The bishop on h6 is powerful because it not only prevents f4 but also stops the knight from going to e3, which would control the d5 outpost. If the knight cannot reach d5, the outpost remains unused.
notes.teaches: A piece can be well-placed not just for its own activity but also for the squares it controls, denying the opponent key outposts.
notes.plans: Black should consider playing ...Bf8-h6 to control the e3 square and thereby limit white's knight from reaching d5, while also preparing to transfer the bishop to a better diagonal.

notes.explains: When considering moves, it's important to come up with at least two candidate moves, even if you have a strong preference for one. This avoids tunnel vision and ensures you consider alternatives.
notes.teaches: Always generate multiple candidate moves before deciding, to keep an open mind and avoid missing better options.

notes.explains: When evaluating a position, don't rush to judge who is better; instead, focus on finding the best plan for your side. Here, black's rooks cannot easily double, and the position may be more comfortable than it appears.
notes.teaches: In positional play, prioritize identifying the best idea for your position over arguing about the evaluation.
notes.plans: Consider transferring the knight to f4, doubling rooks, or advancing pawns to create pressure and restrict the opponent.

notes.explains: The move e6 is strong because it addresses two problems at once: it frees a square for the knight and gives the bishop a target if the pawn is taken. However, it is not immediately problematic because the pawn is hanging, but the resulting position is very comfortable for white.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that improve multiple pieces simultaneously, such as freeing a square for a knight and creating a target for a bishop.
notes.plans: After e6, if the pawn is taken, the bishop recaptures with pressure; otherwise, the knight can use the freed square, and the bishop may become dangerous.

notes.explains: In this position, white has a material advantage (queen up, rook down), so there is no rush to find the best move. The habit of searching for the best move can be replaced by calmly assessing the position and considering piece improvements.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, take your time and look for the most active placement of your pieces rather than forcing tactics.
notes.plans: Consider moves like c4 to activate the bishop, or e6 to free the knight, and evaluate whether opening files is beneficial.

notes.explains: The move c4 is a candidate because it activates the bishop and, if the opponent takes, the bishop recaptures and puts pressure on the file with the rook. However, if the opponent doesn't take, the move may not accomplish much.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn break, think about what happens if the opponent accepts or declines, and whether the resulting open file is actually good for you.
notes.plans: If c4 is played and taken, the bishop recaptures and the rook adds pressure; if not, the pawn may just create weaknesses.

notes.explains: In a comfortable position, even if the advantage is not yet decisive, there may be no better move than a quiet but purposeful one. Moves that merely develop a piece or improve a pawn without a concrete idea do not really accomplish anything.
notes.teaches: Every move should have a short-term plan or a real reason behind it. Avoid aimless moves that just look natural but lack a clear purpose.

notes.explains: Before choosing a move, take in the whole position: evaluate material balance, identify which pieces are good or bad, and notice weaknesses. In the given position, key observations include a weak pawn on d6, a potentially weak pawn on b2, a shaky bishop, a knight stuck defending a bishop, and a rook on an open file.
notes.teaches: Start your thinking process by assessing the position globally: material, piece activity, and weaknesses. Notice what captures your attention before diving into specific moves.

notes.explains: A tactical idea like capturing on d6 may look appealing, but when you try to calculate the continuation, the opponent has resources to neutralize it. For example, after captures, the opponent can defend or counterattack, and the initiative fades.
notes.teaches: Do not rely on intuition alone; support it with concrete calculation. If you cannot find a clear continuation that justifies your idea, set it aside and look for another plan. Later analysis can reveal if your intuition was correct but missed a resource.
notes.plans: If the capture on d6 does not lead to a clear advantage, consider other plans such as improving piece activity, targeting the weak d6 pawn with more pressure, or exploiting the open file.

notes.explains: Intuition can point to a promising idea, but the idea only becomes playable once calculation confirms it leads to a concrete advantage or at least a safe outcome. A flashy move that cannot be backed by a clear follow-up is not worth playing.
notes.teaches: Blindly following instinct or sacrificing material without verifying the end goal will not improve your chess in the long run. Always calculate the critical lines before committing.

notes.explains: In the referenced game, a knight on the rim (or a poorly placed knight) becomes a long-term liability. The side with the better minor piece can use it to dominate key squares and coordinate an attack, while the opponent's piece remains passive.
notes.teaches: A badly placed piece is a permanent weakness. Use your active pieces to restrict the opponent's bad piece and then exploit the extra freedom to build an attack.
notes.plans: Keep the opponent's knight out of the game by controlling its escape squares, then transfer your own knight to a strong outpost and target weaknesses like f7.

notes.explains: When the opponent's pieces are tied down and one piece is completely out of play, even equal material can feel like a decisive advantage. The active side can slowly improve, push a passed pawn, and create threats that the opponent cannot meet.
notes.teaches: Material equality is not the only measure of a position. Piece activity and coordination matter more; if you can keep the opponent's pieces passive, you can convert a static advantage into a win.
notes.plans: Improve your pieces to their best squares, advance a passed pawn, and force the opponent to defend while you keep creating new threats.

notes.explains: In the discussed position, the knight on the edge is badly placed, making all the light pieces for the side with the good knight effective. The key is to exploit the opponent's misplaced pieces rather than rushing into tactics.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a badly placed piece, your pieces gain relative value. Use that advantage by creating threats that force the opponent to keep the bad piece out of play.
notes.plans: Look for ways to attack the weak knight or its supporting squares, while keeping your own pieces active and coordinated.

notes.explains: In the exchange sacrifice line, the key move is to place the queen on a1, a quiet but powerful move that creates multiple threats. This forces the opponent to either retreat the knight or lose a pawn, and after the bishop comes to f4, the opponent's pieces become completely passive.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move in a tactical sequence is a quiet one that improves your position or creates a decisive threat. Look for moves that force the opponent to choose between two bad options.
notes.plans: After the queen goes to a1, follow up with the bishop to f4, maintaining pressure and preventing the opponent from developing their knight.

notes.explains: When solving a position, it's important to first take in the whole board and assess what is beautiful and what is horrible before calculating moves. In a real game, you arrive at a position gradually, so you already have context; in puzzles, you must build that context from scratch.
notes.teaches: Before calculating, pause to evaluate the position: identify strengths, weaknesses, and imbalances. This helps you form a plan and avoid jumping into random moves.

notes.explains: In the puzzle position, both kings are weak, but the white king is currently protected by a knight on f5 that defends the f2 pawn. The question is how long that knight can maintain its defensive role.
notes.teaches: When a piece is overloaded with defensive duties, look for ways to deflect it or undermine its support. The weakness of a king is often relative to the defender's ability to hold.
notes.plans: Consider moves that challenge the knight on f5 or create threats that force it away, exposing the white king.

notes.explains: Both kings are exposed, but the black king is the weaker one because it lacks a defender like the knight on f2 that shields the white king. The knight is currently holding the white position together by guarding f2, but it may not be able to do so forever.
notes.teaches: When both kings are vulnerable, compare the quality of their defenders. A piece that is tied to defense can become a liability if it is overloaded or can be driven away.
notes.plans: Look for ways to undermine the defender of the enemy king, perhaps by attacking the knight or creating threats that force it to move.

notes.explains: The knight on f2 is doing a great job defending the white king, but it is not doing much else. The question is whether to keep it there or reshuffle it to a better square, but moving it would expose f2.
notes.teaches: A piece that is purely defensive may be misplaced if it can be improved without compromising the king's safety. Evaluate whether the defensive duty is truly necessary or if the king can be made safe by other means.
notes.plans: Consider moves like h4 or knight e3 to improve the knight's activity, but only after ensuring the king's safety is not compromised.

notes.explains: In the game, White played queen c5, which led to a strong knight e3 by Black, kicking the queen and creating threats. After the pawn takes f3, the white king becomes very weak, and Black gets a powerful knight on f6. The position becomes unclear, but White has better options.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a dangerous piece that can be kicked, be wary of moves that allow it to jump into a strong outpost. Sometimes it is better to prevent the opponent's idea rather than to try to refute it later.
notes.plans: Instead of queen c5, consider king g1, which is a prophylactic move that prevents the knight from landing on f6 with tempo and keeps the king safer.

notes.explains: After the prophylactic king g1, Black's position is not so clear. If Black tries f5, White has a strong knight f6 move, which is forcing and leads to a powerful attack. Even though White is a piece down, the black king is so weak that White is winning.
notes.teaches: A king that is exposed and lacks defenders can be more valuable than material. When you have a lead in attack, forcing moves can create mating threats that outweigh a material deficit.
notes.plans: If Black plays f5, White can play knight f6, then follow up with rook g6 and queen d6, creating unstoppable mating threats. The key is to keep the initiative and not allow the opponent to consolidate.

notes.explains: Queen h5 is a natural active move, but it allows Black to play e3, which is a strong resource. After e3, White is in trouble because the knight can be kicked and the king becomes weak. The problem is that White often sees such moves but does not take them seriously enough.
notes.teaches: When you see a strong move for the opponent, do not dismiss it just because it looks scary. Take concrete measures to prevent it, even if it means playing a quieter move first.
notes.plans: Instead of queen h5, prefer a move like king g1 that prevents the opponent's key resource, even if it seems less active. This is a common pattern: prophylaxis before launching an attack.

notes.explains: The position is tense because the opponent can play e3, which is a strong move. The player must decide whether to take or avoid it, and there is a plan to play for a win with queen h5.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong move like e3, you don't have to react immediately; you can make a preparatory move like king g1 to stop it, then proceed with your own plan.
notes.plans: Consider playing king g1 to prevent e3, then continue with queen h5 and capture on the next move.

notes.explains: In this position, black has weaknesses: bad bishops, a weak g3 pawn, and a weak square. White has a passed b5 pawn that is a threat. Black must find a plan despite the unpleasant position.
notes.teaches: When your position is worse, focus on improving your worst piece. Identify the piece that can improve dramatically and reroute it to a better square.
notes.plans: Reroute the bishop to a better diagonal, possibly trading light-square pieces, and consider pushing d5 to activate pawns.

notes.explains: The idea of sacrificing a piece to open files is tempting, but without enough pieces to support the attack, it's not practical. The material investment is too high for the return.
notes.teaches: Before sacrificing material, ensure you have enough pieces to create a decisive attack. If the attack lacks support, the sacrifice is likely unsound.

notes.explains: In this position, the light-squared bishop on c8 is bad, and the pawn structure is fluid. Trading light-squared pieces and pushing d5 could make the pawns strong, but it's unclear how the structure will turn out. The open file and potential pins after trades add dynamic possibilities.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed, look for ways to improve it, even with a modest move like bishop c8. Improving a bad piece is often the best practical try, regardless of whether the position is objectively better or worse.
notes.plans: Consider moves that activate the bad bishop, such as bishop c8, and be ready to trade pieces to exploit open files and create pins.

notes.explains: After black's bishop c8, white's best response is queen f2, which preemptively addresses the threat of bishop takes h4 and the resulting pins. Moving the queen away immediately denies black the momentum of a tactical strike.
notes.teaches: When you anticipate a tactical threat, the best move is often to remove the target immediately, not give the opponent the chance to execute it. Prophylactic moves can be the strongest.
notes.plans: White should play queen f2 to avoid the pin and maintain control, then continue developing while keeping an eye on black's counterplay.

notes.explains: After the sequence with queen f2, bishop b7, and rook takes on h2, black plays d5 to eliminate the weakness and potentially create a passed pawn pair. If white captures, black recaptures and gets strong pawns; if white doesn't, black's pawns remain healthy.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn weakness, look for a move that either eliminates it or transforms the structure to your advantage. A pawn break like d5 can be a key resource to improve your position.
notes.plans: Black should play d5, aiming to either create a passed pawn pair or force white to ruin their own pawn structure.

notes.explains: When asked for a plan and feeling clueless, the pressure to find a brilliant long-term idea is self-imposed. Practical play rewards modest, incremental improvements over grand schemes.
notes.teaches: Break the game down into small, concrete improvements — one step at a time. You don't need a deep, distant plan; just find the next small thing that makes your position better.

notes.explains: Positional play can be approached from different angles, such as focusing on piece activity and small advantages rather than only long-term pawn structures.
notes.teaches: Study positional play from multiple perspectives to deepen understanding — for example, thinking about piece placement and short-term maneuvers.

notes.explains: In this symmetrical English structure, the pawn structure dictates the plans. The bishop is well placed, the knight may be kicked away, and the f4 push is a key idea to support the center and kingside play.
notes.teaches: When facing a symmetrical opening, look for pawn breaks like f4 to create imbalances and target the opponent's weaknesses.
notes.plans: Develop pieces harmoniously, aim for f4, and be ready to respond to the opponent's breaks like b5.

notes.explains: Playing a4 to stop b5 is a drastic pawn move that permanently changes the position and gives the opponent a strong outpost on b4 or similar. This is a long-term commitment that may not be worth it if the game is focused on the center and kingside.
notes.teaches: Avoid irreversible pawn moves that weaken your structure or give the opponent outposts unless they clearly serve your long-term plan.
notes.plans: Instead of a4, consider moves that support central and kingside play, like g3 and f4, to build an attack.

notes.explains: After the opponent's knight is placed, you have multiple options: pushing pawns, kicking the knight, or developing pieces. The choice depends on the specific position and your overall plan.
notes.teaches: In middlegame positions, evaluate candidate moves based on how they improve your position and align with your strategic goals.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Qf3, Qg3, or Bd2, each with different ideas, and choose the one that best supports your central and kingside ambitions.

notes.explains: The queen can go to f3, g3, or g4, each with different intentions. The queen on f3 is a 'silent killer' because it supports a pawn break on d4 and keeps an eye on the queenside, while also preparing potential kingside expansion.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for the queen, consider not only immediate threats but also how it supports future pawn breaks and controls key squares on both wings.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to d2, then decide on the queenside plan, possibly with b5, while keeping the option of f5 or h4 later.

notes.explains: A knight move to e2 and then to g3 might look attacking, but it is inaccurate because the opponent can play Bc5, pinning the knight and leaving it vulnerable to attack.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a seemingly aggressive maneuver, check if the opponent can refute it with a pin or other tactical resource.

notes.explains: The move h4 is not yet justified because the position is not ready for it; it could become relevant later, but playing it now would be premature.
notes.teaches: Timing is crucial for pawn storms; only start them when the position is ripe, otherwise you weaken your own king or waste tempo.

notes.explains: After the opponent plays Bc5, the bishop on d2 is strong because it is not on its final diagonal but can be repositioned later; it also helps provoke the opponent to remove the knight, keeping flexibility.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move that seems passive is actually flexible, keeping multiple plans alive and forcing the opponent to commit first.
notes.plans: Keep the position flexible, avoid premature pawn moves like f5, and wait for the right moment to commit to a plan.

notes.explains: Black's king move to h8 is a useful preparatory move, allowing for a future ...Qc7 and ...f5, and it also gets the king off the open file.
notes.teaches: King moves in the middlegame can be prophylactic, preparing for pawn advances and improving the king's safety before launching an attack.
notes.plans: Black plans to play ...Qc7 and ...f5, while White should continue developing and maintain pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: In this position, black has just played f5 to relieve pressure, but white has not committed to either f5 or e5. This creates a psychological burden on black, who must constantly calculate the consequences of white's possible pushes.
notes.teaches: Keeping tension in the position can be a psychological weapon; the opponent has to keep re-evaluating, which can lead to impatience and mistakes.
notes.plans: White should consider maintaining the tension by not immediately resolving the central pawn structure, forcing black to handle the pressure.

notes.explains: If white plays e5, it weakens the d5 square and gives black the a8-h1 diagonal, which could become problematic for white's bishop.
notes.teaches: Before pushing a pawn, consider the long-term weaknesses and the opponent's counterplay, especially open diagonals.
notes.plans: Avoid e5 for now; instead, consider moves that keep the tension and improve piece activity.

notes.explains: Rook to e1 is a useful move because it keeps the option of taking on f5 while also supporting the e4 pawn. If black takes on e4, white can recapture with the pawn and then push f5.
notes.teaches: Place rooks on open or semi-open files where they can support pawn breaks and maintain flexibility.
notes.plans: Play Re1, keeping the tension and preparing for potential captures on e4 or f5.

notes.explains: After the opponent declines to take on e4, the position offers White a choice between recapturing with the pawn or the knight. Taking with the knight places it on e4, where it eyes f5, g5, and h7, and also pressures the weak e6 pawn. The pawn recapture keeps the center solid and prepares a quick f5 push, opening the bishop's diagonal.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice of recaptures, weigh the activity of the piece versus the solidity of the pawn structure. A knight on an advanced outpost can be worth more than a doubled pawn or a slightly looser center.
notes.plans: If recapturing with the knight, follow up with ideas like f5, g5, or targeting h7. If recapturing with the pawn, prepare f5 to open lines for the bishop.

notes.explains: The move Rc1 (or Rook to c1) is a quiet but purposeful move. It doesn't create an immediate threat, but it prepares to double rooks on the c-file or potentially bring the bishop to the kingside. It's a flexible move that improves the position without committing to a concrete plan.
notes.teaches: Not every good move must be aggressive. Sometimes a 'prophylactic' or 'improving' move that prepares multiple ideas is the most effective, especially when the opponent has no immediate threats.
notes.plans: After Rc1, White can double rooks on the c-file, or later play Bc1 and Bh6 to increase pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: White's position has several advantages: a strong bishop on c4, a potential target on d4 (the black pawn is somewhat isolated from the rest of Black's pieces), and the possibility of an attack on the kingside because Black's king is somewhat exposed. Black's queen on c7 is a natural developing move but also a 'sad point' because it can become a target.
notes.teaches: When assessing a position, look for concrete advantages: weak pawns, strong pieces, open files, and king safety. Even if the material is equal, these factors can justify a plan.
notes.plans: White can aim to increase pressure on the d4 pawn, use the bishop on c4 to support a kingside attack, and potentially exploit the queen's placement on c7.

notes.explains: Black's development is awkward: Queen e8 is impossible due to a pawn, and Queen f6 would be a blunder. Thus, Queen c7 is the only natural way to develop the queen, even though it may become a target. This shows that Black is under pressure and has limited good options.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are short on good squares, their 'natural' moves may come with drawbacks. Recognize when the opponent's development is constrained and look for ways to exploit the resulting weaknesses.
notes.plans: White can continue to improve piece placement, perhaps preparing to attack the queen on c7 or to increase pressure on the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: White's advantage is real but fleeting: the open rook file, active bishop, and space edge can evaporate if Black gets two quiet moves like ...Bd7 and ...Re8, turning White's edge into an 'imaginary' one.
notes.teaches: Assess a position dynamically: a static advantage is only meaningful if it can be converted before the opponent consolidates.
notes.plans: White should seek an energetic continuation to exploit the initiative before Black reorganizes.

notes.explains: Taking on f5 with the pawn is tempting but allows Black to use the e-file and the d5 square; the knight on g3 is poorly placed and needs redeployment.
notes.teaches: When a piece is badly placed, consider a multi-move maneuver to a better square, even if it costs time, because the improved piece activity is worth it.
notes.plans: White should play Nh1 and then Nf2-g4-g5, aiming at the weaknesses on h7 and f7.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches g5, Black's king is under pressure; if Black plays ...Bd7, White can continue with Re1, and Black's ...Re8 is bad because White can exchange rooks and then play Qd5, targeting the weak king.
notes.teaches: When attacking, keep pieces coordinated and be ready to exploit open files and weak squares around the enemy king; a simple plan like Qd5 can be decisive.
notes.plans: White should proceed with the knight maneuver to g5, then double on the e-file and use the queen to penetrate.

notes.explains: In this position, the queen on d5 is the strongest move because it directly threatens mate and keeps the initiative. The rook to e8 is weaker because it allows exchanges that reduce attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you have a direct mating threat, prioritize it over slower positional moves. Look for the most forcing and simple continuation.
notes.plans: Play Qd5, then follow up by capturing weak pawns and preparing to bring the bishop to c3 to increase pressure on the weakened kingside.

notes.explains: The move h6 by Black is flawed because it does not address the underlying weakness of the g6 square. White can still play Qg6, and if the pawn on g5 is taken, Qxg5 leads to a mating attack.
notes.teaches: A pawn move like h6 does not eliminate the weakness of the square it was meant to defend; the square itself remains vulnerable. Always check if the opponent's defensive move actually covers the key squares.
notes.plans: If Black plays h6, White should respond with Qg6, threatening mate. If Black captures on g5, White recaptures with the queen and continues the attack.

notes.explains: After Black plays g6 to prevent Qg6, White must find a new plan. The immediate Qg6 is no longer possible, so White should look for other checks, captures, and threats. The move Bxf4 is undesirable because it allows the black queen to re-enter the game actively.
notes.teaches: When your primary plan is blocked, scan for alternative forcing moves: checks, captures, and threats. Avoid moves that bring the opponent's pieces back to life, even if they win material.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Rfe1 or other rook lifts to maintain pressure, while keeping the queen active and preventing Black from consolidating.

notes.explains: The move Bf4 is interesting because it creates threats that force Black to respond. If Black moves the rook, White can play Rae1, and if Black blocks with Bd6, White has Qg6, leading to a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece sacrifice or a move that seems to lose material can be strong if it creates unavoidable threats. Always consider moves that force the opponent to react to your attack.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, and after Black's response, continue with the rook to e1 or the queen to g6 to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In this position, White's queen on g5 gives Black chances to slip away, so a quieter move like Bf4 is preferred. If Black doesn't move the rook, White can play Rae1, and if Black blocks with Bd6, then Qg6 wins the queen.
notes.teaches: When your queen is aggressively placed, consider whether it gives the opponent counterplay. Sometimes a quieter piece move maintains pressure while avoiding tactical complications.
notes.plans: Develop the rook to e1 and keep the queen centralized, ready to exploit any weakness on the g-file.

notes.explains: After Black plays h6, White's options are limited to Qh4 or Qh6. Qh6 allows Qg7, which lets the queen infiltrate the king's position, so Qh4 is preferred to keep the queen active without allowing that.
notes.teaches: When choosing between queen moves, consider not only your own threats but also the opponent's possible defensive resources. A move that allows the enemy queen to enter your position can be problematic.
notes.plans: Play Qh4 to maintain pressure and avoid the queen infiltration on g7.

notes.explains: There is a tactical trick: if Black plays Re8, White can capture on f6 and then play Qh6, threatening the rook on e8 and the knight. If the queen goes to g7, White picks up the rook.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical motifs where a queen can fork pieces or where a discovered attack can win material. Even if the opponent defends, you may gain a piece.
notes.plans: If Black plays Re8, capture on f6 and then Qh6, creating threats against the rook and knight.

notes.explains: After Black plays Kg7 to defend against Qh6, White's knight is better on h3 than g3 because it protects the f4 pawn and gives the queen room to regroup. The knight on h3 also supports the idea of removing the d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Knight placement should be flexible: a knight on the edge can be useful for defense and for freeing squares for other pieces, especially when it supports central pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Consider moving the knight to h3 to protect f4 and allow the queen to reposition, then aim to open the center for the bishop.

notes.explains: Black has two ways to defend the d4 pawn: Qb6 or Nf6. Qb6 is passive, just defending without creating threats. If Black loses the d4 pawn, the game is essentially over because White's bishops become dominant.
notes.teaches: When defending a key pawn, prefer moves that also create counterplay. Passive defense can allow the opponent to build up pressure and win the pawn anyway.
notes.plans: If Black defends passively, continue to increase pressure on d4 with moves like Bc3 or Qb6, and be ready to exploit any inaccuracies.

notes.explains: White is attacking the d4 pawn and should bring more pieces to bear. Bc3 is a strong move, but Bc5 is also possible. If Black plays Bc5, White can capture on d4 and then Qd4, picking up the bishop. Also, Qb6 is a good idea, but Black must be careful because Bc3 and Bc5 are both strong.
notes.teaches: When attacking a pawn, coordinate your pieces to increase pressure. Look for moves that also create additional threats, such as attacking other pieces or squares.
notes.plans: Play Bc3 to increase pressure on d4, and if Black defends with Bc5, capture on d4 and then Qd4 to win the bishop.

notes.explains: If Black plays Qb6, White has several ideas, including Bc3, Bc5, and Qd4. If Black plays Bc5, White can play b4, forcing the bishop to e6, where it becomes passive and only defends the d4 pawn. The bishop was much more active on d6.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece is active, consider forcing it to a worse square. A bishop that is reduced to defending a pawn is often a sign of a positional advantage.
notes.plans: If Black plays Qb6, consider b4 to drive the bishop away, or Bc3 to maintain pressure on d4.

notes.explains: The bishop on b6 is passive compared to its previous post on d6, where it defended key squares like e7 and f5. Its retreat has weakened Black's kingside and left the queen as the main defender.
notes.teaches: A piece's activity is measured by the squares it controls and the defensive duties it fulfills; a retreat to a 'safe' square can leave other pieces overburdened.
notes.plans: White should exploit the bishop's passivity by targeting the weakened kingside, especially the h7 square.

notes.explains: The queen can be reactivated with Qh5, which has a direct impact on the kingside, attacking h7 and supporting the advance g5. This is more direct than other moves like Qe1, which are also interesting but less aggressive.
notes.teaches: When choosing between candidate moves, prioritize those that create immediate threats or improve your attacking potential, even if other moves are also good.
notes.plans: Play Qh5, preparing g5 to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: After Qh5, Black's rook on e8 is a target. White wants to place a rook on the seventh rank, but if Black plays Re8, White can consider g5, attacking h7. However, Black can respond with h6, so the best move is Rxe5, exploiting the weakness of the e5 pawn because Black cannot recapture due to the exposed king.
notes.teaches: When a king is exposed, tactical motifs like pins and discovered attacks become more potent; a piece that appears defended may be vulnerable because the defender is tied to the king.
notes.plans: Play Rxe5, winning a pawn and maintaining the attack, as Black's recapture is impossible due to the king's safety.

notes.explains: After the queen returns to attack d4 and forces the bishop to b6, White's pieces are optimally placed. The knight on g5 is finally achieved, attacking the queen and the h7 bishop, forcing Black's king to g8.
notes.teaches: Patience in maneuvering pieces to their ideal squares can create decisive threats; a well-timed knight jump can be the culmination of a long-term plan.
notes.plans: With the knight on g5, continue the attack by exchanging rooks and bringing the queen back to e1, preparing to activate the bishop on d2.

notes.explains: The bishop on d2 is still inactive, but White has a choice: either find a way to activate it on the long diagonal, or play safely by picking up material, like the bishop on b6, which is a risk-free way to win.
notes.teaches: When an attack is not fully conclusive, converting to a material advantage is a practical and safe way to win; you don't always need the most spectacular move.
notes.plans: If the bishop cannot be activated, capture the b6 bishop and simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: In this winning position, the opponent is down material and trying to prolong the game with moves like ...Qg7. The attacking side has a clear material advantage and can either force mate or simplify to a won endgame.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, the safest and most efficient way to convert is to take the free material and simplify, avoiding unnecessary complications that could allow counterplay.
notes.plans: Take the offered piece, then consolidate by relocating the knight to a strong square like c4, protecting pawns, and exchanging pieces to reach a technically winning endgame.

notes.explains: The move g6 is a powerful idea because it puts pressure on the opponent's king and threatens mate, while also restricting the enemy bishop's activity. It creates a mating net and makes the win much easier.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, look for moves that increase the pressure and create direct threats, such as mating threats, rather than just grabbing material. A move like g6 can be decisive because it limits the defender's options.
notes.plans: After g6, if the opponent tries to defend with ...h5, bring the bishop to the other diagonal to maintain the attack. The threat of mate on g7 forces the opponent to defend passively.

notes.explains: The opponent's king is exposed and under pressure. Moves like ...h5 are attempts to create luft, but they don't solve the fundamental problems of being down material and facing a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When your king is in danger, creating luft can be necessary, but it is often insufficient if the opponent has a sustained attack. You must also address the material deficit and the opponent's threats.
notes.plans: Continue the attack, using checks and threats to prevent the opponent from consolidating. If the opponent plays ...Bd5, respond with Qf6 to maintain the initiative and increase the pressure.

notes.explains: The speaker notes that the winning side did not need to move the king after castling, and the king remained safe on its original square. This highlights the importance of king safety and the fact that a castled king can often stay put while the attack unfolds.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, you don't need to move your king unnecessarily. Keep it safe and focus on the attack, as long as the king is not in immediate danger.
notes.plans: Maintain the king's safety while continuing to press the attack, using the extra material to force a win.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a material advantage and can simplify by exchanging pieces, which reduces Black's counterplay and makes the win easier to convert.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, aim to exchange pieces, especially the opponent's active ones, to reduce their chances and simplify the position.
notes.plans: Relocate the knight to a strong square like c4, protect the pawns, and then target and capture more pawns to increase the advantage.

notes.explains: White's king remained safe after castling, allowing the rest of the army to go on the offensive without concern.
notes.teaches: Once the king is safe, you can commit fully to an attack or active play, using all your pieces for the initiative.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack against the Sicilian, White often develops the bishop to b5 and aims for a pawn structure with a knight on e7 for Black, which can be annoying for White. The position is fluid and semi-closed, with both sides maneuvering pieces and pawns.
notes.teaches: When facing the Grand Prix Sicilian, it's useful to know typical setups: White's bishop on b5 and Black's knight on e7 are common. Understanding these structures helps in planning.
notes.plans: White should consider developing the knight to g2 and castling short, while Black can aim for pawn pushes and piece maneuvers to gain space.

notes.explains: Botvinnik did not consider the Grand Prix Attack a good opening for White, and he was a master of strategy. Against moves like d6, Black can play e5, and White's king's bishop is blocked, while the d-pawn is not a real weakness because it can be defended by multiple pieces.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, Black's d6 and e5 setup can neutralize White's attacking chances, and the d5 square is not a weakness if it can be adequately defended.
notes.plans: Black can aim for e5, and if White tries to exploit d5, Black can defend it with multiple pieces.

notes.explains: Against e6, Black can develop the bishop, then the knight, and if White plays c3, Black needs to find a good response. This is a known plan in similar positions.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Sicilian, Black should be ready to counter White's central pawn advances with piece play and timely breaks.
notes.plans: Black should look for active piece play and potential pawn breaks to counter White's space advantage.

notes.explains: In this line, if Black plays ...e6, White can develop the bishop, the knight comes out, and Black's knight retreats while White prepares c3. The key is that White has a central pawn majority and Black has a weak d6 pawn, while White's bishop is actively preventing ...d5.
notes.teaches: When you have a central pawn majority and the opponent has a weak pawn, you should aim to keep the pressure and avoid trades that relieve the tension.
notes.plans: White should continue with c3, then d4, and if Black captures, recapture and play e5, establishing a strong center and targeting the weak d6 pawn.

notes.explains: After ...b6, Black intends ...Bb7, but White can play Be3, making the d4 break too strong. If Black plays ...d4, White can capture and then Black's position becomes problematic, giving White a comfortable advantage.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's move seems to prepare a natural development, look for a way to make your central break even stronger, possibly preventing their plan.
notes.plans: White should play Be3 to support d4, and if Black plays ...d4, White takes and maintains a comfortable edge.

notes.explains: In the line with ...d6, Black questions ...b6 because ...Bb7 would allow Be3 and a strong d4. Black instead plays ...d6 to solidify the center and avoid the immediate pressure.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must delay a natural developing move to avoid allowing your opponent's central break, even if it means a more modest setup.
notes.plans: Black should continue with ...d6, keeping the position solid and waiting for the right moment to develop the bishop.

notes.explains: If White plays Nh3, Black can develop the bishop because there is no immediate threat on d4. Black can then castle and play ...d6, which is a viable setup. Even if Black plays ...h6, the position may look strange, but as long as the pieces are active and the king is safe, it's playable.
notes.teaches: Don't judge a position by its appearance; what matters is piece activity and king safety. Even unusual moves can be fine if they meet those criteria.
notes.plans: Black should develop the bishop, castle, and aim for ...d6, maintaining a solid but active setup.

notes.explains: When White plays Be3, Black should consider the best response to counter White's central ideas. The bishop on e3 supports d4 and prevents Black's blockading moves.
notes.teaches: In the opening, it's useful to present multiple lines and agree on the general plans for both sides, so you can understand the typical middlegame structures.
notes.plans: Black should find a move that challenges White's center, possibly by preparing ...d5 or ...c5, while White aims to push d4 and maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In this opening setup, White's knight is placed so that it does not block the c-pawn, allowing for a later c3 to support the center and counter Black's blockading maneuvers. This idea was favored in some classical games.
notes.teaches: When developing pieces, consider whether they block important pawn breaks. Keeping the knight flexible can allow for timely pawn advances like c3.
notes.plans: Develop pieces quickly, aiming for a kingside initiative while maintaining central flexibility.

notes.explains: In one possible middlegame, White played too safely by closing the center prematurely, allowing Black to gain counterplay. The position became complex and Black eventually won.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary pawn advances that close the center if they are not part of a concrete plan. Sometimes it is better to wait and let the opponent commit first.
notes.plans: Maintain tension in the center and only close it when it favors your piece placement.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...d6 and castles, White has a choice between f4 and Be3. If White plays Be3 first, Black can respond with ...Nd4, and after trades, White's knight is misplaced and the f4 push is less effective because Black has strong defense on e5.
notes.teaches: The order of moves matters: playing f4 before Be3 can be stronger because it prevents Black from using ...Nd4 to disrupt White's setup. If the knight is not on the way, White can later play c3 to support the center.
notes.plans: Play f4 immediately to gain space on the kingside and prepare e5, rather than allowing Black to block with ...Nd4.

notes.explains: After White plays f4, Black must respond to the threat of f5. Black should play ...f5 to stop the pawn advance, even if it creates weaknesses, because White's f5 is a serious threat. Delaying with ...e6 or ...e5 would allow White to play f5 anyway.
notes.teaches: When facing a serious pawn threat, it is often necessary to stop it immediately, even if it creates holes. Prophylactic moves like ...f5 can be essential to maintain the balance.
notes.plans: Play ...f5 to block White's pawn, then continue development and castle.

notes.explains: White played g4 as a high-risk gambit, but it is not recommended because Black can simply capture the pawn. After ...fxg4, White's f5 push is not effective because Black can defend.
notes.teaches: Be cautious with aggressive pawn moves like g4; they can be refuted if the opponent can safely capture. Ensure that such gambits are sound before playing them.
notes.plans: Black should accept the pawn if safe, then consolidate and maintain the extra material.

notes.explains: The position features a serious threat on f5 that must be addressed. White's g4 push is a high-risk gambit without a clear justification, and Black can simply capture, leaving White overextended.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn thrust like g4, evaluate whether the gambit is sound; if there's no clear compensation, taking the pawn is often correct.
notes.plans: Black should consider capturing on f5 and then developing the queen, with long castling in mind.

notes.explains: Black must be careful about creating new weaknesses. Taking with the bishop might open up another hole, making the position unnecessarily complicated.
notes.teaches: Avoid captures that create new weaknesses in your own camp; prefer simpler recaptures that maintain solid structure.
notes.plans: Recapture in a way that keeps the position solid, and then proceed with development.

notes.explains: White's decision to push f5 and give up control of e5 seems overambitious. Black can later use the e5 square for a knight, which would be strong.
notes.teaches: Be wary of pawn moves that permanently weaken key central squares; the opponent may exploit them with piece activity.
notes.plans: Black should aim to occupy e5 with a knight, while keeping the position closed if advantageous.

notes.explains: Black has many options, but castling is not safe due to tactics involving the g-pawn. A move like knight f6 is too slow because of the immediate threats.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, prioritize forcing moves that maintain your options, rather than routine development that allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Black should look for a move that either castles safely or creates a threat to keep the castling option alive.

notes.explains: The bishop on d4 idea is appealing, but it's not a simple developing move; it must be timed correctly to avoid allowing the opponent's counterplay.
notes.teaches: Even natural developing moves require precise timing; consider the opponent's possible replies and whether they can disrupt your plans.
notes.plans: Black should choose a move that either secures the king or forces a concession, keeping the pressure on White.

notes.explains: In this position, the tempting h5 or knight moves are flawed because they allow ...g6, which prevents castling and leaves the king stuck in the center. The priority is either to castle or to play a forceful move that keeps the castling option alive.
notes.teaches: When the center is unstable, securing king safety by castling is often more urgent than developing a piece or starting an attack. A move that allows the opponent to close the center and trap your king is strategically risky.
notes.plans: Castle kingside first, then look to activate the knights on active squares like b5 or d5, while being aware of pawn breaks like ...f5 that can expose the king.

notes.explains: The knight on c3 is a persistent thorn in Black's position, so eliminating it by taking on c3 is a key idea, even if it costs time. After the exchange, the problem of the knight's influence is removed, but the queen must be careful not to become misplaced.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a well-placed enemy piece is worth more than material or tempo; removing it can relieve long-term pressure. When exchanging, consider whether your queen can then find a good square, like h5, to create counterplay.
notes.plans: After taking on c3, avoid moves that leave the queen without a future. Consider long castling only after playing c4 to prevent the enemy bishop from dominating the long diagonal.

notes.explains: The bishop on g7 (or the corresponding bishop) is a powerful piece that can dominate the long diagonal. Black must prevent it from becoming active by playing c4, which also prepares long castling. If White plays d4, the knight on f3 is well placed to support the center.
notes.teaches: In positions with opposite-side castling, controlling the long diagonal is often a critical strategic battle. A timely pawn move like c4 can restrict the enemy bishop and create a safe haven for your own king.
notes.plans: Play c4 to stop the bishop's activation, then consider long castling. If White pushes d4, the knight on f3 can maintain a strong central presence.

notes.explains: Playing c4 before the bishop can take the long diagonal prevents the bishop from becoming dominant. If the opponent later pushes d4, the knight on f3 is well placed to handle it.
notes.teaches: Prevent your opponent's bishop from occupying a strong diagonal by using a pawn move that controls the key squares.
notes.plans: After c4, consider castling long if the center remains stable.

notes.explains: When the opponent offers a bishop exchange on d4, taking it can weaken your central pawns and reduce your counterplay. In this position, the exchange leaves the pawns vulnerable and the position passive.
notes.teaches: Before accepting a piece exchange, evaluate how it affects your pawn structure and your potential for active play.
notes.plans: If possible, avoid the exchange and seek active piece play, such as rerouting a knight to a better square.

notes.explains: King placement matters in the endgame. A king on f7 can be more exposed than on d7, especially if enemy rooks are active. The safer king square avoids unnecessary threats.
notes.teaches: In endgames, keep your king on a safer square, away from open files and enemy rook activity.
notes.plans: If the king is on f7, be cautious about rook checks and consider moving it to a more sheltered spot.

notes.explains: A knight that is poorly placed, like on e6, can be described as 'biting on granite'—it attacks nothing and has no influence. Meanwhile, having a rook on an open file is valuable.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activate your rook on open files and avoid placing pieces on squares where they have no prospects.
notes.plans: Prepare to double rooks or invade on the open file, and use pawn moves like h6 to prevent enemy knight outposts.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king is misplaced, trading rooks can simplify into a winning pawn endgame. Here, exchanging rooks leads to a favorable pawn structure with a two-versus-one on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for trades that accentuate your pawn majority or exploit the opponent's king position.
notes.plans: After trading rooks, advance your pawns and use your king actively to support them.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's rook is active on the open c-file, and the knight is heading to d5, a strong central outpost. White's king is exposed and misplaced, while Black's pieces coordinate well.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's king is exposed, prioritize activating your pieces and targeting weaknesses rather than defending passively.
notes.plans: Continue improving piece activity, aim to trade rooks to reduce counterplay, and use the knight on d5 to control key squares.

notes.explains: Black plays h5, which frees the rook and prevents knight g4 ideas because the king is on g3. This move also creates potential mating threats.
notes.teaches: When your king is safe, use pawn moves like h5 to gain space, activate your rook, and restrict your opponent's piece play.
notes.plans: After h5, continue pressuring White's weak pawns and prepare to push the kingside pawns to create mating threats.

notes.explains: Black plays g3, a move that defends the h-pawn and sets up mating threats. If White takes, there is a checkmate pattern. The king cannot take the pawn because it is defended.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for pawn moves that both defend your own pieces and create threats against the enemy king. Defended pawns can be crucial for mating nets.
notes.plans: Use the g-pawn to support the king and prepare further mating threats, while keeping the rook active.

notes.explains: Black plays a6, a quiet move that ignores the immediate action. It prevents any knight moves and leaves White with few options, as the rook is the only active piece.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is a quiet waiting move that maintains pressure and forces the opponent to worsen their position. Avoid unnecessary complications when you have a clear advantage.
notes.plans: After a6, prepare to push the pawns and continue increasing pressure, while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: Black chooses a safe route to victory rather than flashy but risky continuations. The king is exposed, and Black has multiple threats, so simplifying is best.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning advantage, prefer the safest and most forcing continuation. Do not give your opponent unnecessary chances to complicate the position.
notes.plans: Trade pieces if beneficial, push the pawns, and convert the material advantage without taking risks.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: In the Catalan, White's light-squared bishop on g2 is typically more active than Black's counterpart on c8. Black often tries to trade or activate this bishop to neutralize White's advantage.
notes.teaches: When playing the Catalan, be aware of the imbalance between the light-squared bishops; Black's main plan is to activate their bishop, while White should try to maintain its advantage.
notes.plans: White aims to keep the bishop on g2 active and prevent Black from trading it off or activating their own.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: After White plays Nc3 instead of the more common castling, Black faces a choice: take on c4 and enter a line where they must play accurately for equality, or avoid it with a solid move like c6. The latter gives White more central space.
notes.teaches: Sometimes deviating from the main lines can put the burden on your opponent to find precise moves just to equalize. If they avoid the challenge, you may get a comfortable advantage.
notes.plans: White will continue with central expansion, aiming for e4 to open the long diagonal for the bishop.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: Black's a5 aims to gain queenside space and prepare b6 and Ba6 to activate the light-squared bishop. White responds with b3 to defend the c4 pawn and prepares to play e4, which would open the long diagonal for the bishop on g2.
notes.teaches: In the Catalan, White's typical plan is to push e4 to gain central space and activate the bishop. Black's counterplay often involves activating the light-squared bishop via a6.
notes.plans: White will play e4, possibly after Nbd2, to open the center and increase the scope of the g2 bishop.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: Black's b5 is a pawn sacrifice that can be dangerous if White is not careful. After bxc4, bxc4, Qb6, White must handle the pressure on the d4 pawn and the knight. White chooses b3 to avoid complications and keep the position under control.
notes.teaches: Be cautious of pawn sacrifices that create dynamic counterplay. Sometimes it's better to decline a pawn and maintain a solid position rather than grab material and face active piece play.
notes.plans: White will continue with e4, aiming to consolidate the space advantage and keep the bishop active.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: In this position, White's bishop on g2 is not necessarily better than Black's bishop on a6; both are somewhat passive. White wants to play e4 quickly to gain space and activate the bishop, but must first deal with pressure on the c3 knight and the b3 pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's bishop is not worse than yours, prioritize central expansion (e4) to create a spatial advantage and give your pieces more scope.
notes.plans: White should aim to play e4, but first must resolve the tension around the c3 knight and the d4 pawn.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: After Black plays Qb6 attacking the knight, the natural defensive move a4 fails because Black can play Ba6, renewing the attack on the knight and leaving White's position passive. Instead, White should move the knight to c3, allowing Black to take on d4, but then White can develop the bishop to b2, defending the knight and creating a battery.
notes.teaches: When your piece is attacked, consider moves that create counterplay or improve your position rather than just defending. Developing with tempo (Bishop b2) can be stronger than a passive defensive move.
notes.plans: White plays Nc3, allowing ...Nxd4, then Bb2, defending the knight and preparing potential tactical shots.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: After Bb2, if Black plays Bb7, White has a tactical resource: Nxd5! If Black recaptures with the queen, White can take the queen with the bishop on b2. This works because the bishop on b2 is part of a battery along the diagonal, and the queen is overloaded.
notes.teaches: Always look at the whole board for tactical opportunities. A piece that seems passively placed (like the bishop on b2) can become a key attacker. When your opponent's queen is on a diagonal with your bishop, consider knight sacrifices to deflect it.
notes.plans: White should calculate Nxd5, and if Qxd5, then Bxd5, winning the queen. If Black declines, White has won a pawn and disrupted Black's position.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Benjamin Defense
notes.explains: Black avoided the immediate tactics by moving the queen to b4, but spent a lot of time on the clock, which later became a problem. White has a slight lead in development and both knights are active.
notes.teaches: Time management is crucial in chess. Spending too much time on a single move can lead to time pressure later, causing mistakes. Also, a lead in development is a temporary advantage that should be used to create threats.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and look for ways to exploit the lead in development, perhaps by increasing pressure on Black's position.
