notes.plans: After …Bg4, White can play Nc3, and eventually the queens will be exchanged, leading to a similar endgame. The main line remains the focus, but the alternative is worth exploring.

notes.explains: The game under discussion is from 1914, and the opening is the Ruy Lopez Exchange, which has deep lines and interesting endgames. The speaker notes that they have never played this variation themselves, highlighting its complexity.
notes.teaches: Even strong players may not have experience with every variation; it's valuable to study and try new lines to broaden understanding.
notes.plans: Focus on the main line of the exchange Ruy Lopez, but if time permits, explore the alternative …Bg4 line and the endgame from a 1909 world championship match.

notes.explains: In this Ruy Lopez exchange variation, White has an extra pawn and wants to use it, but Black is not lost and has resources. The position is still full of pieces, so calling it an endgame is misleading.
notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn, your plan is to activate your pieces and use the pawn advantage, but you must also respect the opponent's counterplay.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop harmoniously and prepare to push the kingside pawns, while Black should seek active piece play and decide on a safe king placement.

notes.explains: The knight on c3 is well placed; from d2 or e3 it would not be as effective. Keeping the knight on c3 supports central control and future operations.
notes.teaches: Piece placement matters: a knight on c3 is often better than on d2 or e3 because it controls key central squares and supports pawn advances.
notes.plans: White should keep the knight on c3 and then decide on castling and pawn pushes based on Black's setup.

notes.explains: Black has several reasonable moves, including castling long or short, playing f6, or developing the knight to e7. Long castling has become more popular in modern practice, though historically it was less explored.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez exchange, Black has flexible plans: castling long can lead to sharp play, while short castling with rook to d8 and a pawn storm is also viable. The choice depends on style and concrete analysis.
notes.plans: Black should decide on a castling side and then prepare to counter White's kingside pawn push, often with f6 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: Playing f6 can be problematic because if White later pushes f4 or e5, Black's e-pawn might become isolated. The knight is better placed on e7 than f6 because on f6 it would be restricted by the pawn and White could more easily push e5.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that create weaknesses like isolated pawns. Place knights on squares where they are not blocked by your own pawns and can fight against enemy pawn advances.
notes.plans: Black should develop the knight to e7 to prepare f6, challenging White's center and preventing an easy e5 push.

notes.explains: In this opening, Black wants to avoid allowing White an easy e5 pawn push. If the knight goes to f6, then e5 becomes much easier for White, so keeping the knight on e7 allows Black to challenge the center with f6 later.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn majority, piece placement should hinder your opponent's pawn breaks. Keep pieces flexible to support your own counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play f6 to challenge the e5 square, while developing pieces harmoniously.

notes.explains: Black considers playing ...e5 to fix the pawn structure, but must be careful about tactical tricks. For instance, if Black plays ...Nf5, White can simply take on f5, winning a piece. So Black must keep the knight on e7 to avoid such tactics.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a pawn break, check for tactical vulnerabilities in your piece placement. A seemingly active move can lose material if the opponent can capture.
notes.plans: Black should prepare ...e5 carefully, ensuring that the knight on e7 is not exposed to captures.

notes.explains: After White plays f5, Black's bishop and knight are blocked, so Black must find a way to activate the pieces. The move ...b6 is suggested to develop the bishop to c5, but the knight on e7 still needs a route.
notes.teaches: When your opponent restricts your pieces, prioritize piece activity. Look for pawn moves that open lines for your bishops and knights.
notes.plans: Black should aim for ...b6 and ...c5 to activate the bishop, and consider rerouting the knight to a better square, perhaps via g6 or f5, if possible.

notes.explains: After black plays f5 and white responds with b6, black must decide how to develop the queen's bishop. The tension is between keeping the pawn structure solid by allowing bishop exchanges and seeking piece activity by developing the bishop to b7.
notes.teaches: In the opening, piece activity often outweighs a fixed pawn structure. A bishop that is free to develop and participate in the game is more valuable than a rigid pawn chain.
notes.plans: Black should aim to develop the bishop to b7 or c8, then follow with c5 to gain space and free the pieces. The knights can later go to e5 or d4, but must avoid blocking the bishop.

notes.explains: The move f6 is generally discouraged in many openings because it weakens the kingside and can be a target. However, there are exceptions when it is necessary to challenge the center or prevent the opponent from playing e5, especially if the opponent's light-squared bishop cannot exploit the diagonal.
notes.teaches: General rules like 'never play f6' have exceptions. Evaluate the specific position: if the opponent can occupy the center or if the f6 pawn is not a weakness, it may be playable.
notes.plans: If f6 is played, ensure it supports the center and does not leave the king vulnerable. Otherwise, prefer developing pieces and maintaining a flexible pawn structure.

notes.explains: In this position, black had the opportunity to exchange bishops on f4, which would have fixed the pawn structure but also freed the bishop and allowed for a smooth development with c5. Instead, black chose to avoid the exchange, focusing on a solid pawn structure but neglecting piece activity.
notes.teaches: When considering an exchange, weigh the value of piece activity against the solidity of the pawn structure. A fixed pawn structure is not always an asset if it leaves your pieces passive.
notes.plans: Black should have taken on f4 and then played c5, freeing the bishop and preparing to develop the knight to e5 or d4. This would have given black a more active and comfortable position.

notes.explains: After white's knight goes to d4, black is in a difficult spot because the pieces are not coordinating well. The move bishop c8 is a good defensive resource, preventing the knight from jumping to e6 and preparing to challenge the center with c5.
notes.teaches: When your position is cramped, look for defensive moves that also create counterplay. Pushing back against the opponent's pieces is often necessary to gain space and activate your own.
notes.plans: Black should play bishop c8, then follow with c5 to challenge the center. If white's knight retreats, black can continue with rook d8 and eventually push e6, aiming to free the position.

notes.explains: Even world-class players like Capablanca can make positional mistakes under pressure, such as choosing a passive move that neglects piece activity. This shows that psychology and pressure affect decision-making at all levels.
notes.teaches: Always prioritize piece activity and dynamic factors over static pawn structure, especially in the opening and middlegame. Recognize that even strong players can err when they focus too much on one aspect of the position.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's pieces are passive and the knight on e6 is a strong outpost for White. Black's attempts to create counterplay, such as pushing pawns or rerouting pieces, are too slow and leave weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a powerful knight outpost, you must either challenge it or neutralize it, even if it costs material. Passive moves that allow the knight to remain will slowly lose.
notes.plans: Black should consider trading off the strong knight on e6, even at the cost of a pawn, to gain piece activity and relieve the pressure.

notes.explains: Black's move bishop a8 is a sign of desperation, as it retreats the bishop to a passive square and does nothing to address the central tension. White is free to improve their position, such as bringing the king to f2, while Black shuffles pieces.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that further restrict your own pieces. If you find yourself making such moves, it's a signal that your position is already critical and you need to find a radical solution.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve their position, using the space advantage and the strong knight to increase pressure. Black should look for active counterplay, even if it involves sacrifices.

notes.explains: Black's idea of playing b5 and then trying to activate the knight is too slow because the knight on e6 is defended and the bishop is blocked. The position is already difficult for Black, and these slow maneuvers allow White to consolidate.
notes.teaches: In a cramped position, you must seek immediate counterplay, not slow plans. If your pieces are tied down, look for tactical blows or exchanges to free your game.
notes.plans: Black should consider pawn breaks like c5 or even sacrificing the exchange to eliminate the knight on e6, aiming for piece activity rather than passive defense.

notes.explains: In this position, White is better because the king is actively participating and White has more space. Black is shuffling pieces without a clear plan, while White is building pressure on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and a safer king, you should look to increase the pressure, often by advancing pawns on the side where you have more space.
notes.plans: White should continue improving piece activity and prepare a pawn push on the kingside, such as g4-g5, to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: Black's rook maneuver to a7 and then back to a7 (after going to a7 and then returning) is inconsistent and loses time. Black had a better try in taking on e6, which would have been a more practical attempt to change the course of the game.
notes.teaches: In a difficult position, it is important to find the most active defensive resource, even if it means giving up material for activity. Wasting time with piece shuffles only makes the position worse.
notes.plans: Black should seek counterplay, perhaps by trading pawns or pieces to relieve pressure, rather than making pointless rook moves.

notes.explains: White's pieces are all optimally placed: the knight on d5 restricts Black's play, the rook on e7 ties Black down, and the king is ready to join the attack. The immediate plan is to push the g-pawn to g5, but White needs more support, so the king goes to f4.
notes.teaches: When you have a bind, you should improve your pieces to their maximum potential before executing the breakthrough. The king can be a powerful attacking piece in the middlegame if it is safe.
notes.plans: White should bring the king to f4 to support the g4-g5 push, and then continue with rook to h1 to exploit the open file after the pawn break.

notes.explains: Black tries to create counterplay with g6 and possibly g5, but White can simply respond with rook g3, maintaining the pressure and preventing Black from freeing their position.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create counterplay, you can often neutralize it by placing your pieces on flexible squares that both defend and attack, keeping the opponent tied down.
notes.plans: White should continue with the plan of pushing g5, using the rook on g3 to support it, and then open the h-file for a decisive attack.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a structural advantage with a passed pawn on the g-file, while Black's pieces are passively placed. White's king is safe, and the rook on g3 is well-placed to support the advance of the g-pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, use your pieces to support its advance rather than rushing to push it prematurely. Keep the tension and improve your pieces first.
notes.plans: White should continue with rook to h3, preparing to double rooks on the h-file and then advance the g-pawn. Black's pieces are tied down to defense, so White can build up pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays g5 to block the pawn's advance, but White wisely declines to capture immediately. Taking would open lines for Black's pieces and allow the knight to become active on e5, giving Black counterplay.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to capture pawns if it opens lines for your opponent's pieces. Sometimes it's better to maintain the tension and keep your opponent's pieces passive.
notes.plans: White plays king to f3, keeping the king safe and maintaining the pressure. The g-pawn remains a thorn in Black's side, and White can later decide when to capture or push.

notes.explains: White's rook goes to h3, and Black plays rook d7. White finds a strong maneuver with the knight to g3, aiming for the outpost on d5. This avoids the crossfire of a check and prepares to double rooks on the h-file.
notes.teaches: Look for knight maneuvers to strong outposts, even if they take a few moves. A knight on a central outpost can dominate the position and support an attack.
notes.plans: White doubles rooks on the h-file and then plays e5, bringing the last piece into the attack. If Black captures, the knight recaptures and jumps to f6, creating a decisive attack.

notes.explains: White's attack culminates in a beautiful combination involving knight sacrifices and checks, leading to a forced mate. The key is to include all pieces in the attack and use the open files.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, bring all your pieces into play and look for tactical blows. Sacrifices are often necessary to break through the defense.
notes.plans: White continues with the attack, using the knights to create threats and eventually delivering checkmate. Black's defenses are overwhelmed.

notes.explains: In this position, the attacker has a decisive initiative. The knight on c5 is a powerful outpost, and the rook on d7 is poised to deliver checkmate threats. There are multiple mating ideas, such as knight to b7 or e6, making the defense very difficult.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong initiative, look for ways to bring all your pieces into the attack, especially rooks on open files and knights on strong outposts. Multiple mating threats can overwhelm the defense.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing the rook to d7 and using the knight on c5 to create threats. Look for the quickest mate, such as knight to b7 or e6.

notes.explains: The speaker recalls a personal game where moving rooks around a lot was effective, illustrating that active rook play is a common winning theme.
notes.teaches: Rooks are powerful when they are active and can switch between files to create threats. Don't be afraid to move rooks multiple times to find the best attacking square.

notes.explains: In the endgame, fatigue and time pressure often lead to missed opportunities, such as agreeing to a draw when one side is winning or resigning in a drawn position.
notes.teaches: Always re-evaluate the position objectively before agreeing to a draw or resigning, especially in the endgame where small advantages can be decisive.

notes.explains: White has the bishop pair and a passed pawn on h5, while Black's knight is misplaced, far from the action and unable to blockade the passed pawn effectively.
notes.teaches: In bishop-versus-knight endgames, a misplaced knight can be a permanent weakness; the side with bishops should aim to exploit the knight's poor placement by creating threats and advancing passed pawns.
notes.plans: White should target the f5 pawn and use the bishops to dominate the knight, while advancing the h-pawn to tie down Black's pieces.

notes.explains: White correctly chose the direct bishop move to attack the f5 pawn, rather than a slower maneuver that would give Black time to consolidate.
notes.teaches: In endgames, concrete and direct moves are often better than slow preparatory ones; every tempo counts when there are passed pawns and weaknesses to exploit.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring the f5 pawn and prepare to advance the h-pawn further.

notes.explains: Black had to decide whether to defend the f5 pawn or ignore it; ignoring it would allow White to win the pawn and create a dangerous passed pawn, so Black chose to defend.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn attack, weigh the cost of defending versus ignoring; sometimes defending a weak pawn is necessary to prevent a greater danger, but it may also lead to passivity.
notes.plans: Black should try to activate the king and coordinate pieces to counter White's initiative.

notes.explains: White played h6 at the right moment, preventing Black's king from catching the h-pawn. If White delayed, Black could approach and neutralize the passed pawn, possibly even winning.
notes.teaches: Timing is critical in endgames with passed pawns; the push of a passed pawn must be timed to prevent the opponent's king from stopping it.
notes.plans: After h6, White will force Black to give up the knight for the pawn, leaving White with a material advantage and active pieces.

notes.explains: In the final position, White is winning but the players agreed to a draw. White has a clear plan: take on f5, then use the king and bishops to create further threats while Black's knight is still misplaced.
notes.teaches: Do not agree to a draw in a winning position; instead, calculate a concrete plan to convert the advantage. In bishop-versus-knight endgames, the bishop pair and a passed pawn can be decisive if handled precisely.
notes.plans: White should capture the f5 pawn, then advance the h-pawn or use the bishops to restrict the knight, while bringing the king to support the passed pawn.

notes.explains: In this bishop-and-king endgame, White's king needs to penetrate to a key square (like e5) to attack the f5 pawn, while the bishop controls both black pawns. Black's king tries to stay active to defend, but White can use triangulation or zugzwang to force progress.
notes.teaches: In king-and-bishop versus king-and-pawns endgames, the king's activity is paramount; use the bishop to restrain enemy pawns while your king marches to attack them. If the opponent's king is tied to defense, look for a zugzwang or a maneuver to gain a tempo.
notes.plans: White should aim to bring the king to e5 (or similar) to attack the f5 pawn, using the bishop to control the other pawns. If the black king tries to oppose, use bishop moves to put Black in zugzwang, forcing the king to give way.

notes.explains: White considered several king routes (e.g., Kf2, Kh5) to approach the f5 pawn, but had to calculate whether Black could counterplay by advancing his own pawns. The key was to find a plan that prevents Black's counterplay while making progress.
notes.teaches: When planning a king march in an endgame, always check the opponent's counterplay—especially pawn advances. If a line allows dangerous counterplay, abandon it and look for a more solid plan.
notes.plans: White should choose a king route that avoids allowing Black to roll his pawns, possibly by first improving the bishop to control key squares, then bringing the king to the queenside or directly to the f5 pawn.

notes.explains: White missed a winning maneuver: by playing the bishop to d2, then to c3, and back to e1, White could force Black into zugzwang, allowing the king to reach e5 and win the f5 pawn. The game ended in a draw because White took a draw instead of finding this.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for bishop maneuvers that put the opponent in zugzwang, forcing them to make a bad move. Even if a position seems drawn, there may be a subtle winning idea; always search for such tactics before agreeing to a draw.
notes.plans: White should have played a bishop maneuver (e.g., Bd2, Bc3, Be1) to force Black's king to move, then penetrate with the king to e5, winning the f5 pawn and the game.

notes.explains: In the next example, Black is an exchange down but has dangerous passed pawns on b4 and c3. However, the knight on b3 is blockading them effectively, so it's not clear how Black can advance. Black played f6 to open the position, but White's blockade seems solid.
notes.teaches: In material imbalances, a well-placed blockading piece can neutralize dangerous passed pawns. When facing a pawn mass, look for ways to blockade them with a piece that also has other active roles.
notes.plans: White should maintain the blockade on the b4 and c3 pawns with the knight, and aim to consolidate the material advantage by activating the other pieces. Black should look for ways to break the blockade, possibly by advancing the f-pawn to create weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this endgame, black is down an exchange but has dangerous passed pawns on b4 and c3, though the knight on b3 is effectively blockading them, making their advance unclear.
notes.teaches: Material imbalances in endgames require careful evaluation of the activity and potential of each piece, not just counting points.
notes.plans: Both sides should seek to activate their kings and improve their least active pieces while keeping an eye on the opponent's pawn breaks.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to open the position, and later g5 to stop white's pawns, but the final move g5 is actually a blunder, allowing white to win.
notes.teaches: Even in complex endgames, a single move can change the evaluation drastically; always check for tactical resources before committing to a move.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to exploit the weakened kingside, possibly by targeting the e6 pawn or creating threats against the black king.

notes.explains: White's best chance is rook f6, attacking the e6 pawn, and if black captures with the knight, the pawn recaptures and the resulting passed pawn is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: In rook endings, active rook play and targeting weak pawns can create decisive threats, especially when the opponent's pieces are tied down.
notes.plans: White should play rook f6, forcing the issue on e6, and then evaluate whether to convert the material advantage or continue pressing.

notes.explains: In this rook versus pawn endgame, the rook must immediately attack the e6 pawn with Rf6, forcing the knight to capture and allowing the pawn to advance. The black king is far away, but the knight can try to stop the pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, prioritize pushing it, but be aware of the opponent's pieces that can stop it. Sometimes you need to use your king to support the pawn's advance.
notes.plans: White should play Rf6, forcing ...Nxf6, then push the e-pawn. Black must use the knight to try to stop it, but the pawn is decisive.

notes.explains: The white knight needs to reach f3 to deliver checkmate. The move d5 is the most beautiful because it frees the d4 square for the knight, while also opening lines. Black must capture the d-pawn, allowing the knight to go to d4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you need to sacrifice a pawn to create a mating net. Look for moves that open squares for your pieces and force the opponent's response.
notes.plans: White plays d5, and if black captures, the knight goes to d4, then f3, and checkmate follows. If black doesn't capture, the d-pawn will be decisive.

notes.explains: The final combination involves promoting the f-pawn to a queen, which delivers checkmate. The black knight cannot defend both the promotion square and the mating threats.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, promotion is a primary goal. Use threats of promotion to force the opponent into a position where they cannot defend against mate.
notes.plans: White plays f7, and if ...Nxf7, then c1=Q is checkmate. Otherwise, the pawn promotes with mate.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn ending, the position is objectively a draw, but both players thought Black was winning. The key is that only one king move loses; the others draw.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endings, a single tempo can decide the outcome. Always look for the precise king move that maintains the draw or win, even when the position seems lost.
notes.plans: White should play Kf1 to be ready to meet f3 with the king on the faster route to the queenside. If Black plays Kg3, White must not play Kg1, as that loses a tempo.

notes.explains: The a4 pawn break is a critical resource in this ending. By playing a4, White creates doubled pawns on the a-file, eliminating Black's winning chances.
notes.teaches: In pawn endings, a well-timed pawn break can liquidate to a drawn structure. Look for such resources even when the opponent has a space advantage.
notes.plans: After the king is on f1 and Black plays f3, White should eventually play a4. If Black takes on a4, the doubled pawns draw; if Black ignores, White can exchange and get the king to c1 in time.

notes.explains: In the game, White resigned in a drawn position. This highlights the psychological difficulty of assessing complex pawn endings correctly, especially after a long game.
notes.teaches: Never resign in a pawn ending without checking for drawing resources. Fatigue can lead to misassessment, so rely on concrete calculation rather than intuition.

notes.explains: In the Averbakh game, Black is an exchange up but White has a dangerous h4 pawn. White has two defensive ideas: Bf5 to defend the pawn or e5 to exchange pawns.
notes.teaches: When worse, exchanging pawns can be a drawing mechanism. Defending a pawn may be less effective than simplifying the position.
notes.plans: White should consider e5 to trade pawns and hope for a draw, rather than passively defending with Bf5.

notes.explains: In this rook versus bishop ending, black is up the exchange for a pawn, but white has a dangerous passed h-pawn. The placement of the pawn (h4 vs h5) and the color of the bishop are critical: with a dark-squared bishop, h4 might be a fortress, but here the bishop is light-squared, so the h4 pawn is not enough to hold.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop endings, the defender's pawn structure and bishop color determine whether the position is a fortress or a win. A pawn on h5 with a dark-squared bishop can be a draw, but with a light-squared bishop, the h4 pawn is vulnerable and the attacker can often win.
notes.plans: Black should aim to bring the king to f4, then use the rook to harass the bishop and create mating threats, while keeping the h-pawn under control.

notes.explains: The natural defensive move bishop f5 holds the draw, but white instead chose to exchange pawns with e5, which was a mistake. After the exchange, black's winning plan involves bringing the king to f4 and then using the rook to force the bishop off the key diagonal, leading to a decisive penetration.
notes.teaches: When worse, exchanging pawns can be a drawing resource, but only if the resulting position is truly drawn. Here, the exchange gave black a clear path to victory, so white should have kept the pawn and defended with bishop f5.
notes.plans: White should have played bishop f5 to defend the h-pawn and maintain the blockade. Black, after the exchange, should proceed with king f4, then rook b2, and force the bishop away to win.

notes.explains: In the line after bishop f5, black tries rook g3 check, but white has only king f2. Then black plays rook d3, attacking the bishop. White must not move the king toward the rook; instead, the king should stay near the h-pawn. The correct move is bishop e6, keeping the bishop on the h3-c8 diagonal to prevent black's king from reaching g4.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop endings, the defender must keep the bishop on the diagonal that controls the key squares, and the king should stay close to the passed pawn. Moving the king to hunt the rook can allow the pawn to advance and lose the game.
notes.plans: White should play bishop e6, maintaining the blockade. If black tries rook d5, white must avoid taking on c5, as the resulting pawn ending is lost.

notes.explains: In this rook-and-bishop versus rook endgame, the defender's king is near the corner and the attacker threatens to mate or win material. The defender must find precise moves to avoid losing, and the presence of a passed d-pawn can be a crucial resource to distract the enemy rook and allow the king to escape.
notes.teaches: When defending a cramped king in the corner, look for counterplay with a passed pawn to deflect the enemy rook, rather than passively waiting. The king's ability to move only one square at a time means timing is critical.
notes.plans: The defender should aim to activate the king, using the passed pawn to create threats that force the rook away, then run the king to safety.

notes.explains: A specific trap exists: if the defender's king goes to g2, the attacker can play rook to d5, and after pawn takes c5, the king goes to f5, winning. The defender must avoid this by choosing a different king move or a bishop move like bishop e6, which holds the draw.
notes.teaches: In endgames, be alert to tactical tricks that exploit the king's position. Sometimes the most natural-looking king move loses, while a quieter move or a piece move maintains the balance.
notes.plans: The defender should play bishop e6 to neutralize threats and keep the position drawn, rather than moving the king to g2.

notes.explains: The defender's plan involves playing h3 as a try, but the attacker must immediately address the pawn with king g1, then go to g2 and take the pawn. Exchanging pawns on e5 with a check can simplify to a drawn pawn ending.
notes.teaches: When facing a dangerous passed pawn, it's often best to neutralize it quickly, even if it means giving up a pawn, to reach a drawn pawn ending. Check moves can force favorable exchanges.
notes.plans: The attacker should play e5 to eliminate the pawns, then take the h3 pawn with check, leading to a drawn king and pawn endgame.

notes.explains: In this Grünfeld, black has given up the center, allowing white to control it, with the plan of using the bishop on g7 and a later c5 to pressure the white center. The move b6 is somewhat slow because it doesn't immediately challenge the center; c5 or castling are more natural.
notes.teaches: In the Grünfeld, black's compensation for conceding the center comes from dynamic piece play and the c5 break. Moves like b6 that don't contribute to that plan can give white time to consolidate.
notes.plans: Black should aim for c5 and develop the bishop to b7, while white will try to maintain the central pawn duo and develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: White's bishop check on b5 is a useful provocation: if black responds with c6, the pawn is deflected from its ideal square c5, and the bishop can retreat to c4, a better square. This disrupts black's intended setup, especially if black had wanted the bishop on b7.
notes.teaches: A checking move that forces a pawn to a less useful square can be a strong way to disrupt the opponent's plan, even if it costs a tempo to move the bishop twice.
notes.plans: After c6 and Bc4, white has a slight edge in development and black's pawn on c6 may become a target. Black should look for ways to play c5 anyway or develop pieces to natural squares.

notes.explains: Black offers to exchange bishops with Ba6. In general, exchanging pieces is good for the side with less space, but here it can leave black with weaknesses. If white takes on a6, black's knight recaptures, and the queen can go to d3, attacking the knight on a6, which is misplaced.
notes.teaches: Not all exchanges are equal: even if you have less space, you must consider whether the resulting piece placement is favorable. A piece that ends up on a poor square can be worse than the space disadvantage.
notes.plans: White should consider taking on a6 and then using the queen to harass the knight, while black must find a way to redeploy the knight or create counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's a6 move offers an exchange of bishops, which could be beneficial for Black due to having less space, but it risks leaving weaknesses and can worsen the position of Black's pieces if not handled well.
notes.teaches: When considering trades, evaluate whether the exchange improves the location of your remaining pieces; avoid trades that leave your pieces poorly placed.
notes.plans: If the bishop exchange occurs, the queen may go to d3 to attack the knight, or Black might play Qc8 to keep pressure on the center.

notes.explains: White's moves like Qa4 and Bg5 develop pieces while simultaneously attacking Black's pieces, creating threats and gaining tempos.
notes.teaches: Develop with threats: if you can develop a piece and attack an opponent's piece at the same time, you gain time and put pressure on the opponent.
notes.plans: Continue developing while maintaining threats; White aims to consolidate and push central pawns.

notes.explains: After Black plays Qb7 defending the pawn, White plays Re1 to protect the e4 pawn, ensuring it is not lost and setting up future threats.
notes.teaches: Protect central pawns; they are valuable and should not be traded off lightly. A move like Re1 can both defend and prepare future attacks.
notes.plans: With e4 protected, White can proceed with threats like Bxe7, exploiting Black's overloaded pieces.

notes.explains: Black considers moves like e6 or Re8, both harmless to White's position. Moving a pawn like e6 can prevent d5 ideas but also creates a permanent weakness, whereas moving a piece develops and keeps pawn structure flexible.
notes.teaches: When defending, prefer moving a piece over a pawn if possible, because pawn moves are irreversible and can leave weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should aim to put pressure on the center to prevent White from consolidating and pushing pawns.

notes.explains: White's rook to b1 is a prophylactic move, moving the rook off the bishop's diagonal to avoid hidden threats, especially since White plans to advance central pawns.
notes.teaches: In openings like the Grünfeld, be aware of the bishop's diagonal and move rooks out of potential pins or attacks, especially when planning pawn advances.
notes.plans: White can now proceed with e5, c4, and d5, pushing the center pawns, while Black's knight remains misplaced on a6.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a strong passed pawn on d5 and a powerful bishop on the long diagonal, while Black's knight on a6 is misplaced and Black has less space. The rook on b1 is useful because it supports the b-pawn and keeps the queen tied to the defense of the knight.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear positional advantage, avoid giving material for unclear compensation. Instead, maintain the pressure and improve your pieces with prophylactic moves that restrict the opponent's counterplay.
notes.plans: White should aim to advance the d-pawn, supported by the rook on d1, while keeping the bishop on the strong diagonal. The rook on b1 can later support a b-pawn push or switch to the d-file if needed.

notes.explains: Black played c5 to challenge the center, but White should not capture because that would give the knight a nice square. Instead, White can continue with d5, which is a strong central breakthrough, supported by the rook on b1 and the bishop.
notes.teaches: In the Grünfeld structure, it's sometimes acceptable to give up the opponent's c-pawn, but only if you get concrete compensation. Here, the strong d-pawn and active pieces provide that compensation.
notes.plans: White should push the d-pawn forward, aiming to create a passed pawn that ties down Black's pieces. The rook on d1 will support the pawn's advance, and the bishop on the long diagonal controls key squares.

notes.explains: After Black plays f6, it's a natural defensive move to stop the d-pawn's advance, but it also weakens the kingside. White's plan is clear: continue pushing the d-pawn, and if Black's pieces are tied down, White can create threats on the kingside or exploit the weak squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is forced to make defensive moves like f6, it's a sign that your plan is working. Keep the pressure and look for ways to increase it, either by advancing your passed pawn or by switching to other weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should continue with the d-pawn push, possibly preparing to open lines or create mating threats. The rook on d1 and the bishop on the long diagonal support the advance, and the queen can join the attack if needed.

notes.explains: Black's pieces are tied down: the queen is stuck defending a knight, the knight lacks good squares, and the d-pawn is close to promoting. Black played ...f6 to block the bishop's control of the queening square, but this creates a potential weakness on e6.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are passive and tied to defense, you should seek to increase the pressure rather than trade pieces. Avoid unnecessary trades when you have an initiative or a material advantage.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to exploit the pinned and overloaded black pieces, possibly by infiltrating on the seventh rank or creating threats that force black to further weaken their structure.

notes.explains: The move ...f6, while necessary to block the bishop, weakens the e6 square and the kingside. The bishop was black's strongest piece, and now it is blocked.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must make a weakening move to parry a direct threat, but you should be aware of the long-term consequences. The opponent will try to exploit the new weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should target the weakened e6 square and consider maneuvers that increase pressure on black's position, especially along the e-file or diagonals.

notes.explains: White considers moves like Rc1 to infiltrate on the seventh rank, but the key is to find a move that increases pressure without allowing black to free their pieces. The move g5 is suggested, putting pressure on the f6 pawn and potentially creating threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are stuck, a pawn thrust can be a powerful way to open lines or further restrict their mobility. Look for moves that create multiple threats or force the opponent to make concessions.
notes.plans: White might play g5 to attack the f6 pawn, forcing black to respond and potentially weakening their kingside further. This could open lines for the rooks or the queen.

notes.explains: In this position, the advanced pawn on d7 is a powerful asset. It cuts the board along the d-file, separating the two sides and restricting the enemy queen's movement. The pawn is also close to promotion, and it supports a future knight jump to f7, which is hard to defend.
notes.teaches: When you have a far-advanced passed pawn, use it to restrict the opponent's pieces and to support your own attacking pieces. The pawn can act as a wedge that divides the board.
notes.plans: Push the pawn forward, double rooks on the d-file, and prepare a knight to f7. If the opponent takes the pawn, the resulting open diagonals can be used for your bishops.

notes.explains: The bishop on the long diagonal looks active but actually attacks nothing because the opponent lacks a light-squared bishop to oppose it. The key diagonal is the one that supports the passed pawn and the attack.
notes.teaches: Evaluate bishops not just by their activity but by whether they have targets. A bishop on an open diagonal is only useful if it can influence the critical squares.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on the useful diagonal, supporting the pawn's advance and the knight's maneuver to f7.

notes.explains: If the opponent declines to take the pawn and instead plays a knight move like ...Ne4, White can respond with Qb3+ and then Bf4, maintaining a positional advantage. The queen will later regroup to b3 and e6, controlling key squares around the pawn, while the enemy queen on b7 is passive.
notes.teaches: In positions with a strong passed pawn, centralize your queen and coordinate your pieces to control the squares around the pawn. Compare the activity of the two queens to assess who has the better chances.
notes.plans: Play Qb3+ to force the king to move, then place the bishop on f4. Double rooks on the d-file and use the queen to control e6 and other key squares, preventing the enemy knight from returning to c6.

notes.explains: There is an alternative plan involving a pawn push to g5 and a later knight to f7, but after a sequence of trades it is not as clear as the d7 plan. The position offers two pawns for the exchange, but the simpler path is to keep the pawn on d7 and build up.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear, strong plan, prefer it over a murky tactical alternative. Sometimes the most straightforward continuation is the best.
notes.plans: Stick with the d7 pawn plan, building up pressure rather than entering unclear complications.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, White has sacrificed material for active pieces and threats. The immediate knight jump to f7 is tempting, but Black can respond with ...Kg7, and White's attack fizzles, leaving White in trouble. Therefore, the knight should instead go to e6, maintaining pressure and avoiding a premature strike.
notes.teaches: When attacking, do not rush the first forcing move if it allows the defender to consolidate. Look for a more flexible square that keeps multiple threats alive.
notes.plans: Play the knight to e6, keeping the initiative and preparing further threats against the black king.

notes.explains: Black tries to give back material to simplify and defend. The knight on e6 is poorly placed, so Black maneuvers it to c7, where it is more active and can be traded off for White's strong knight. If that trade happens, Black's position improves significantly because White's knight was the key attacking piece.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for opportunities to return material to neutralize the opponent's most active piece. A trade of a bad piece for a good one can be a major defensive resource.
notes.plans: Black aims to provoke or force the trade of knights, while White should avoid it and keep the pressure.

notes.explains: White has a clear winning plan with rook to d6, which cuts off the black knight on c7 and prepares to double on the sixth rank or bring the queen to e6. This is more straightforward than the complicated queen takes e5 line, which allows Black a tricky resource that makes the win less clear.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear, forcing plan that leads to a win, prefer it over speculative complications. Even if a tactical idea is tempting, clarity and simplicity are virtues in winning positions.
notes.plans: Play rook to d6, followed by doubling rooks or bringing the queen to e6, maintaining the bind on Black's position.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a passed pawn and a safer king, but immediate captures lead to unclear complications. The opponent's pieces are active, and the king is exposed, so there are two main ideas: promoting the passed pawn and attacking the weak king.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple advantages, look for a way to combine them rather than forcing a single plan. Sometimes it's better to avoid complications if a clearer path exists.
notes.plans: Consider advancing the passed pawn further to gain space and activate your pieces, while also preparing to bring the rook to the seventh rank to attack the king.

notes.explains: The key idea is to sacrifice the passed pawn to open lines and improve piece placement. After pushing the pawn to d8, the opponent is forced to capture, allowing the rook to reach the seventh rank and join the attack on the king.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must give up a material advantage to shift the nature of your advantage. A passed pawn can be used as a decoy to activate your pieces and create a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to d8, let it be captured, then use the open files to bring the rook to the seventh rank and coordinate an attack on the king.

notes.explains: With only three pieces left, reckless sacrifices are risky because you may not have enough material to deliver checkmate. The rook sacrifice on the pawn is tempting, but the opponent can defend, and the attack fizzles out.
notes.teaches: When you have few pieces, be careful with sacrifices. Ensure you have enough material to sustain the attack before giving up material.
notes.plans: Instead of sacrificing, look for a quieter move that improves your piece coordination, such as repositioning the rook to a more active rank.

notes.explains: The queen maneuver to f4 is strong because it creates a pin and attacks the c7 pawn. This is only possible after the rook is activated to the seventh rank, which was achieved by the pawn sacrifice.
notes.teaches: Piece activity is often more important than material. By improving the rook's position, you enable your queen to reach a dominating square that creates multiple threats.
notes.plans: After the rook reaches the seventh rank, bring the queen to f4 to pin a piece and attack the c7 pawn, forcing the opponent to defend.

notes.explains: In this position, the pin on the f-file is a key tactical motif. The queen can regroup to f4, creating a stronger pin because it also attacks c7, making it hard for Black to defend everything.
notes.teaches: When a pin is combined with an attack on another weakness, the defender's task becomes much harder. Look for ways to reinforce a pin by adding pressure on other targets.
notes.plans: White should continue to exploit the pin and the attack on c7, aiming to increase pressure and force Black into passivity.

notes.explains: Black's best defensive try was bishop to g7, ignoring the knight, to allow the queen to recapture on c7 and enter an endgame. Although White remains better, this gives Black the most hope.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best defense is to give up material to reach a simplified position, even if the endgame is worse, rather than allowing a devastating attack.
notes.plans: If Black plays bishop g7, White should continue with rook f1 to prevent counterplay, then target the a-pawn and use the rook actively.

notes.explains: If Black tries rook d8, White can capture with the bishop, and then the queen can come to f7, threatening mate because the bishops are on the back rank. Black's pieces are stuck on the other side, unable to defend.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are far from the king, a queen invasion can be decisive. Look for checks and threats that force the king into a mating net.
notes.plans: White should continue with rook to d-file to control it, or queen to f7, both leading to a win. The key is to maintain the initiative and not allow Black to consolidate.

notes.explains: After the queen comes to h6, the knight is hanging but irrelevant because there is no way to stop the mate threats. Black's queen to a6 was a blunder that allowed this decisive move.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, do not be distracted by material. Focus on the most forcing continuation that leads to mate or a decisive gain.
notes.plans: White should play queen h6, threatening mate, and if Black tries to defend, continue with checks and threats to force resignation.

notes.explains: Throughout the game, White was willing to give up material, like a pawn, to open the position and seize the initiative. This is a typical style where activity and attacking chances outweigh material.
notes.teaches: In open positions, initiative and piece activity can be worth more than material. Be willing to sacrifice for long-term pressure.
notes.plans: Maintain the initiative by keeping the pieces active and creating threats, even at the cost of material.

notes.explains: In this game, White willingly gave up a pawn to open the position and seize the initiative, a hallmark of aggressive play. The resulting open lines made it easy for White to infiltrate and put constant pressure on Black.
notes.teaches: Material can be sacrificed for initiative and attacking chances, especially when the opponent's king is exposed or development is lagging. The side with the initiative often has more freedom to improvise, while the defender must be extremely precise.

notes.explains: Black's early move b6 was criticized as too slow; the more active c5 was preferable. This allowed White to gain a tempo and left Black's pieces, particularly the knight on a6, awkwardly placed for the rest of the game.
notes.teaches: In the opening, moves that are too passive or slow can cede the initiative and lead to lasting positional problems. Prefer moves that fight for the center and develop actively.

notes.explains: Black defended tenaciously for a long time without making a single large blunder, yet White's relentless pressure and accurate play gradually squeezed Black. The defender's task is harder because every move must be precise, and time pressure can exacerbate the difficulty.
notes.teaches: A strong attacker can win by accumulating small advantages and maintaining pressure, even without a decisive mistake from the defender. Defending requires extreme accuracy, and time trouble can be a decisive factor.

notes.explains: In the f3 Nimzo-Indian, Black's immediate ...c5 challenges the d4 pawn and aims for a dark-square strategy, often provoking d5. This leads to a wide variety of complex structures, making it hard to navigate.
notes.teaches: When an opening move leads to many possible structures, study the less popular lines first to understand the typical plans before tackling the main lines.
notes.plans: White should consider d5 as the main try, but a3 is a practical alternative that leads to more linear positions.

notes.explains: After …c5, White can play a3 instead of d5. This avoids the complex main lines but gives Black a comfortable position, as White is a couple of tempi short compared to similar lines where the bishop can develop to d3.
notes.teaches: Tempo is critical in the opening; being a move behind can make a standard development like Bd3 unplayable because a pawn hangs.
notes.plans: If White wants a simpler game, a3 is viable, but the main line with d5 is more ambitious.

notes.explains: After d5, Black can play ...Bxc3, forcing a specific pawn structure immediately. This removes fluidity but costs a tempo because the bishop capture is unprovoked.
notes.teaches: Voluntarily giving up the bishop for a knight without gaining something concrete is often a waste of time; the opponent can use that tempo to improve their position.
notes.plans: White should exploit the extra tempo to build a strong center, while Black aims for ...d6 and ...e5 to establish a solid structure.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian structure with ...c5, Black often plays Bxc3 to double White's c-pawns, but doing so unprovoked wastes a tempo. White can use that extra tempo to build a strong position, so Black should not rush this capture.
notes.teaches: Avoid giving up the bishop for the knight on c3 without a concrete reason; the tempo loss can be exploited by White.
notes.plans: White aims to use the extra tempo to develop actively and maintain a healthy pawn structure.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...d6 and ...e5, the center becomes blocked. White should not try to capture on d5 because Black's extra c-pawn supports the center, making White worse. Instead, White should play e5 to fix the structure.
notes.teaches: In blocked centers, avoid pawn captures that open lines for the opponent; instead, solidify your own pawn chain.
notes.plans: White will develop the bishop to d3 and prepare kingside play.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...h6 or ...Nf8, White's h4 is a key move. It prevents Black from playing ...g5, which would give Black active kingside play against White's king. This is a prophylactic move that stops Black's plan before it starts.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like h4 can prevent the opponent's typical expansion and keep your king safe.
notes.plans: White will continue with Be3, Qd2, and castle queenside, while Black struggles for a plan.

notes.explains: Black's move ...Kd7 is unusual but justified because the center is blocked, so castling is not urgent. Black plans to place the king on c7 or queenside, where it is safe. However, Black's pieces lack active prospects, and Black is reduced to waiting.
notes.teaches: In blocked positions, king safety can be handled flexibly; but if you have no plan, you may end up shuffling while the opponent improves.
notes.plans: White castles queenside and aims to break through on the queenside or center, while Black waits.

notes.explains: In this structure, Black has no clear strategic plan and is forced to shuffle pieces, while White can slowly improve and seek a breakthrough. If White fails to break through, the game may end in a draw; if White succeeds, Black is likely lost.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has no plan, you should improve your pieces and create threats without rushing; patience is key.
notes.plans: White will double rooks on the b-file or prepare a pawn break, while Black waits.

notes.explains: In this structure, White has a space advantage and Black is passively shuffling. White's plan is to slowly improve and eventually break through, while Black has no active counterplay.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and the opponent is passive, you should not rush to open the position; instead, improve your pieces and create threats at your own pace.
notes.plans: White can play f4 to create tension, but should not open the f-file prematurely. Continue developing with moves like Be3, Rg1, and then advance g4 to gain more space.

notes.explains: White has a strong tactical resource with Nd4, preparing Nf5, which hits key squares and creates threats of g5 and sacrifices on h6. Black's position becomes very difficult to defend.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a surprising knight maneuver can be the most effective way to exploit a passive opponent, especially when it targets weaknesses and creates multiple threats.
notes.plans: After Nd4, White threatens Nf5, and if Black captures, White recaptures and continues with strong pressure, often leading to a decisive attack.

notes.explains: In this specific Nimzo-Indian structure where Black has taken on c3, White's doubled c-pawns are not a real weakness because Black cannot easily attack them. White's structure is solid and White has no concessions.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always weak; if they cannot be attacked, they may be a non-issue. Focus on the dynamic factors of the position rather than static pawn structure.
notes.plans: White should continue with h4 to keep the kingside locked down and then proceed with a patient buildup, as Black has no active plan.

notes.explains: Black's attempts to exploit the doubled pawns, such as Qa5 or putting a knight on e5, are not effective because White can easily neutralize them with moves like Bd2. If Black does not play e5, White can take over the dark squares with f4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to attack a perceived weakness, simple defensive moves can often nullify the threat. Also, be aware of the opponent's possible dark-square weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should be ready to respond to Black's ideas with simple moves like Bd2, and if Black neglects e5, White can play f4 to gain a strong grip on the dark squares.

notes.explains: In this structure, neither side has a clear way to attack the opponent's pawns directly; attempts like queen a5 are met by bishop d2, and a knight on e5 fails to generate real pressure.
notes.teaches: When a pawn structure is solid and closed, piece play alone often cannot break through; you need a concrete pawn break or a favorable structural transformation.
notes.plans: If Black delays the e5 break, White can seize the dark squares with moves like f4, so Black should consider timely pawn advances.

notes.explains: With the pawns already committed, Black's earlier plan of knight a5, b6, and bishop a6 is no longer viable because the structure has changed.
notes.teaches: Opening plans are highly dependent on the exact pawn structure; a plan that works in one variation may be obsolete in another.

notes.explains: After Black takes on c4 and d5, the structure appears to favor White: Black has weaknesses on d7 and c5, and the d5 square is a strong outpost for a White knight. Black's compensation is piece activity and White's king still in the center.
notes.teaches: When accepting structural weaknesses, you must have concrete piece play to justify them; otherwise the opponent's long-term trumps will tell.
notes.plans: Black should play knight c6 and aim for active piece play, while White should complete development and prepare to exploit the d5 outpost.

notes.explains: White's knight to e2 is a flexible move: it prepares castling, defends the c3 knight, and prevents Black's knight from landing on d4.
notes.teaches: In the opening, a single move can serve multiple purposes: king safety, piece defense, and controlling key central squares.
notes.plans: Black's best try is bishop a6 to pressure White's position; if Black castles too early, White can castle and enjoy the better structure.

notes.explains: In this line of the Nimzo-Indian, Black's early ...c5 and ...Bb4 aim to create pressure along the long diagonal and hinder White's castling. If Black castles normally, White can achieve a favorable structure with more central control and fewer weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When facing a setup where the opponent tries to prevent castling, it's important to evaluate whether their commitment to that plan creates other weaknesses. If you can safely complete development, the resulting structure may favor you.
notes.plans: White should aim to complete development and castle, maintaining central control and exploiting Black's potential weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black's ...Ba6 is a direct attempt to stop White from castling, as the bishop pressures the long diagonal. However, this commits Black to a structure prematurely, and White can challenge the bishop on b4 before Black has finished development.
notes.teaches: When an opponent uses a piece to prevent castling, you can often challenge that piece before completing your own development, forcing them to deal with the threat and potentially gaining time.
notes.plans: White can play a3 to attack the bishop on b4, forcing Black to either retreat or capture, and potentially winning the c5 pawn if Black retreats to a5.

notes.explains: Black's best response to a3 is ...Bxc3, after which White recaptures with the knight. Black then faces difficulty defending the c5 pawn, so ...Qb6 is the standard move to guard it. White can then play Kf2, even though it seems counterintuitive with the queen on b6, but it's the best move.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the most natural-looking move (like Kf2) is correct even if it appears to walk into a check, if the king is actually safe and the move helps consolidate your position.
notes.plans: White plays Kf2, and if Black gives check with ...c4+, White can move the king to g3, finding a safe square where the king is protected and the opponent's pieces are ineffective.

notes.explains: After ...c4+ and Kg3, White's king is surprisingly safe on g3. The knight has no path to attack it, the bishop is shut out, and any dark-square check can be met by Bf4. Black's counterplay on b2 is a recurring theme, but White can handle it.
notes.teaches: In some structures, a king can be safe in front of the pawns if the opponent's pieces lack coordination. Evaluate the actual attacking chances rather than relying on general principles.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and aim to neutralize Black's counterplay on b2, while maintaining the safe king position.

notes.explains: When the king has to run out in front of the pawns, it usually signals trouble, but here the king is safe because the enemy knight has no path to attack it and the bishop is shut out. Any check on the dark squares can be met by Bf4, so the king is perfectly secure.
notes.teaches: A king that appears exposed can still be safe if the opponent lacks the pieces to exploit the open lines. Evaluate concrete attacking resources before fearing a king on the run.
notes.plans: Proceed with development and central play, knowing the king is not in danger.

notes.explains: Black's attempt to create counterplay with Qb8+ and Qxb2 fails because after the king is no longer checked, Bf4 is fine, and Rc1 traps the queen. In the game, Nb4 and Rab1 left white close to winning, with ideas like Bd6 and Nb5, while black's king remained stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen tries to raid your pawns, look for tactical refutations like trapping the queen with a rook. Also, a king stuck in the center is a major liability when the opponent has active pieces.
notes.plans: White should continue with central activity and target the weaknesses in black's camp, especially the weak b2 pawn is not a real issue.

notes.explains: After black castles kingside, white's knight on a4 kicks the queen, and then Nc5 gives white a clear advantage due to extra central space. Black's weaknesses force them to play catch-up, as seen with moves like Rf6, Bd2, Qa5+, Bf4, Qb6, and Bd6, leaving white clearly better.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, use it to restrict the opponent's pieces and force them to defend weaknesses. Active piece play in the center is often more important than material gains like a weak b2 pawn.
notes.plans: White can continue with h4 to bring the king back to safety and then attack on the kingside, but the main plan is to exploit black's structural weaknesses with active pieces.

notes.explains: In the line with ...d6 and ...c5, white often prefers Ne2 over Bd3 because it keeps the bishop flexible and avoids the possibility of black playing b5 and Bxc4, which would give black counterplay. The move Ne2 is more accurate in this specific structure.
notes.teaches: In the opening, consider the opponent's typical plans and choose moves that prevent them. Sometimes a knight move is more accurate than developing the bishop if it avoids a known pawn break.
notes.plans: White will continue with development and aim to maintain the central space advantage, while being ready for black's potential ...b5 break.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian structure, black's plan of b5 and Bxc4 is a key idea. If white develops the bishop to d3, black can immediately play b5, gaining a tempo because white has wasted a move to reach a similar position. Therefore, the more accurate move is Ne2, which avoids this and prepares to meet black's plan more effectively.
notes.teaches: When choosing a developing move, consider whether it allows the opponent to gain a tempo with a thematic pawn break. Sometimes a more flexible move, like Ne2 instead of Bd3, is better because it doesn't commit the bishop to a square where it can be attacked.
notes.plans: White plays Ne2, and black typically continues with b5, but only after completing development (castling and playing d6 to prevent e5). This is an improved version for black because it delays the pawn break until the king is safe and the center is solid.

notes.explains: After Ne2, black's main plan is to play b5 and then Bxc4, but only after developing. This is better than playing b5 immediately because black first ensures king safety and prevents white's e5 break. This is the most logical and common approach for black.
notes.teaches: In the opening, it's often better to complete development and secure the king before initiating pawn breaks in the center or on the flank. This avoids weakening your position or giving the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Black castles kingside, plays d6, and then initiates b5 and Bxc4. White must be prepared for this plan and choose a setup that can handle it.

notes.explains: After black's b5 and Bxc4, white has two main options: Nf4 or Ng3. Nf4 is more popular, but Ng3 is actually better because it prepares kingside play and avoids some tactical issues. Black has several possible responses, including Bxc4, Bb7, exd5, or waiting moves like Re8 or a6, making the position complex and fluid.
notes.teaches: When facing a flexible opponent, you must be prepared for multiple plans. Choosing a move that is less popular but more principled can be better if it addresses the key ideas of the position.
notes.plans: White plays Ng3, ready to castle and possibly launch a kingside attack with Nh5. Black must choose among several viable plans, each leading to different types of positions.

notes.explains: After ...c5 and ...cxd4, Black's structure remains weak in the center, and White has extra development and kingside chances. The move Nh5 is strong because it prepares Qg5 to force weaknesses and supports a future Nd5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a compromised pawn structure, prioritize completing development and applying pressure to those weaknesses rather than rushing to win material.
notes.plans: Play Nh5, then Qg5 to provoke g6, castle kingside, and aim for Nd5 to exploit the dark-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: In a line where Black delays ...bxc4 and White plays exd5, Black can castle and try to go pawn hunting with Qxb2. After Qb3, if Qxa1, White can develop the bishop to f1, and after Kxf1, Black must play ...e5. The resulting position has White with a queen for two rooks, but White is better because Black's pieces are uncoordinated and underdeveloped.
notes.teaches: Material imbalances like queen vs. two rooks are often decided by coordination and development; the side with better piece activity and safer king can be better despite the material deficit.
notes.plans: After ...e5, play Bg5 to create awkward threats, and if ...Nd7, then Nf5 to pressure the weak squares.

notes.explains: After castling kingside, White need not fear ...Bxc3 because the resulting position still favors White due to superior structure. In the game, Black played ...Ba6, and after Bxa6, Qxa6, and exd6/exd6, the position resembles earlier lines but with Black's pawn on e6 instead of f7. White's plan remains the same: pressure the d6 pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a structural advantage, you can often ignore threats to your pieces and focus on finishing development; the opponent's pawn weaknesses will remain a long-term liability.
notes.plans: Play Qb3 to pressure d6, then Bf4 and Rfd1 to increase the pressure, potentially winning the d6 pawn.

notes.explains: If Black plays the immediate ...Ba6, White can simply take with Bxa6, and after ...Nxa6, Black has not prevented castling. White castles and is slightly better due to the superior central structure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's move does not address your main plan, proceed with your development and rely on your structural edge to maintain an advantage.
notes.plans: Castle kingside and continue with standard development, using the central pawn majority to create pressure.

notes.explains: In this line, after Black plays ...Ba6 and White responds Bxa6 Nxa6, Black has not prevented White from castling. White's central pawn structure is superior, giving a slight edge.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's piece placement fails to disrupt your development, prioritize castling and rely on a sound central structure for a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: White should aim to pressure the d6 pawn and prepare a timely e5 break to attack the kingside.

notes.explains: Black's ...d5 push is a typical resource, but it does not solve all problems because the d5 pawn can become a target just like d6 was.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn break, evaluate whether the resulting pawn will be weak or strong; a pawn that becomes a target may not relieve pressure.
notes.plans: White should be ready to meet ...d5 by maintaining pressure on the center and possibly attacking the newly created weakness.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...exd5 and White recaptures cxd5, a new structure arises. White's plan is to pressure Black's queenside pawns with a4, exploiting the open bishop.
notes.teaches: In structures where the opponent has opened a diagonal for your bishop, use moves like a4 to create queenside pressure and target weak pawns.
notes.plans: White should play a4 to attack the queenside pawns, while Black must find a way to counter this pressure, often with moves like ...Ba5.

notes.explains: The line with ...exd5 is considered inferior for Black because Black is a couple of tempi short of organizing a useful response to White's a4.
notes.teaches: Tempo deficits matter in the opening; if the opponent's plan arrives faster than your counterplay, the position can become difficult.
notes.plans: White should proceed with a4 and maintain the initiative, while Black must seek active counterplay to avoid being overrun.

notes.explains: In this line, Black's bishop to a5 is the best way to avoid losing a pawn, as it prevents White from capturing on b5 without allowing Black to push a5 and create a pin on the a-file.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is attacked, sometimes the best defense is to place a piece so that the capture allows a counter-pin or a pawn push that regains the material.
notes.plans: After bishop a5, White can simply develop with bishop e2, maintaining the tension and leaving Black without a clear way to resolve the pressure.

notes.explains: Black has two typical ways to deal with the pressure on the light squares: b4 or c4. Both create weaknesses, but c4 is generally better because it doesn't weaken the light squares as much as b4 does.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two defensive pawn moves, prefer the one that leaves fewer permanent weaknesses in your camp, even if it is slower.
notes.plans: If Black plays c4, White can respond with king h1 to vacate the diagonal, then follow up with a5 and knight f5, targeting the weak d6 pawn.

notes.explains: After Black plays b4, White can reroute the knight to d2 and then to c4, exploiting the weakened light squares. Black's position becomes difficult because the light squares are permanently weak.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens their pawn structure, reroute your pieces to exploit the newly created weaknesses, even if it takes a few moves.
notes.plans: White can then play f4, a typical Benoni break, to challenge Black's central knight on d5, and follow up with b3 to prepare knight c4.

notes.explains: In the game, White chose to take on c4 with the pawn, but taking with the knight would have been even stronger, as it would have led to a nearly winning position.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece should do the recapturing based on the resulting piece activity and pawn structure. Sometimes the more active recapture is worth more than maintaining a pawn duo.
notes.plans: If White recaptures with the knight, the knight can go to e4, and after exchanges, White can develop the bishop to d3 and b2, maintaining strong pressure.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a strong center and active pieces. The move Nxc4 is much stronger than Bxc4 because it maintains the initiative and creates overwhelming activity, even if it doesn't win material directly.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and central control, prioritize maintaining the initiative over winning a pawn. Piece activity can be more valuable than material.
notes.plans: Continue to build pressure with moves like Bd3 and Bb2, aiming to keep Black's pieces passive and exploit the activity.

notes.explains: Black's setup with ...b5 and ...Bb7 aims to pressure the d5 pawn, but this plan is somewhat premature. White can respond with a3, forcing the bishop to make a decision and preventing Black from comfortably trading on c3.
notes.teaches: When an opponent tries to pressure a central pawn, you can use a pawn move like a3 to gain a tempo on the attacking piece and disrupt their plan.
notes.plans: After a3, if Black takes on c3, White can recapture and then use the intermezzo exf6 to create a favorable structure. If Black retreats the bishop, White can proceed with dxc6 and then a3, maintaining a solid center.

notes.explains: In this structure, White's pawn on c3 is valuable because it controls the d4 square, preventing Black from ever comfortably pushing ...d4. This gives White a lasting structural advantage.
notes.teaches: A pawn that controls key central squares can be a long-term asset. Even if it seems modest, it can restrict the opponent's plans and improve your own piece activity.
notes.plans: Aim to maintain the pawn on c3 and use it to support central and kingside operations.

notes.explains: After White plays a3, Black's bishop should retreat to a5 rather than capture on c3, because Black cannot comfortably push through to d4; White controls that square too well. The plan is to meet ...c6 with dxc6, forcing Black to recapture suboptimally with the f-pawn after the bishop leaves the defense of e6, and then White can claim the b5 pawn.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, retreating it can maintain pressure and force the opponent to weaken their structure. Punish an opponent's extra tempo by targeting the weaknesses they create.
notes.plans: After ...Bxd6, White will take on b5, gaining a pawn. If Black does not play ...d5 immediately, White will simply continue developing, relying on the favorable structure.

notes.explains: Black's immediate ...d5 is the correct response, creating a scary center and threats like ...d4. However, White has a tactical solution because the f-pawn has been drawn away: White can capture on d5. After exd5, White plays Be2, ignoring the threat of ...d4, and if Black plays ...d4, White has the tactic Be2-b4, exploiting the pin on the knight.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn break, look for tactical resources that exploit the opponent's weakened pawn structure. A pin can turn a scary-looking position into a favorable one.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...d4, White plays Bb4, and after the exchanges, White can play Qb3+ first to avoid a knight fork. Black may respond with ...Kh8 or ...Nd5, leading to a simplified but favorable position for White.

notes.explains: In the game, Black plays ...Kh8, and White continues with axb4, forcing the bishop back to c7, then White plays Na4, gaining time. Black tries ...Nbd7, castles, and ...Ne5, but White's structure is better: White is up a pawn, and the d4 pawn is a target. If Black does nothing, White can improve with Nc5, Qc2, Bb2, and rook to the center.
notes.teaches: When you have a structural advantage, you don't need to rush; improve your pieces and let the opponent feel the pressure. A protected passed pawn or a target like d4 can be a long-term asset.
notes.plans: White should finish development, bring the bishop to b2, and place rooks on central files, maintaining the structural edge. Black's attempt with ...Nh5 is a desperate tactical try that doesn't work.

notes.explains: In this position, White's structure is favorable due to the strong d4 pawn and active rooks, but the light squares around the king are vulnerable. Black's knight to h5 is a tactical resource that can lead to a knight fork on f3, undermining White's control of those light squares.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical shots that exploit weaknesses around the king, even when the overall structure seems favorable. A seemingly quiet move like Nh5 can carry hidden threats.
notes.plans: White should consider maintaining the extra piece with gxf3 if possible, rather than recapturing with the rook, which gives up the advantage. After Bh2+, Kf2 is a good try to keep things under control.

notes.explains: The tactical sequence involving Nh5, Nxf3+, and Bh2+ can lead to a draw by perpetual check or similar, as seen in the game. White's best defense is to keep the king safe and avoid material loss.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a tactical flurry leads to a drawish outcome and be willing to accept it if the alternative is worse. Also, be cautious about recapturing with the rook when a pawn recapture maintains material advantage.
notes.plans: If White can survive the attack, the better structure and extra piece should tell in the long run. Focus on consolidating and completing development.

notes.explains: In the opening line with a3, exd5, and cxd5, White gets a reasonable position. The threat of d5-d4 can be met by b4 with Qb3+ to save the position and finish development.
notes.teaches: In the opening, be aware of tactical resources that help you complete development while maintaining a sound pawn structure. Moves like b4 can create counterplay and deflect threats.
notes.plans: White should aim to finish development and then use the better structure to create pressure, while remaining vigilant about the light squares around the king.

notes.explains: The move …c5 in the Nimzo-Indian leads to complex positions with many possible structures. Historically, some lines were thought to be excellent for White, but Black has found ways to create counterplay.
notes.teaches: In complex openings, it's important to understand the typical structures and plans rather than memorizing long variations. Be ready for a wide range of setups.
notes.plans: White should be flexible and choose plans based on the specific structure that arises, often involving h4 to prevent Black's pawn breaks or a3 to challenge the bishop.

notes.explains: In the main line with d6, O-O, and b5, White's knight is best placed on g3, where it defends e4 and eyes the f5 square. Black's main options include Bxc4, exd5, and Bb7.
notes.teaches: Knight placement is crucial in the opening; a knight on g3 can be both defensive and offensive. Understanding the key squares for your pieces helps guide your plans.
notes.plans: White should continue with development, aiming to complete kingside castling and then decide on the best way to exploit the position, possibly with e5 or other central breaks.

notes.explains: In the …c5 variation of the f3 Nimzo-Indian, black's dark-squared plan leads to a rich landscape of possibilities. The position can branch into several distinct structures depending on black's choices, such as ...b5, ...Re8, ...a6, or immediate ...exd5, and even ...Nh5. Each of these creates different strategic motifs that must be understood separately.
notes.teaches: When studying a complex opening variation, break it down by the resulting pawn structures and piece placements. Instead of memorizing long move sequences, focus on the key ideas that arise from each structure.
notes.plans: Prepare to handle the main lines after ...c5, including the sharp ...b5 with e5, the flexible ...Re8, and the side moves ...a6, ...exd5, and ...Nh5. Recognize that the move order chosen by black may transpose to similar positions, so understanding the underlying plans is more important than exact move orders.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 f3 d5, if White plays a3 and Black captures, then after White recaptures, Black's choice of recapturing on d5 matters. If Black castles kingside first, then White can meet ...Nxd5 with e4, trapping the knight because it has no retreat squares. The tactical sequence involves sacrificing the c3 pawn, then using a bishop pin and a rook to eventually win the knight.
notes.teaches: When a knight lands on a central outpost with no retreat, look for ways to trap it, even if it requires a temporary pawn sacrifice. The key is to remember the pattern: if the opponent castles before taking on d5, you can punish ...Nxd5 with e4.
