notes.explains: After e4, the opponent's bishop on e5 is loose and the knight on d2 is poorly placed. Playing Nf3 attacks the bishop with tempo, improving the knight and preparing to open the center with d5.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed, look for a move that improves it while attacking an enemy piece, gaining time.
notes.plans: After Nf3, if the bishop retreats, take on d5 to open the center and activate the rook on d1.

notes.explains: The opponent is planning to castle kingside, but White has few attackers there. Instead of chasing the king, White can let the opponent castle and win material by taking on c5, winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: If you cannot attack the king, consider a positional approach: allow the castling but punish it with a tactic that wins material.
notes.plans: Play Be3, preparing to take on c5 if the opponent castles, winning the rook.

notes.explains: White played e4 to open the e-file and use the rook on e1. The opponent took the pawn on e5, but White can respond with Nf3, attacking the bishop and improving the knight.
notes.teaches: When you have a rook on an open file, try to open the file further to increase its power, even at the cost of a pawn.
notes.plans: After Nf3, if the bishop retreats, take on d5 and use the rook on d1 to pressure the queen side.

notes.explains: A knight on d2 can be poorly placed, and a bishop on e5 may be loose. By playing Nf3, the knight attacks the bishop and gains a tempo, improving its position while forcing the bishop to move.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that improve your worst-placed piece while gaining a tempo by attacking an enemy piece. This is a common way to increase pressure without committing pawns.
notes.plans: After the knight improves, consider opening the center with a capture on d5 and activating the rook on d1 to target the enemy king.

notes.explains: The bishop on a6 is passive and not contributing. The ideal scenario is to trade the dark-squared bishops, leaving the opponent with a useless bishop while our knight dominates the dark squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a bad piece, aim to trade off the pieces that are actually useful to them, leaving them with the bad ones. Control of a color complex can be decisive.
notes.plans: Seek to trade the dark-squared bishops and then exploit the dark-square weaknesses, using the knight to dominate the bishop.

notes.explains: Playing h3 is not just a defensive move; it prevents the opponent from gaining counterplay with ...Bg4 or ...h3. It takes away all counterplay and solidifies our space advantage.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like h3 can be crucial in positions where you have a space advantage. Preventing the opponent's counterplay is often more important than immediate attacking moves.
notes.plans: After h3, continue improving pieces and preparing an attack, knowing the opponent has no active resources.

notes.explains: The rook on a1 has been ignored, so bringing it to d1 improves it and creates a sneaky threat: the knight on d2 can jump to e4 and then to d6, a strong outpost.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to activate your rooks, especially in the middlegame. A rook lift can also create hidden tactical threats, such as a knight maneuver to a key square.
notes.plans: Play Rfd1, threatening Ne4 followed by Nd6, and if the opponent prevents it, the rook still exerts pressure on the d-file.

notes.explains: The rook on a1 has been idle while the other pieces developed. Moving it to d1 improves the rook and creates a concrete threat: the knight on d2 can jump to e4, aiming for d6, a strong outpost that would be very annoying for the opponent.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to bring your least active piece into play, especially when it also creates threats. A quiet rook move can set up tactical ideas like a knight hopping to a dominant square.
notes.plans: If the opponent ignores the threat, play Ne4 and then Nd6, establishing a powerful knight. If they prevent it, use the rook to support central or queenside expansion.

notes.explains: The opponent is low on time and relying on a defensive resource like Rh8 to hold. The immediate tactical strike Ne4 is tempting, but it doesn't work because of that defense. Instead, playing c4 opens the position and exposes the enemy king, especially after the d5 pawn disappears.
notes.teaches: When a direct tactic fails due to a specific defensive move, look for a quieter move that improves your position and increases the pressure. Opening the position can be more effective than forcing a line that the opponent can defend.
notes.plans: Continue to open lines and bring more pieces to the attack. The opponent's passivity means they will struggle to find active counterplay, so keep creating threats and avoid allowing them to consolidate.

notes.explains: The opponent's pieces are poorly placed: the rook on h8 has never moved, and the other rook has only made a useless move. They are trying to stay solid but have no active plan. Moves like Bb6 or Qb7 don't solve the fundamental problems of passivity and exposed king.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is passive, avoid giving them counterplay. Keep your pieces coordinated and look for ways to increase the pressure without allowing them to trade off or escape. Patience is key when you have a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: Bring the remaining pieces into the attack, especially the rook on e1. Aim to create threats that force the opponent to defend, and be ready to exploit any inaccuracies they make under time pressure.

notes.explains: The rook on e1 has done its job, so it's time to bring the other rook into the game. The move Rd6 is provocative: it invites the opponent to play Be7, which would allow a tactical finish: Rxe6, fxe6, Qg6, winning material. The opponent instead plays Rf5, but then the rook on d1 is redeployed to d1, preparing Rd7 or other invasions.
notes.teaches: In an attack, every piece should have a role. When one piece has fulfilled its purpose, redeploy it to a more active square. Provocative moves can lure the opponent into mistakes, especially when they are short on time.
notes.plans: Continue to build pressure, aiming for a decisive invasion. If the opponent takes on e5, Qf4 attacks the rook and threatens to invade on h6 or f8. Be alert to tactical motifs like back-rank mates or discovered attacks.

notes.explains: The opponent plays Rh5 to cover the h6 square, but this allows Rxe6, which is decisive because it leads to mate. The attack has reached its climax, and the opponent's defensive resources have run out.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, keep calculating concrete variations. The opponent's defensive moves may create new weaknesses, so be ready to switch from positional pressure to direct tactics. A single oversight can end the game.
notes.plans: Execute the winning tactic and convert the advantage. After Rxe6, the threats are overwhelming, and the opponent resigned.

notes.explains: In this London System setup, after an early ...c5 and a trade on c5, White's d4-pawn is gone, so the usual central structure is altered. Black's ...Qc7 prepares ...Nbd7 and ...e5, a typical freeing idea.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent's move order aims for a central break like ...e5; if you can prevent or preempt it, you keep the initiative.
notes.plans: White should avoid passive moves like castling short, which would concede the center for nothing; instead, look for active central play with e4.

notes.explains: With the center fluid, White plays Qe2 to support an immediate e4-e5 push. After Black takes on g3, White recaptures, increasing pressure on h7. King safety becomes key: castling short would reduce the attack, so long castling is preferred to keep the initiative.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and an attack, prioritize keeping the initiative over king safety; long castling can maintain attacking chances.
notes.plans: White aims to launch e4 before Black's ...e5, then continue the attack against the black king.

notes.explains: In the critical moment after the e4-e5 exchange, White must choose between recapturing with the queen or the bishop. Queen takes is natural but allows ...Nf6, forcing the queen to move and losing time. Bishop takes is sneaky, setting a trap.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece maintains the attack best; sometimes a less natural recapture sets a trap and keeps pressure on the opponent's position.
notes.plans: White plays Bxf6, creating a tactical threat that Black may overlook by playing the obvious ...Nf6.

notes.explains: The queen is placed on e2 to support the e4-e5 push and to stay in front of the bishop for potential mating threats. Queen c2 would not support these ideas and would be less active.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for the queen, consider which pawn breaks and attacking ideas it supports. A queen that only defends without creating threats is often misplaced.
notes.plans: Support the e4-e5 break and keep the queen active for attacking chances.

notes.explains: Black's knight maneuver to f6 and then e5 is a natural but flawed idea. After the bishop is captured, Black falls behind in development and has no active pieces, while White's pieces are all aimed at the king.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, development and activity matter more than material. A natural-looking move that loses time can be punished by a direct attack.
notes.plans: Continue the attack against the black king, using the lead in development to create threats before Black can coordinate.

notes.explains: Black's queen e7 aims to play f6 and e5, but this is too slow. White's attack on the kingside is faster, and Black's queenside play (like b5) is not a real threat because White can block with c4 and b3.
notes.teaches: When attacking, it's a race: who gets to the king first. Don't be distracted by slow counterplay on the other side; focus on the attack.
notes.plans: Continue the kingside attack, possibly with g4-g5, and be ready to meet queenside pawn pushes with c4 and b3 to keep the position closed.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king is exposed and their pieces are undeveloped, the priority is to attack the king rather than chase material on the queenside. The race is about who delivers mate first, not about pawn grabbing.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions with opposite-side attacks, focus on the king attack; if your attack lands first, the opponent's queenside play is irrelevant.
notes.plans: Continue the attack against the enemy king, using pieces to create threats and force weaknesses.

notes.explains: The opponent's move queen e7 aims to prepare f6 and e5, but it is passive and allows a strong pawn break with f4. This break prevents the freeing move f6 and opens lines against the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a freeing pawn break, use your own pawn break to preempt it and open attacking lines.
notes.plans: Play f4 to stop f6, then follow up with rook lifts and sacrifices to expose the king.

notes.explains: After the opponent's pieces remain undeveloped, the attacker can simplify to a winning endgame or keep the pressure. Trading queens is a way to convert while maintaining a material advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a material or positional edge, offering a queen trade can be a practical way to convert, especially if the opponent's pieces are stuck.
notes.plans: Offer queen trades to reach a won endgame, or use the queen to create mating threats if the opponent declines.

notes.explains: The London System is a solid opening that requires less preparation than sharp mainlines, making it suitable for players with limited study time. It still offers attacking chances if the opponent errs.
notes.teaches: Choose openings that fit your practical needs; a sound, easy-to-play system can be effective even at high levels.

notes.explains: When you have limited time to study, choose an opening that is easy to play and requires less memorization, allowing you to focus on other aspects of the game.
notes.teaches: Select openings that are straightforward and reliable, so you can play them confidently even with minimal preparation.

notes.explains: After the opponent offers a queen trade, you can decline if you have a strong attack or better piece activity. Here, the knight on d6 controls key squares and prevents the opponent from using the d-file, as any rook entry would be met with a capture that wins material.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are well-placed, don't be afraid to avoid queen trades to keep the initiative and maintain attacking chances.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece coordination and look for ways to exploit the opponent's weakened king position.

notes.explains: In a winning position, there may be multiple good moves. Here, both knight c8 and knight f5 lead to strong threats, but the chosen move (knight f5) sets up a mating net while keeping the bishop on the board for aesthetic reasons.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive advantage, look for the most forcing and elegant continuation, but ensure it is still objectively winning.
notes.plans: After the opponent's reply, deliver checkmate or win decisive material.

notes.explains: The opponent had a defensive resource (king g8) that would have allowed a beautiful mating sequence: queen f8, king takes, rook d8 mate. This shows the importance of considering the opponent's best defensive tries and having a plan for them.
notes.teaches: Always anticipate the opponent's most stubborn defense and prepare the most forcing continuation to convert the win.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays king g8, execute the queen sacrifice and rook mate.

notes.explains: The London System is often considered a solid, even boring opening, but it can be played dynamically with sharp ideas and tactics, leading to a good advantage.
notes.teaches: Even 'boring' openings can be played aggressively if you look for tactical opportunities and dynamic piece play.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 c3 d5, if White plays cxd4, Black should avoid allowing doubled pawns on c6. Instead, Black can play …Ne5, hitting the bishop on f3, forcing it to retreat, and preventing the doubling.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, avoid creating permanent weaknesses like doubled pawns unless necessary. Proactive moves that harass the opponent's pieces can help maintain a sound structure.
notes.plans: Black should consider …Ne5 to keep the pawn structure intact and gain a tempo on the bishop.

notes.explains: After …Nf6, White's most testing reply is e5, attacking the knight. Black has two main options: …Ne4 or …Nd5. If Black plays …Ne4, White can respond with Qe2, harassing the knight. Black must then support it with f5 or d5; otherwise, moving the knight again wastes time and allows White to capture on d4 with a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, it's often better to support it with a pawn move that also gains space, rather than retreating and losing tempo. Central pawn advances can be more valuable than flank pawn moves.
notes.plans: Black should choose between …f5 and …d5 to maintain the knight on e4. Prefer …d5 after …f5? Actually, the idea is to play f5 first, then after exf6, play d5, keeping a central pawn supporting the knight.

notes.explains: In the line with …Nd5, White should prioritize rapid development over material gains. For example, after Qb3, Black can play …Nb6 and then …d6, putting pressure on the center. White should instead develop minor pieces to coordinate an attack.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, development is paramount. Grabbing pawns or wasting time can lead to a poor position. Focus on getting pieces out quickly and creating threats.
notes.plans: White should develop pieces harmoniously, aiming to castle quickly and create pressure on Black's position.

notes.explains: In a line where White has sacrificed a pawn for development, White should not greedily grab the g7 pawn. After ...Bxg7, Black gets pressure on c3 and a lead in development, making it hard for White to catch up. Instead, White should continue developing, e.g., with Nbd2, and after ...Qxf6, recapture on e4, etc.
notes.teaches: When playing a gambit, the compensation comes from activity and development, not from regaining material. Avoid distractions like capturing flank pawns if it allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: White should aim to complete development, castle, and use the open files and diagonals to create threats.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 c3 d5, White has several tries. One is Qb3, but this neglects development; Black can calmly play ...d6, pressuring the center and opening the bishop, leaving White to deal with the position.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, prioritize developing minor pieces before bringing the queen out; a premature queen sortie can be met by solid central play.
notes.plans: White should focus on development, e.g., Bb5, while Black can develop naturally with ...Be6, ...Qd7, ...Be7, and castle.

notes.explains: If White plays Bb5, the game can transpose into a Marshall-like attack in the Ruy Lopez. Black can respond with ...a6, ...Nge7, or ...Nb6, and after ...Nxd4, White recaptures, leading to a sharp position where both bishops target the kingside.
notes.teaches: Recognize transpositions to familiar attacking setups; in such positions, g3 is often necessary to blunt mating threats, and h3 can be too slow.
notes.plans: Black should aim for ...d5 to open the center, then develop with ...Be6 and ...Nd4, while White must address the kingside pressure with precise moves like g3.

notes.explains: The main move is cxd4, giving White a solid center. Black can then play ...Bb4+ check, or choose ...d6 to keep more pieces on the board and maintain fighting chances.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, you can either simplify to equality or keep pieces on to preserve winning chances; both are viable depending on your style.
notes.plans: After ...Bb4+, White has limited options; the natural Nc3 is losing due to tactics, so White must find the correct response. If Black plays ...d6, the game continues with normal development, and White's bishop can become a strong attacker.

notes.explains: After the gambit is declined with …d5, White should not grab the d4 pawn because Black recaptures on e4, leaving the knight misplaced. Instead, White should develop and keep the bishop pair, as trading the bishop for the knight is favorable for White.
notes.teaches: In the Göring Gambit declined, prioritize development and the bishop pair over winning back a pawn immediately. A natural-looking recapture can lead to a loss of initiative.
notes.plans: Develop with moves like Nf3, Bd3, and castle, aiming to put pressure on Black's center and queenside.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight, and White must choose between Bd2 or Nbd2. Nbd2 is preferable because it keeps the bishop on the board, and if Black trades the bishop for the knight, White gets the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: When facing a pin, consider which piece to block with based on long-term piece value. Keeping the bishop pair can be a strategic asset.
notes.plans: After resolving the pin, continue development and prepare to castle, then target Black's queenside weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black's knight on d5 is a key piece. White can provoke it to move by attacking it with c4, but if Black retreats, White's bishop on c4 hits the knight, forcing it to move again, misplacing Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: Use pawn breaks to challenge an opponent's central knight, forcing it to move and disrupting their coordination.
notes.plans: Play c4 to attack the knight, and if it retreats, follow with Bc4 to keep it under pressure.

notes.explains: After a sequence of trades, White can trap Black's knight on a1 with Bd3, preventing Black from playing c6 to fork. This is a key tactical resource that gives White an advantage.
notes.teaches: In tactical skirmishes, look for ways to trap an enemy piece that has gone deep into your position. A retreating bishop can be a powerful tool.
notes.plans: Play Bd3 to trap the knight, then develop the rook and prepare to exploit the extra piece.

notes.explains: After White castles and gives up the e5 pawn, the resulting endgame has both sides with two rooks and a minor piece, but Black has a slightly worse pawn structure. White can develop the rook and attack Black's weak pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity and pawn structure are key. Sacrificing a pawn to activate your rook can be a sound strategy.
notes.plans: Develop the rook to an open file, target Black's doubled or isolated pawns, and use the minor piece to support the attack.

notes.explains: After …d5, White should not play exd5? because Black recaptures with the knight, and White's knight is forced to move to g5, allowing Black to develop with initiative via Bb4+. White's pawns become targets.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, be wary of recaptures that give the opponent the initiative. Sometimes it's better to decline the pawn and maintain a solid structure.
notes.plans: Instead of capturing on d5, consider developing pieces and keeping the center fluid.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 c3 d5, White's attempt to keep the center closed with e5 is weak. Black can respond with …Nxe5, and after dxe4, Black plays …d4, gaining space and attacking. White must try to win the pawn back, but Black can develop with ...Bc5, holding everything. White ends up just developing while being pushed around, and Black's position is solid with no weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When a gambit pawn is offered, sometimes the best way to refute it is to return the material to gain a central pawn majority and active piece play. A pawn on d4 supported by pieces can be a strong asset.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing, aiming to maintain the strong d4 pawn and exploit White's lack of central control. White should focus on completing development and finding counterplay against Black's center.

notes.explains: Another White idea is Bd3, supporting the e4 pawn. This is a developing move but somewhat passive. Black can respond with …Bg4, pinning the knight, and after White castles, …Nf6 hits the e4 pawn again. White supports with Re1, placing the rook on a semi-open file. Black should play …Be7, closing the e-file before White can capture on d5. If White plays e5, the knight retreats, and White may try Bb5, aiming to double Black's c-pawns.
notes.teaches: In the opening, when your opponent has a central pawn chain, it's important to challenge it with piece pressure. Also, preventing your opponent from opening a file against your king is a key defensive idea.
notes.plans: Black will maintain the solid structure, possibly accepting doubled c-pawns to keep the king safe and open the b-file for the rook. White will try to exploit the doubled pawns as a long-term target.

notes.explains: After …d5, White's main try is exd5, and Black's only good response is …Qxd5. There's no need to move the knight and waste time; just recapture with the queen. Normally, this would allow White to gain time with Nc3, but because White's c-pawn is already on c3, that move is not available. Black can then develop with ...Bc5 or ...Bb4, and ...Bg4 is a natural move, preparing to castle queenside.
notes.teaches: When recapturing in the center, consider using the queen if it doesn't lose time due to the opponent's pawn structure. Also, developing pieces with tempo and preparing a safe king position (queenside castling) can be part of a solid opening strategy.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing, aiming to castle queenside and put pressure on White's center. White will try to complete development and find active play, possibly targeting Black's queen.

notes.explains: In the line after exd5 Qxd5, Black can allow White to double the c-pawns with ...Bxc3+ and ...Qxc3, because this prevents White from castling. The white king remains stuck in the center, which is a significant drawback. Black can then castle queenside and develop normally, not fearing the doubled pawns. This position is at least equal for Black, as confirmed by a top-level player.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always a weakness; they can be acceptable if they come with concrete benefits, such as preventing the opponent from castling or opening a file for your rook. King safety is often more important than pawn structure.
notes.plans: Black will castle queenside and aim to open the center while White's king is vulnerable. White will try to trade queens and find a safe square for the king, but this is difficult.

notes.explains: In the Göring Gambit accepted, after …dxc3 Nxc3, White may also try Bc4, leading to a position similar to the Danish Gambit. However, Black is one move faster than in the normal Danish, so White's attacking chances are reduced. White might have ideas of castling queenside and playing h4, but the typical sacrifices on f7 are not as effective here.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, the exact move order matters. A single tempo can make the difference between a sound attack and a dubious one. Recognizing when the opponent's attack is too slow is key to defense.
notes.plans: Black should aim to consolidate and complete development, being careful not to fall for tactical tricks. White will try to generate kingside attacking chances, but Black's extra tempo should allow for a solid defense.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 c3 d5, White's bishop to c4 is a natural developing move, but Black's early ...d5 has accelerated the counterplay compared to the Danish Gambit. White's attacking chances on f7 are less potent because Black is a tempo ahead.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, the speed of development is critical. If the opponent has advanced a central pawn early, it can blunt your attacking ideas, so you must adjust your plans accordingly.
notes.plans: White should focus on rapid development and castling queenside, while being aware that the f7 sacrifice is not as effective as in the standard Danish Gambit.

notes.explains: Black has several defensive options after Bc4. The move ...Bb4 transposes to a London Defense setup, which is a solid choice. Other moves like ...Bc5 or ...Be7 lead to different tactical possibilities, but ...Nf6 is the most natural developing move.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, you can often transpose to known solid setups. Developing knights and bishops to natural squares is usually reliable, while trying to hold onto the pawn with artificial moves can backfire.
notes.plans: Black should aim for ...Nf6, ...d6, ...Be7, and castling kingside, consolidating the extra pawn.

notes.explains: White's best move is to recapture with the knight on c3, developing a piece. Taking back with the pawn is a mistake because it leaves White with a poor pawn structure and no compensation for the pawn deficit. Immediate queen attacks like Qb3 are too slow.
notes.teaches: In gambit play, you must prioritize development over material. Recapturing with a piece that develops is often better than with a pawn, and slow queen sorties rarely generate enough pressure.
notes.plans: White should play Nxc3, developing the knight, and then continue with Bc4, Nf3, and Qb3 to create threats against f7.

notes.explains: After …d6, Black intends a defensive setup with ...Be7. White can build pressure with Bc4, Nf3, and Qb3, attacking f7. Black's best response is ...Qd7, keeping e7 free for the bishop, rather than ...Qe7 which blocks the bishop and hinders castling.
notes.teaches: When defending against an attack on f7, it's important to keep lines open for your pieces. Placing the queen on d7 can be more flexible than e7, as it allows the bishop to develop and castling to occur smoothly.
notes.plans: White can try Ng5 to increase pressure on f7, while Black should aim to consolidate with ...Be7 and ...O-O.

notes.explains: In the sharp line after ...d6, White can play Ng5, and Black can respond with ...Ne5, defending f7 and attacking the queen. White might then try Bb5, c6, and f4 to break through. Black should avoid trading queens prematurely, as being a pawn up means keeping queens can create winning chances.
notes.teaches: In tactical battles, every move must serve a dual purpose. Defending a key square while attacking an enemy piece is a common motif. Also, when you are up material, you often want to keep pieces on the board to increase your winning chances.
notes.plans: White can aim for f4 to open lines, while Black should maintain the extra pawn and seek to simplify only if it leads to a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: In this Göring Gambit line, White has sacrificed a pawn for development. Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3, and White's compensation depends on active piece play. The position is balanced if White can develop harmoniously, but Black's pin and extra pawn give them a comfortable edge if White falters.
notes.teaches: When you are down a pawn, you should avoid creating additional weaknesses and keep pieces active to generate counterplay. Conversely, when you are up material, trade pieces and simplify to reduce your opponent's attacking chances.
notes.plans: White should aim to castle, break the pin, and prepare central play, while Black should look to consolidate the extra pawn and exchange pieces to reach a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: Black's move d6 is a key prophylactic move, preventing White from playing e5 and kicking the knight on f6. This mirrors the Sicilian Defense idea where d6 controls e5 and prepares to develop the bishop to g4.
notes.teaches: In open games, a timely d6 can prevent a central pawn push that would gain space and harass your pieces. Always consider prophylactic moves that restrict your opponent's pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Black should follow up with Nf6, Bg4, and natural development, while White should castle and seek active piece play to justify the pawn deficit.

notes.explains: White has the option of an exchange sacrifice on f6 to double Black's kingside pawns and open the f-file for attack. This is a critical resource that both sides must be aware of, as it can create long-term attacking chances for White despite the material deficit.
notes.teaches: Exchange sacrifices can be a valid way to create weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure and open lines for your pieces. When considering such sacrifices, evaluate whether the resulting pawn structure and open files give you sufficient compensation.
notes.plans: White may prepare f4-f5 or Rxf6 to initiate the sacrifice, while Black should be vigilant and consider moves that prevent the f-file from opening, such as timely pawn moves or piece placement.

notes.explains: White's bishop on c4 eyes the f7 pawn, and Black must be careful about tactics involving Qd5 or Bxf7+. Black's d6 move also protects the bishop on c5, preventing such tactics.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, look for tactical motifs like bishop sacrifices on f7 and queen checks. Defenders should anticipate these threats and make prophylactic moves that guard key squares.
notes.plans: Black should ensure their king's safety and avoid weakening squares around the king, while White should look for opportunities to exploit the f7 weakness if Black errs.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3, and Black has the option to capture on c3, doubling White's pawns and creating permanent weaknesses. White must avoid this by breaking the pin or moving the knight to a better square like d5.
notes.teaches: Pins can be used to create structural damage in the opponent's camp. When you have a pin, consider whether capturing the pinned piece will leave your opponent with lasting weaknesses. The defender should prioritize breaking the pin or relocating the pinned piece.
notes.plans: Black should consider Bxc3 to inflict structural damage, while White should aim to castle and then possibly play Nd5 to avoid the pin and centralize the knight.

notes.explains: White's queen on b3 attacks f7, but Black can defend with Qe7 or block with c5. White's attempts to create threats are often met with accurate defense, leaving White without sufficient compensation for the pawn.
notes.teaches: When you are down material, you need concrete threats to justify the deficit. If your opponent can defend accurately and neutralize your pressure, you should reassess and possibly simplify to a more tenable endgame.
notes.plans: White may try to maintain pressure, but if Black defends accurately, White should consider consolidating and minimizing weaknesses. Black should look to trade queens and transition to a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: In this Göring Gambit position, Black has just played d5, returning the pawn to reach a comfortable setup. White's queen on b3 attacks f7, but Black can defend with Qe7, and after Ba3, c5 blocks the bishop's pressure. The resulting exchanges leave Black with a sound position and no real weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, returning the pawn to reach a solid, active position is often a good practical choice. Defending accurately against immediate threats can neutralize the attacker's initiative.
notes.plans: Black should aim to complete development and maintain the extra pawn if possible, or ensure a healthy pawn structure if material is equalized.

notes.explains: Black has a strong tactical resource: Ne4, hitting the bishop on c3 and the pawn on c3, while also threatening Nxd2 forking the queen and rook. This move creates multiple threats and puts White under pressure.
notes.teaches: Centralized knights can create powerful tactical threats. When a knight lands on a central outpost, it can attack multiple targets and force the opponent to respond defensively.
notes.plans: Black should play Ne4 to create threats, and if White defends with Qa3, Black can continue with Qc6 to pressure the bishop, maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: White's counterintuitive defensive move Qa3 is the only way to stop Black's threats: it protects the c3 pawn, covers d2, and indirectly defends the bishop. This shows that sometimes the best defense is a non-obvious move that addresses all threats simultaneously.
notes.teaches: When facing multiple threats, look for a move that addresses all of them at once, even if it seems unnatural. Defensive resources can be creative and counterintuitive.
notes.plans: White should play Qa3 to neutralize Black's Ne4 idea, then continue with development and try to consolidate.

notes.explains: After Qc6, White can take on a7, but must be careful because Black can try to trap the bishop with b6. White can navigate the complications with Rf1, f6, Qb4, and eventually give up the bishop for the knight on f2, reaching a position where material is equal but Black's pawns are healthier.
notes.teaches: In sharp tactical battles, it's important to calculate forcing sequences accurately. Sometimes sacrificing material for activity or to reach a favorable pawn structure is the best practical outcome.
notes.plans: White should aim to survive the complications and reach an endgame where the extra pawns are not enough to win, while Black should press for a win with the better pawn structure.

notes.explains: In the resulting endgame, although material is equal, Black's pawns are healthier and more mobile. White's doubled or isolated pawns are difficult to advance, while Black can slowly push a pawn majority. This makes Black's position preferable, and White should play for a draw.
notes.teaches: Pawn structure is a long-term factor that can outweigh material equality. In endgames, healthy pawns and pawn majorities are crucial for winning chances.
notes.plans: Black should advance the pawn majority and create a passed pawn, while White should aim to blockade and trade down to a drawn endgame.

notes.explains: After d4, Black must play actively or White will consolidate and remain a pawn up for nothing. The most active move is Bd6, attacking the rook on e5 and clearing the way for Qh4.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions with a material deficit, development and activity matter more than material. Look for moves that combine attack and development.
notes.plans: Black plays Bd6, then Qh4, aiming at h2 and preparing Bg4. White should play Re1 to meet the threats.

notes.explains: Qh4 is a justified early queen sortie because Black's development is nearly complete and the queen supports the light-squared bishop's future move to g4. It also creates immediate mating threats on h2.
notes.teaches: The rule 'don't bring the queen out early' has exceptions when the queen participates in a direct attack and supports piece development.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with f5-f4, increasing pressure on the kingside. White must find precise defensive moves, often starting with g3.

notes.explains: If White fails to play g3 and tries h3 instead, Black can play Bxh3, and if White recaptures, Qxh3 wrecks the kingside. White's best defense is g3, creating a pawn barrier for the bishop.
notes.teaches: When facing a mating attack, the correct defensive move is often a pawn move that blunts the attacker's pieces, not a move that appears to block the immediate threat.
notes.plans: White plays g3, and Black continues with Re5, sacrificing the exchange to maintain the attack.

notes.explains: After g3, Black plays Re5, and if White captures, Black recaptures and then plays Rae8, pressuring the e-pawn. This rook lift is a common and automatic move for Black in this structure.
notes.teaches: Rooks belong on open files and can be used to increase pressure on weak pawns. In attacking positions, it's often worth sacrificing material to keep the initiative.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Rae8, then capture on d5 with the pawn, keeping the queen active. White must develop pieces (e.g., Bf4) to defend.

notes.explains: In the ensuing play, Black's rook swings to g6, and after f5-f4, the bishop on g3 is trapped. White must be careful about recapture options; en passant allows Rxg3, and other captures lead to a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked by a pawn, consider all recapture options and the resulting king safety. Inserting checks (like Qh3+) can be crucial to avoid counterplay.
notes.plans: Black pushes f4, and if White takes en passant, Rook takes g3. If White doesn't, the pawn advances to f4, winning the bishop. Black must ensure the correct move order to avoid letting White escape.

notes.explains: In this sharp Marshall Attack position, Black has a mating attack building against White's king. The immediate capture on f6 is tempting, but White can defend with Qh5, so Black must first insert Qh3+ to force the king to g1 and remove that defensive resource.
notes.teaches: When executing a mating attack, check for the opponent's defensive resources before committing to a capture. Inserting a check can force the king to a worse square and neutralize key defensive moves.
notes.plans: Black should play Qh3+ first, then after Kg1, take on f6 with the rook, continuing the attack.

notes.explains: White cannot defend with h3 because it allows the mating attack to proceed; instead, g3 is necessary to give the king an escape square and attack the queen. After g3, Black's queen retreats to h3, preparing Bg4 and Bf3, threatening mate on g2.
notes.teaches: When facing a mating attack, consider pawn moves that create luft and also attack the enemy queen. Prophylactic thinking is crucial: anticipate the opponent's threats and find moves that address multiple issues.
notes.plans: White should play g3, and after Qh3, be ready to meet the Bg4-Bf3 plan with Qd3 and Qf1.

notes.explains: White's bishop belongs on e3, not g5, because on g5 it can be kicked away by h6 and has no influence. From e3, it solidifies the position and allows the knight to maneuver to d2 and f1 for defense.
notes.teaches: In cramped defensive positions, place pieces on squares where they are secure and support the king's defense, even if it means giving up the bishop pair. Development should serve the immediate needs of the position.
notes.plans: White plays Be3, then after Bg4, Qd3, keeping an eye on f1 to meet Bf3 with Qf1.

notes.explains: After Be3, Black continues with Bg4 attacking the queen. White's only move is Qd3, because the queen must keep an eye on f1 to meet the threat of Bf3 with Qf1. Other moves like Nd2 hang the queen, and f3 allows Bxg3 with a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the queen must be placed on an awkward-looking square to fulfill a defensive role. Recognize when a piece has a critical function and avoid moving it without a replacement.
notes.plans: White plays Qd3, and if Bf3, then Qf1, neutralizing the mate threat.

notes.explains: If Black's knight captures on e3, White should recapture with the rook, not the f-pawn. Taking with the f-pawn opens the king and allows Bxg3, leading to a lost position because the king cannot escape to e2 and Black can bring the rook to the e-file.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, prefer the piece that keeps the king's pawn shield intact. Avoid pawn recaptures that expose the king and create weaknesses.
notes.plans: White recaptures with the rook on e3, maintaining a solid defense.

notes.explains: In this Marshall Attack tabiya, black's knight on e3 is a poisoned gift: if white recaptures with the f-pawn, black plays Bxg3, and after the forced recapture with the queen, the white king is exposed on f1 and cannot escape to e2. White's rook on e5 is well placed to recapture on e3, keeping the kingside pawn structure intact.
notes.teaches: When a piece is offered on a square that a rook can recapture, prefer the rook over a pawn recapture if the pawn recapture opens the king. Always check if the recapture square is safe for the king before taking with a pawn.
notes.plans: If black captures on e3, white recaptures with the rook, then plays Nd2 and Re1 to complete development and neutralize black's initiative.

notes.explains: Black's rook lift to e8 is a standard attacking move that also prepares to double rooks or swing to e6. White's best response is Nd2, because the rook on e8 does not create an immediate threat, allowing white to catch up in development.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a non-threatening developing move, you can often use the tempo to improve your own position. Recognize when a move is 'automatic' for the opponent and not a real threat.
notes.plans: Black will follow with Re6, putting pressure on the e-file and eyeing the bishop on e3. White should continue with Nd2 and then consider a4 to start queenside counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's queen to h5 is a key attacking move with two purposes: it keeps the queen and bishop coordinated on the b1-h7 diagonal, and it ensures that if white captures on d5, the queen can recapture without compromising the c6 pawn structure. White's bishop to f3 is not good because it allows black to force a queen trade after Qf1, which reduces black's attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for the queen in an attack, consider both coordination with other pieces and the ability to recapture on key squares. Avoid forcing queen trades when you have the initiative.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Re6 and Qh5, maintaining pressure. White should play a4 to start queenside play and prepare f3 to disrupt black's coordination.

notes.explains: In the line with Qf1 first, black has the surprising rook move Re7, which defends the bishop and prepares to meet f3 with captures on e3. After f3, black can sacrifice the piece on e3, but white's queen to f2 creates a double attack, forcing black to give up material. This leads to an endgame where white is not mated but is likely worse.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn thrust like f3, look for tactical resources that allow you to sacrifice material to maintain the initiative or force a favorable endgame. Sometimes giving up a piece is better than allowing a mating attack.
notes.plans: If white plays Qf1 first, black should play Re7, and after f3, capture on e3, leading to a complex endgame where black has good chances. White should prefer a4 to avoid this.

notes.explains: The position is dynamically balanced: both sides have only moves that stop the opponent's threats. White is not passive because they are actively preventing black's mate threats while creating their own counterplay, and black also has to be precise to stop white's ideas.
notes.teaches: Having only moves does not mean you are passive; it means the position is sharp and both sides are under pressure. Evaluate activity by whether your moves are creating threats or just waiting.

notes.explains: Black's queen goes to h5 instead of h6 to keep the bishop pair together on the diagonal and to be able to recapture on d5 without compromising the c6 pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a queen, consider both the immediate tactical threats and the long-term structural consequences of pawn recaptures.
notes.plans: Black will use the queen on h5 to pressure the kingside and maintain flexibility in the center.

notes.explains: White cannot play on the kingside without compromising king safety, and the center is blocked by active black pieces, so the only viable plan is queenside counterplay with a4.
notes.teaches: When one side is attacking on the kingside, the defender should seek counterplay on the opposite wing rather than passively defending.
notes.plans: White plays a4 to create pressure against black's queenside pawns and pieces.

notes.explains: Black's queen on h5 anticipates a future queen to f1 by black, saving a tempo, and overdefends d5 to keep the pawn structure clean.
notes.teaches: A well-placed queen can serve multiple purposes, including saving tempi and reinforcing key squares.
notes.plans: Black continues to consolidate the center and prepare further kingside pressure.

notes.explains: After white survives the initial kingside attack, the main line involves knight to f1, and black's bishop goes to f5 attacking the queen, leading to a sequence where white's bishop goes to d1 with tempo.
notes.teaches: In tactical sequences, look for moves that gain time by attacking the opponent's queen or other valuable pieces.
notes.plans: White aims to consolidate and trade off pieces to reduce black's attacking potential.

notes.explains: In the main line, black's bishop goes to f4, a surprising move that sets a trap: if white takes on h5, black plays queen g6, and white must play knight g3 to protect, but then black can win material.
notes.teaches: Be wary of captures that open lines for the opponent's queen or allow tactical blows on critical squares.
notes.plans: White should avoid the trap and instead play bishop g2, leading to a repetition of moves and a draw.

notes.explains: Black, as the attacker, avoids trading off attacking pieces, so when white offers queen trades, black declines and instead attacks the rook with queen to c8.
notes.teaches: The side with the initiative should avoid simplifying into a worse or equal endgame, and instead maintain the tension.
notes.plans: Black continues to press, while white seeks to consolidate and possibly force a repetition.

notes.explains: In this Marshall Attack tabiya, White's attacking pieces are the queen and bishop; trading them off would blunt the initiative. Black's queen to c8 attacks the rook on e1, forcing it back to a1 to guard the back rank, while Black's rook to e8 pressures the queen on e2.
notes.teaches: When attacking, avoid unnecessary trades of your most active pieces. Coordinate rooks on open files and use queen checks to drive the opponent's pieces to passive squares.
notes.plans: White can maintain the tension with queen to c2, inviting a repetition after bishop f5 and queen d1, bishop g4. If White wants to avoid the draw, queen b3 keeps the game going with balanced chances.

notes.explains: Black's idea of playing f5 and f4 to attack can be neutralized by White's bishop to f4. If Black captures on d5 first, White can recapture and then play bishop f4, after which Black's bishop takes on e6 is met by rook e1, and after gxf4, White's queen or knight can go to g3 to consolidate.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn storm, look for a piece placement that blocks the pawns and covers key squares. A well-timed bishop to f4 can defuse Black's kingside ambitions.
notes.plans: White should aim for bishop f4, possibly after capturing on d5, and then bring the queen to g3 to secure the position.

notes.explains: Refusing the Marshall Gambit is a reasonable practical choice. Strong players, including Kasparov, have avoided giving Black the chance to play it, preferring to steer the game into other lines.
notes.teaches: In the opening, you can choose to avoid sharp theoretical battles if you prefer a different type of position. Knowing your own style and the opponent's preparation matters.
notes.plans: White can choose an anti-Marshall setup to sidestep Black's main attacking plans.

notes.explains: After the Marshall Gambit sequence, black's most promising try is Rxe4, attacking the pinned bishop on e4. Capturing immediately with the bishop would trade off all the attacking pieces and leave white with a healthy center pawn and the bishop pair, so black instead keeps the pin and adds pressure.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, don't rush to win material; add more attackers to increase the pressure. The side with the pinned piece must often give back material to escape.
notes.plans: Black plays Qg6 to reinforce the pin on the e4-rook, then Nf6 to add another attacker. White must decide whether to defend with f3 or move the queen to safety.

notes.explains: White can choose to move the queen to f1, allowing black to take on e4. White is up material (the exchange) and can afford to give it back to simplify into a favorable position. After Bxe4, white develops the bishop to f4, the only active square given the pawn structure on b2, c3, and d4.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, you can return it to neutralize the opponent's attack and reach a safer, more comfortable position. Piece activity matters more than maintaining a material edge at all costs.
notes.plans: White aims to reach a balanced endgame where the extra center pawn is not enough to win because both sides have bishops that can defend and trade off. The position is equal with best play.

notes.explains: An alternative for white is Qe3, after which black can take on e4 and force a similar equal endgame. However, black has a tactical resource: Bg3, offering the bishop to force a draw. If white takes, black recaptures with the queen and creates a perpetual check or a mating net on the first rank.
notes.teaches: In equal positions, be alert to tactical drawing resources. A bishop sacrifice can lead to a perpetual check or a repetition when the opponent's king is vulnerable.
notes.plans: White should avoid taking on g3 and instead find a way to keep the position balanced, but black has forced drawing lines. The position is dynamically equal.

notes.explains: In the Marshall Attack main line after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 c6 Bxd5 cxd5 d4 Bd6 Re1 Qh4 g3 Qh3, White has two main setups: Bf4 (or Be3) and Re4. The rook to e4 idea aims to play Re4-h4, driving the queen off the h-file, but Black can meet it with g5, stopping the rook and creating tactical threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen sits on an open file, a rook lift can challenge it, but be alert to pawn breaks like g5 that refute the idea and create counterplay.
notes.plans: White should consider Re4 as an alternative to Bf4, but must be ready for Black's g5 response and the resulting tactics.

notes.explains: After Re4, Black's g5 is strong: if White takes the pawn, Qf5 forks the rook and bishop; if White tries Rg4, Qxg4 wins because the queen is protected by the bishop. Thus White must find other moves, with Qf3 and Qf1 being the main tries.
notes.teaches: A pawn move that attacks a rook can also create tactical threats against other pieces; always calculate captures carefully before taking.
notes.plans: White should avoid taking on g5 and instead consider Qf3 or Qf1 to maintain the position.

notes.explains: White's natural developing move Nd2 is too slow; Black can immediately play f5 and start a kingside attack. White is forced to play Re3 to defend, but Black can then play Kh8, a key preparatory move that gives the king safety and flexibility, enabling the attack to proceed.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, development must be balanced with meeting immediate threats; a quiet king move like Kh8 can be crucial to avoid tactics and prepare an attack.
notes.plans: Black should aim for f5 and Kh8 to build the attack, while White must find accurate defensive moves like Re3.

notes.explains: If Black rushes f4 without Kh8, White can generate active defense: after gxf4, Black cannot recapture because of Rxh3, so the queen must move. Then Ne4 attacks d6 and g5, and Bf4 stops both threats. After Rg3, Black can give up the exchange for a solid position, but White has blunted the attack.
notes.teaches: Timing is critical in attacks; a premature pawn break can allow the defender to consolidate, so prepare with moves like Kh8 first.
notes.plans: Black should prefer the slow Kh8 approach rather than immediate f4, to keep the attack rolling.

notes.explains: With Kh8 played, Black's threat of f4 is real. If White tries Re1, it's too slow and f4 tears the position apart. More accurate is Rd3, but even then f4 breaks through. White struggles to find a defense, and Black can continue with Qg6 or Ra7, while White tries for queenside counterplay with a4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a strong pawn break, you must find the most resilient defense; sometimes even good-looking moves are too slow, so look for active counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should proceed with f4 after Kh8, while White must seek counterplay on the queenside with a4.

notes.explains: In this Marshall Attack position, White's knight on d2 line is too slow after ...f5, which gives Black a strong initiative. White's pieces are passive and Black's threats are real.
notes.teaches: When facing an aggressive pawn break like ...f5, you must have active counterplay; slow moves allow the opponent to tear your position apart.
notes.plans: White should avoid slow moves like Re1 and instead seek active defense, possibly with Qf1 or Qf3 to trade pieces.

notes.explains: White's queen to f3 idea to trade queens runs into ...Bf5, attacking the rook. If White tries Re1, Black's ...Rae8 offers a trade and White is too far behind in development.
notes.teaches: When you are behind in development, trading pieces can relieve pressure, but you must ensure the trade doesn't allow tactics against your pieces.
notes.plans: White might consider giving up the exchange or trying Bxd5 to gain time and save the rook on e3.

notes.explains: After Bxd5, Black recaptures and White saves the rook, but Black's ...Be4 threatens mate on g2, forcing White to give up the exchange. However, White gets the center pawn or counterplay with Qf6.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up the exchange is the best practical choice to avoid worse outcomes and gain compensation.
notes.plans: White should take the compensation and seek active play, possibly with Qf6 to attack the bishop and pawn.

notes.explains: White should not take the bishop on d6 because of ...Qd1. Instead, White can try Qxg5 to trade queens, but that leads to equality with Black's advanced pawns. Better is Nd2 first, keeping the queen for counterplay.
notes.teaches: When your opponent offers a piece trade, evaluate the resulting endgame and your piece activity. Sometimes keeping queens on the board gives you more chances.
notes.plans: White should play Nd2, develop pieces, and secure the position, while Black will aim to use the bishop sacrifice to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: After the bishop sacrifice on d6, white must be careful: if white plays e3 and black recaptures with the rook on e3, black gets strong pressure on the first rank, with ideas like rook to e2 or rook to g3, pinning everything and preventing development.
notes.teaches: When facing a sacrifice, do not rush to recapture if it opens lines for the opponent's pieces; consider returning material to maintain a solid position.
notes.plans: White should play Nf3, giving back the piece to neutralize black's initiative, after which the position is fine for white.

notes.explains: After Nf3, if black takes on f3, white recaptures with the bishop on e3, which acts as a 'tall pawn' — a solid defensive piece that keeps the position secure and prevents black from breaking through.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece that seems passive is actually valuable for its defensive role; don't undervalue a piece that holds the position together.
notes.plans: White can consider Kh1 to avoid perpetual check, or Qf2 to defend, leading to an even endgame where black has checks but white has a passed d-pawn.

notes.explains: Black does not need to sacrifice the exchange; instead, black can play Re6 to attack the queen, forcing it to move to c5, then play h6 to solidify the position, resulting in a balanced game.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, you don't always need to force tactics; you can consolidate and maintain the advantage with simple developing moves.
notes.plans: Black should avoid the direct f5, which allows white to push d5 and gain a strong initiative; instead, play h6 and prepare to convert the exchange advantage.

notes.explains: If black plays f5 prematurely, white pushes d5, and after the rook moves to e5 to pin, white plays Bd4, creating dual threats: the queen can go to e7 with mate threats on g7 and also attack the pawn on g5, leaving black unable to defend both.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening pawn moves that give your opponent a target for a pawn break; always consider the opponent's possible pawn pushes before advancing your own.
notes.plans: Black should play h6 instead of f5 to keep the position solid, while white should look for ways to create dual threats against the king and loose pawns.

notes.explains: In the main line with Qf1, black avoids queen trades and plays Qh5, leading to a complex middlegame. White can give up the exchange but gets a strong pawn center and easy development.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up material for a strong pawn center and piece activity is a good trade, especially if the opponent's pieces are passive.
notes.plans: White should develop harmoniously with Ne4 or Nf3, Bd2, and Rf1, while black tries to create counterplay against the e4 pawn and the king side.

notes.explains: In the line with Nf6, Qg2, Qg6, Rook e3, and Nd5, a trade on d5 is acceptable for white even though it gives up the bishop for a knight, because the rook has already moved to e3 and retreating would lose tempo.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's worth trading a bishop for a knight to maintain the initiative and avoid losing time; piece trades should be evaluated based on the resulting position, not just piece values.
notes.plans: White continues with Nb3 heading to c5, Bd2, and doubling rooks, while black tries to stop the knight's advance and create counterplay on the c-file.

notes.explains: After the rook lands on e3, the knight on d5 attacks it. Trading the bishop for that knight is justified here because retreating the rook to e1 would lose time; the rook has already committed to the third rank.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, accept a trade that would normally be undesirable if it preserves the initiative and avoids wasting a tempo.
notes.plans: White will develop the knight to b3 heading for c5, while black prepares counterplay on the queenside with ...Rac8 to discourage the knight's jump.

notes.explains: White's queen goes to f2 to support the knight's outpost on c5. This is chosen over doubling rooks because it allows the knight to remain on c5, a key square for pressuring black's position.
notes.teaches: Supporting a strong outpost with the queen can be more valuable than routine rook development, especially when the knight's presence cramps the opponent.
notes.plans: Both sides will expand pawns on opposite wings, leading to an endgame with queen, bishop, and rook versus the same, with pawns distributed across the board.

notes.explains: After a4, if black tries ...d5, white can simply take on b5, and black cannot recapture because the rook on a8 hangs and the knight on c6 is attacked. Thus the Marshall attack is prevented.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez, a4 is a direct way to challenge black's queenside structure and stop the Marshall, because it exploits the pin on the a-file and the loose rook.
notes.plans: Black should avoid the immediate ...d5 and instead play ...Bb7 or ...b4, leading to a different type of middlegame where white has a comfortable edge in development.

notes.explains: After White plays a4 in the Ruy Lopez, Black's Marshall Attack is neutralized because the typical ...d5 break is no longer effective. This is the anti-Marshall setup.
notes.teaches: The move a4 is a direct way to avoid the Marshall Attack, steering the game into different structures.
notes.plans: Black can choose between Bb7, preparing to recapture on b5 with the bishop or queen, or the more common b4, leading to a distinct pawn structure with ...a5.

notes.explains: In the anti-Marshall, after a4 Bb7, White should not play c3 because it allows ...d5, which is fine for Black. The move c3 is inaccurate in this specific setup.
notes.teaches: In the anti-Marshall, White's c3 is often a mistake because it does not address the central tension and allows Black to seize the initiative with ...d5.
notes.plans: Black should be happy to play ...d5 after White's c3, as it leads to active piece play.

notes.explains: The Marshall Attack has a vast body of theory because it is a very serious gambit that can quickly punish inaccurate play by White. White must be precise if facing it.
notes.teaches: Some openings require deep preparation because they are inherently dangerous for the defender; the Marshall is one such opening.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian position, Black has just played Bb4, pinning the knight on c3. White can capture the c5 pawn, and normally Black would recapture later, but here White can make it awkward for Black to regain the material.
notes.teaches: When a pawn capture is normally not critical because the opponent can recapture, look for ways to make the recapture awkward, turning a temporary pawn grab into a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: White should consider capturing on c5 and then supporting the pawn with moves like e4, while being aware of Black's queen to a5 attacking c3 and c5.

notes.explains: After Black plays Qa5, White can play e4, forcing the knight to move. If Black captures on c3, White can respond with Qd2, and after Bb2, the knight on c3 is stuck and Black's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a seemingly hanging pawn is not really hanging because capturing it allows the opponent to develop with tempo and create strong pressure.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop the bishop to b2 and rook to c1, putting pressure on the c-file and the knight.

notes.explains: After e4, Black's main retreats are Ne7 and Nf6. The knight on c7 is badly placed. White can simply develop with Be3, and the c3 pawn is not worth Black's time to capture because the queen will have to move later.
notes.teaches: In the opening, a pawn is often not worth capturing if it costs time and allows the opponent to develop naturally.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, with bishops aiming at the queenside, and be ready to support the c5 pawn.

notes.explains: After Black plays Nd7, White can defend the c3 pawn with Qb3. If Black tries to capture on c5, White has the surprising Qb4, forking Black's pieces and fixing the pawn structure favorably.
notes.teaches: Look for non-standard forks and queen moves that create threats and improve your pawn structure, even if they seem unusual.
notes.plans: White should consider Qb4 to force a favorable pawn structure or win material, and otherwise maintain pressure with the open bishops.

notes.explains: White has a 'terrible' pawn structure in this variation, but it is acceptable because White has more pawns and active pieces. The character of the line is that if Black can recapture the pawn on c5 without problems, Black is fine; if White can make ...Nxc5 a bad move, White gets an advantage.
notes.teaches: A bad pawn structure can be compensated by other factors like material, piece activity, or attacking chances. Evaluate the position dynamically, not just statically.
notes.plans: White should aim to make Black's recapture on c5 difficult, either by maintaining the pawn or by gaining a different advantage after ...Nxc5. Black should try to equalize by safely recapturing on c5.

notes.explains: In the theoretical main line, after the moves d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4, White plays f3, and Black often castles kingside, which is better than the ...Nd7 maneuver seen in the earlier game. Castling helps Black avoid the king being stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: In sharp opening lines, prioritize king safety by castling early, especially when the center is fluid and the opponent has active pieces.
notes.plans: White should continue with natural development, aiming to maintain pressure and exploit any inaccuracies. Black should complete development and castle to bring the king to safety.

notes.explains: In this line of the Nimzo-Indian, after the moves d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4, the position is rich with tactical and strategic ideas. The immediate threats and piece activity are crucial, and both sides must navigate carefully to avoid falling into disadvantageous structures.
notes.teaches: The opening is a battleground for piece activity and pawn structure. Recognizing key squares like d5 and the importance of castling early can prevent tactical disasters.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain pressure and possibly exploit the bishop pair, while Black should prioritize castling and developing harmoniously to neutralize White's initiative.

notes.explains: After the sequence leading to a position where Black has played Qa5 and White has responded with e4, Nc3, Qd2, and Bc3, the position is critical. Black's queen on a5 is active, but White's pieces are well-coordinated. The move Qxc3 by Black would allow White to play Kf2, gaining time and leaving White with a more active position and a fine pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen ventures out early, it can become a target. Sometimes it's better to avoid capturing material if it allows the opponent to improve their king's safety and piece activity.
notes.plans: Black should look for a safe way to develop and castle, while White should continue to build pressure and avoid unnecessary exchanges that give Black counterplay.

notes.explains: In the position after Black has castled and White has played Qb3, Black's move Qc7 is a paradoxical but correct choice. It prepares to attack the c5 pawn and also keeps the queen on a useful square, avoiding the fork on b4 that would occur after Nd7. This move maintains Black's chances of equalizing.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet-looking move that prepares threats is better than an aggressive one that walks into tactics. The queen on c7 is well-placed to support a pawn push and avoid harassment.
notes.plans: Black will aim to challenge White's center and create counterplay, while White will look to maintain the extra pawn and develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: In the position after Qb3 and Qc7, White's best move is Bb5. This move is superior to other bishop placements because it puts pressure on the knight on c6 (if it goes there) and also prepares to trade the bishop for a knight, which would hinder Black's ability to recapture on c5. Other bishop moves like Bd3 or Bc4 are less effective: Bd3 is passive and can become a target, while Bc4 is vulnerable to a knight jump to a5, attacking the light squares and creating forks with the queen on b3.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a bishop, consider its activity, potential targets, and the opponent's possible responses. Sometimes a bishop is best used to trade off a key defender rather than to stay on the board.
notes.plans: White will aim to trade the bishop for a knight if possible, to weaken Black's control over c5 and reduce Black's light-square pressure. Black must be careful to avoid falling into a worse endgame.

notes.explains: After Bb5, Black's main move is Nc6, but there is a tricky alternative in e5. This move can lead to sharp play, as seen in a famous game where Black's light-square pressure became overwhelming. In that game, Black's bishop came to e6, and after a series of moves, Black's knight reached a5, attacking the light squares and causing White serious problems. White's attempt to save the day with Nd5 was prevented by active play from Black.
notes.teaches: In sharp opening lines, be aware of the opponent's potential to seize control of key complexes (like the light squares). Sometimes a pawn sacrifice or a dynamic move can give long-term positional pressure.
notes.plans: If Black plays e5, White must be very precise to avoid being overrun on the light squares. White may need to consider returning material or finding active counterplay to survive.

notes.explains: In the f3 Nimzo-Indian, if Black manages to play ...Bg4? Actually, the key is Black's light-squared bishop to e6 and knight to a5, gaining control of the light squares. If White allows this without a plan, Black's pieces become very active and White's position can collapse, as seen in a famous game where Black's light-square control was decisive.
notes.teaches: When facing the Nimzo-Indian with f3, you must be alert to Black's plan of ...Be6 and ...Na5, which targets the light squares. If you allow it without a counter, you risk being worse.
notes.plans: White should look for a way to challenge Black's light-square control, such as the thematic sacrifice N d4, which undermines Black's bishop on e6 and knight on a5.

notes.explains: The move R a b1 is a nonchalant option that doesn't address Black's light-square plan. After Black continues with ...Na6, ...Qa4, and ...Nc4, White can feel lost, wondering why they played this opening.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a clear plan, you must have a concrete response. Playing a move that doesn't address the threat can lead to a passive position.
notes.plans: Instead of R a b1, White should consider the active idea of N d4, which sacrifices a knight for two pawns and central control, regaining the light squares.

notes.explains: The knight sacrifice N d4 is the key idea. After exd4, cxd4, White has a massive pawn center. Black's pieces are disorganized, and the bishop on e6 is useless after d5. White doesn't need to rush; supporting the pawns with moves like Q c3 and R fd1 gives a long-term advantage.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a piece for two pawns can be justified if it gives you a powerful pawn center and leaves the opponent's pieces poorly placed. You don't need to force immediate material gain; just support the center and let the opponent suffocate.
notes.plans: White should continue with d5, pushing the pawns, and use the rook to support from behind. Black's pieces are stuck, and White can slowly improve.

notes.explains: In the game, White avoided playing d5 immediately, because Black's only chance to equalize is to sacrifice a piece back for two pawns. By keeping the pawns, White denies Black that resource.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage in pawns, sometimes it's better to keep the tension and not allow the opponent to simplify. If they offer to give back material, you can decline and maintain your advantage.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and improving piece placement, while keeping the pawns intact. Black's pieces remain passive, and White can slowly convert.

notes.explains: In the F3 Nimzo-Indian, after Black plays ...Bb4, the move ...Be6 is a common plan aiming for ...Nc4 and ...Nb3, which can give Black strong light-square play. If White allows this, White risks being worse.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to Black's plan of ...Be6 followed by a knight to c4/b3. Preventing this plan is a key priority for White.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to stop ...Be6 and the knight's entry to c4, such as playing Nd4 or other prophylactic moves.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...Na6, attacking both the bishop on c4 and the pawn on b4, White should consider Bxa6, giving up the bishop to double Black's b-pawns. This creates a structural concession for Black, but Black still has the same idea of ...Be6 and ...Nc4.
notes.teaches: Doubling the opponent's pawns can be a good trade-off, but you must remain vigilant against their piece activity, especially on the light squares.
notes.plans: After Bxa6, White should aim to prevent ...Be6 and ...Nc4, possibly with moves like Rad1 or even d6 to disrupt Black's coordination.

notes.explains: In the game, White played Rad1 to stop ...Be6, but this allowed Black to get counterplay. A stronger idea was d6, attacking the queen and forcing ...Qc6, then c4, leading to a fork with Qb4 if Black takes on c5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a specific plan, look for active countermeasures that disrupt their pieces, even if it involves a pawn sacrifice. Tactical motifs like forks can turn the game in your favor.
notes.plans: White can aim for d6, c4, and Qb4 to win material or gain a decisive advantage, leading to a favorable endgame with two pieces for a rook.

notes.explains: The central theme is that Black's plan of ...Be6 and ...Nc4 is dangerous, and White must constantly prevent it. In the main line, White's best play involves proactive moves that stop Black's light-square play.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, controlling the light squares and preventing the opponent's knight from reaching strong outposts is crucial. Always be on the lookout for ways to neutralize the opponent's plans.
notes.plans: White should continue to develop harmoniously while keeping an eye on Black's potential ...Be6 and ...Nc4. If Black plays ...Be6, consider Nd4 to challenge it.

notes.explains: In the f3 Nimzo-Indian, after White plays e4 and recaptures on c5, Black's main plan is to play ...e5, ...Be6, and ...Na5, targeting the light squares and the c4-pawn. White must prevent this at all costs, often with moves like Nd4 or Rd5, which can give White a pleasant edge.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to Black's typical freeing/attacking ideas in the opening. If you can prevent them with a concrete move, do so, even if it costs some material, because the resulting pawn structure and piece activity can favor you.
notes.plans: White should aim to keep the position locked and maintain the knight d4 idea, while being ready to sacrifice material for mobile pawns if needed.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Ne7, Black's key idea is to play ...e5, ...Be6, and ...Na5. White can counter with Nd4 or Rd5 to stop ...Nc4, and this gives White a slight edge. The move Qa4 is a strong improvement over other moves because it keeps the position locked and maintains the Nd4 idea.
notes.teaches: When facing a specific plan, look for a move that both prevents the opponent's idea and improves your own position. Sometimes a quiet move like Qa4 is more effective than a flashy one.
notes.plans: After Qa4, if Black tries ...Nc6 and ...Na5, White can play Nd4 with a good position. If Black goes after the c-pawn, White can give up the piece and play Qc2, with near-balance.

notes.explains: In the game, Black played ...e5 and ...Be6 quickly, and White's response c4 got into trouble. The improvement is Qa4, which prevents Black's main plan and keeps White's position solid.
notes.teaches: When your opponent uses move-order tricks to reach a favorable setup, you need to find a move that addresses the threat directly. Qa4 is such a move because it stops ...Na5 and keeps the knight d4 idea alive.
notes.plans: White should continue with Qa4, keeping the position locked and preparing Nd4. If Black tries to win the c-pawn, White can sacrifice the piece for activity.

notes.explains: In the ...Nf6 variation, the ideas are very similar to ...Ne7. Black still aims for ...e5, ...Be6, and ...Na5, and White must prevent it.
notes.teaches: Recognize that different move orders can lead to similar strategic ideas. The same preventive measures apply.
notes.plans: White should apply the same principles: prevent ...Be6 and ...Na5, and be ready to sacrifice for activity.

notes.explains: In the F3 Nimzo-Indian, after the main theoretical lines, black can equalize if well-prepared. The main line with queen b3 leads to long forcing variations where black is not worse. To avoid this, white can choose a more offbeat move.
notes.teaches: When facing well-prepared opponents, it's practical to choose less theoretical lines that make equality harder to find, even if they are not objectively better.
notes.plans: White plays queen b3 first, then after knight fd7, plays knight h3, avoiding the main theoretical path.

notes.explains: The move knight h3 is a perfectly normal developing move, though it has been played in only about 17 games. It avoids the long theory where white pushes the a-pawn and trades queens. Black's best response is queen c7, stepping out of a queen b4 idea.
notes.teaches: Developing moves that are slightly unusual can be a good practical choice to steer the game into less charted territory.
notes.plans: White continues with queen c4, defending the c-pawn and creating a different type of position than the main lines.

notes.explains: The key difference between black's knight on e7 and on d7 is that on d7 the knight blocks the bishop's path to e6, so black's typical idea of attacking c5 with the bishop is not available. This changes the plans for both sides.
notes.teaches: Piece placement affects the viability of certain plans; a knight on d7 can hinder the bishop's development, altering the character of the position.
notes.plans: Black may try knight e5 to challenge the queen on c4, while white can respond with queen b4, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: With a knight on d7 instead of c6, Black's typical idea of ...e6 followed by ...Bb6 is less effective because the knight blocks the bishop's path. White no longer needs to worry about that plan and can focus on other ideas.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece placement blocks their own typical plans, you can adjust your own strategy accordingly, as the usual threats may no longer be relevant.
notes.plans: White can consider moves like Ne5 to challenge the queen on c4, or develop with Bb5, aiming to maintain the extra c-pawn and pressure.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Nd7, White can play Bb5, and if Black plays ...Na5, White can respond with Qb4, defending the c-pawn. After ...Nc6, White can give up the bishop with Bxc6, as preserving the extra pawn on c5 and maintaining space is more important.
notes.teaches: In this opening, don't be afraid to trade a bishop for a knight if it maintains a structural advantage like an extra pawn or central space.
notes.plans: After Bxc6, White can play Rd1 to centralize the rook, then use the queen actively (e.g., Qd4, Qd5) while keeping the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black could have equalized with ...Bd7 or an earlier ...Na6, but the line with ...Nd7 gives White a significant edge. White's pieces are centralized, and the extra c-pawn provides lasting pressure.
